title: Penn State RB Carson Hansen, DE Yvan Kemajou probable for game against Michigan
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's first availability report for its game against Michigan has been released.

Running back Carson Hansen, defensive end Yvan Kemajou, cornerback Josiah Zayas and defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim are all probable ahead of Saturday's game.

Linebacker Cam Smith and kicker Cristiano Rosa are questionable. Matt Campbell said Smith returned to practice this week, participating in the first two days.

Wide receiver Koby Howard remains out as the headlining name on the list.

Defensive end Max Granville, linebacker Alex Tatsch and offensive lineman Will Tompkins are all out and have been ruled out for the year by Campbell.

Defensive ends LaVar Arrington II, Mason Robinson and Dayshaun Burnett, cornerbacks Joshua Johnson, Christian Askew and Tyler Armstead are also out for the game. Tight end Cooper Alexander and defensive tackle Liam Andrews round out the players who will be sidelined for Saturday's contest.

title: Penn State men’s soccer notebook | Rob Dow discusses recent play, future outlook
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returned from Ann Arbor with their first draw of the season, and points in the Big Ten.

This is the first match the Nittany Lions haven’t lost since their game against Yale on Sept. 4, and it will show whether they has carried that momentum into the rest of the season. Since then, the blue and white have endured a five-match losing streak.

Coach Rob Dow sat down to talk about the upcoming match against Northwestern and the look ahead as the postseason approaches.

Here is what was discussed.

Reflecting on Michigan

While the Nittany Lions were able to stay away from another loss, the team was still disappointed with how they performed.

“We created enough to win the game. Our first 65 minutes we were in control of the game and with the ball, the attacking actions even defensively,” Dow said. “With high-percentage scoring chances you expect to win the game, we were disappointed, but we are in a position where we have to win against Northwestern.”

In the game, Michigan was able to fend off the blue and white by filling in their box, blocking any chance of a goal. The team made it a point in practice this week to focus on getting into those areas before the pressure builds, and get to the goal quicker.

Strategies and preparation

Penn State has been putting in the work at training this week to prepare for the quick turnaround between traveling to Chicago to take on Northwestern Friday to being back in State College for its game against Rutgers on Tuesday.

“Less is more, but we had a hard week of training; we needed to step up,” Dow said. “We’ve been fading in matches in the last 15 minutes and losing control. We needed to pick up the training intensity so we have that taken care of.”

Unlike teams they’ve played before, Northwestern will pose a new challenge for the Nittany Lions, as they are a combative and direct group.

“They overload the midfield then play forward very quickly. I heard it’s pretty windy when you play against a team where the ball’s in the air a lot, meaning there’s a lot of things you can’t predict,” Dow said. “We just have to overcome it and be stronger and execute our game plan, despite how disruptive they will be.”

Players to look out for

While the team has leaders in players like Etienne Reck and captains Joe Sheridan and Grant McIntosh, some players have seen the most growth over the season and are players to look out for in the upcoming games.

Senior defender Morgan Marshall joined the team this season after playing for West Point and has been an important part of the back end.

“He does his job, executes game plans, very coachable,” Dow said. “We haven’t coached him up until January and he’s important to start matches with because he sets the match intensity. He’s really stepped up in an exemplary leadership role.”

Another breakout player has been first-year midfielder Peter Doran. Even though he is just starting his college career, Doran has already started two games.

“He has a good chance of starting the game against Northwestern, and this guy hasn’t played a lot of soccer last year for the Philadelphia Union, but the best attributes we saw in him are coming out right now and that is a really good sign of a healthy team,” Dow said. “He’s such a good example for all the young guys within our group and how to go through this process.”

Playoffs

With only four remaining matches of the regular season, Penn State has to fight for their chance at having a run in the playoffs. The blue and white will need to bring their A game in the next month.

“Winners find a way to execute the plays between the plays, marking their guy, contesting in the first, the little things you don’t see. We haven’t given a 90-minute performance toward that and we’re going to have to,” Dow said. “Every team’s fighting for playoff … that grit will come through, and it’s needed to be a playoff team.”

Currently, Penn State is last in the Big Ten standings and needs to make a push, as only nine teams make the conference tournament.

Calendar change

The Division I cabinet voted against a proposal to extend the playing season from the fall to the spring, with championships occurring in the spring.

The decision was disapproved and will now go into a 30-day recess before being made permanent, unless 2/3 of the eligible schools vote against the new changes.

“We will not vote to support the rescission, and are supportive of the flex model,” Dow said.

title: Penn State women's hockey notebook | Jeff Kampersal talks goalkeepers, Lindenwood, finishing games
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State coach Jeff Kampersal spoke to the media Wednesday following a road series against AHA opponent Syracuse where the Nittany Lions split the series with the Orange. The blue and white lost the first contest in a 5-4 overtime thriller and won the second handily 4-0.

This week, the Nittany Lions gear up to take on the Lindenwood Lions in Pegula Ice Arena and look to get back on track.

Is Campbell ahead in goalkeeper competition?

There has been a debate in the early season of who should start in net for the Nittany Lions but after the Syracuse series one candidate might have taken the lead in the competition.

“Maddy (Campbell) has emerged in the competition but we still count a lot on Morgan (Stickney),” Kampersal said. “I think in that first Syracuse game we didn't do (Stickney) any favors in terms of giving up a couple odd man situations and breakaway opportunities we didn't give up many chances that game but the ones we did give up were doozies, we’re still looking for them to compete with one another because we’ll need both down the stretch of the season”.

The Syracuse game Kampersall is referring to was the one in which the Orange upset the Nittany Lions putting five goals past Stickney. While Kampersall acknowledged that the defense didn't help Stickney, Campbell's shutout performance the following day may have given her the edge in the competition.

With both goalkeepers still in the picture, Campbell's performance could mark a turning point in the battle for the starting spot as Penn State looks towards the rest of the season.

Lindenwood

Kampersall was asked about the next task at hand for the Nittany Lions, which is a 4-4 Lindenwood team that is coming off of two losses against Mercyhurst. Kampersal seemed to have a high level of respect for the program.

“You look at their program, and it looks like they're having fun; obviously, they've enjoyed a little success so far this season. On tape, they look quick, and they look like they're moving the puck well,” the Penn State skipper said.

Kampersall also talked about strategy for the upcoming series as well, highlighting potential dangers and things the team needs to do correctly in order to win.

“Like all the AHA teams we play, we don't want to take penalties and give them power-play opportunities because that's more likely when they will strike,” Kampersal said. “So we need to essentially lock it down from the beginning defensively so we can play a good offense and prevent them from having the puck too much, but they'll present issues like Syracuse did with their speed.”

Lindenwood has an assortment of players that have done damage offensively this season, so being able to possess the puck and keep it out of the d-zone will be important for Penn State.

Players like Sofia Ismael and Kylie Amelkovich will be important in this series, as both players played really well in the last series against Syracuse

“Amelkovich is such a thoroughbred skater; she's strong on her skates. She can take care of the D-zone and then lead the offensive rushes. She looks to move the puck; we’re trying to get her to obviously make the right hockey plays but also trying to get her to shoot a little bit more,” Kampersal said. “Ismael is just super talented right now in terms of her ability to pull people towards her, to free other people up. Like she's kind of a mini magician with the puck, and she's a sharpshooter, too.”

Finishing close games

This year the blue and white haven’t lost a game by more than one goal, with all losses being very close and two out of the three going to overtime; when asked about this, Kampersal acknowledged the overtime woes.

“I mean what we really need to work on and what we have been working on is the 3-on-3 overtime, taking away time and space,” Kampersal said. “Both in Ohio State and Syracuse, we didn't really do a good job in the overtime; we want to be a team that's hard to play against.”

It is encouraging that every Nittany Lions loss this season has been close, and if they can tune up and refine the little things, they can be elite in the coming months.

“We’re learning lessons, and as long as we learn from the losses and correct those areas, then that's a good thing," Kampersal said. "Then we’re really building for when we get back from Christmas, January, February to be elite at that point.”

title: Malachi Goodman focusing on technique, cohesion, amidst OL struggles
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Malachi Goodman arrived at Penn State in May 2025 with a lot of expectations. He was a 6-foot-5.5, 320 lbs and a 4-star per 247sports composite, already having the size needed to succeed as an offensive lineman in the Big Ten.

After redshirting his first year, Goodman was in a position battle during the summer months and throughout fall camp, eventually earning the starting left tackle spot. He’s started in all six games so far this year.

“I think (the coaching staff) handled (the transition) fairly well,” Goodman said Wednesday. “Just getting all the reps in camp and in the spring and spring ball. It was definitely an adjustment at the time, but I felt like I picked it up very quickly.”

While Goodman is the youngest of Penn State’s five offensive linemen, with redshirt sophomore center Brock Riker the next youngest, Goodman had a strong start to the season during nonconference play.

Against Temple, Goodman earned his first highlight with a big block during a run play. He cut behind the offensive line and laid down cornerback Nakeel Lawrence, sending his 190-pound body flying backward.

“I feel like I had a great start the first few games,” Goodman said. “My goal is just keep honing on the techniques, being detailed, giving my all every day, trying to get better.”

However, not everything was perfect for the young starter. According to On3’s Thomas Frank Carr, Goodman was occasionally tipping off plays during early downs, giving the defenses an idea of whether a pass or rush play would be coming, which Goodman said was somewhat true, but not 100% accurate.

Pre-snap while lined up on the line of scrimmage, Goodman frequently put his right hand on his face mask before run plays and kept his hand down prior to passing plays.

“I kind of laughed at it,” Goodman said. “We looked over and I fixed it, and it won’t be happening anymore. It was easy.”

While Goodman has worked to correct his individual mistakes, Penn State’s offensive line has also struggled collectively, particularly in establishing a consistent rushing attack. Campbell has pointed to the running backs as part of the cause, but has also shared blame with the offensive line, saying things have “been a hair off.”

Those issues have only been exacerbated as Big Ten play has begun, as Goodman described the players he’s faced as “great talent all over the world.”

“We look at the film and evaluate everything, but we got to do our jobs too,” Goodman said. “We focus on ourselves, trying to get better. Tendencies, techniques, all that stuff. We gotta clean up technique, especially me.”

Six weeks through the season with a nearly nonexistent run game, Goodman said the team is “working every day for it to get fixed.” He particularly cited discipline and tight hands as two areas of growth for himself.

But while he emphasized the need for individual improvement from each player, he also harped on the necessity of chemistry and cohesiveness between himself and the other four linemen.

“There’s always room for improvement,” Goodman said. “But I definitely feel like we have a good connection and relationship in my room.”

Throughout practices, things have clicked at times where all five have worked together as one offensive line. With struggles in various aspects of Penn State’s play, that cohesiveness is the goal for the squad.

“(The potential cohesiveness) looks amazing,” Goodman said. “It’s just very fluent, really fluent.”

title: Report: Josh Reed currently eligible to play for Penn State men's basketball
author: Will Horstman | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State received good news Wednesday regarding the status of fifth-year forward Josh Reed.

The college athletes suing the NCAA in Ohio are currently eligible to play this upcoming season after the Supreme Court of Ohio stayed the decision by the First District Court of Appeals, according to Ohio-based basketball reporter Paul Fritschner.

This means that Reed is currently eligible to play for the Nittany Lions in 2026-27. However, this could change as the legal process continues to play out.

Reed and the other athletes involved in the lawsuit were originally granted an injunction by an Ohio trial court. The NCAA appealed, and the Ohio Court of Appeals reversed that decision by the trial court.

The players then filed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Ohio, which has now reversed the decision to reverse the trial court ruling. This isn't a final ruling, as both sides can continue to provide information to the Ohio Supreme Court. As for next steps, both sides must submit briefs addressing this order by Oct. 19.

Reed, who wasn't given a fifth year in the 5-in-5 eligibility changes, is currently eligible to play, which is a massive development for Penn State. Reed averaged 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds per game last season with the Nittany Lions, and he is projected to be a starter this upcoming season.

title: Penn State’s DL working on playing tough ‘through all four quarters’ ahead of Michigan
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim was clear Tuesday about Penn State’s biggest problem on the defensive line — finishing games.

It was a glaring issue in the second half against USC and Wisconsin, as the Nittany Lions looked strong, primarily at the beginning of the first and second half, but fell apart as time went on.

Nnodim said it comes down to the team “not being tough enough,” and how they haven’t displayed equal physicality throughout all four quarters.

“I believe this team has been, especially on the defensive front, playing for the first half and probably the third quarter,” Nnodim said. “We’ve just got to play through all four quarters.”

Nnodim cited how the team features a lot of talent, with both players and coaches alike, but it doesn’t matter when things fall apart late.

“The response that we're trying to do is just go back to work and figure out how we can finish better,” Nnodim said. “We have talented players, talented coaches, but none of that can be put into play if we don't know how to finish.”

Physicality was a big topic of discussion after Penn State’s loss to Northwestern, when the team didn’t feel practice was physical enough, and it led to an explosive run game by the Wildcats.

In the week of practice leading up to playing Michigan, defensive tackle Dallas Vakalahi said Wednesday they’ve made a change in perspective in an attempt to fix the team’s longevity concerns. He noted how the defense has been consciously starting and ending practice with physical play.

“Just like any good game, you have to play all four quarters, and it's something that's required of us if we want to win,” Vakalahi said. “Practicing that, it'll transfer over to the game.”

After finding the level of intensity they want to play at, the Nittany Lions are now working on maintaining it throughout the game. Additionally, Vakalahi said the defensive line has been practicing having an attacker’s mindset, as well as refining fundamental mechanics.

“The biggest thing is just getting off the ball, getting hands-on first, and making sure that we're the ones striking and not being struck,” Vakalahi said. “As we've been in practice, a lot of the things that we have seen are just being able to snatch off and to make sure that we're in our gap and that there's nothing else that's going to take us out of it.”

Vakalahi said reaching and staying in the level of physicality required of the Big Ten isn’t a concern for him, despite understanding the difference in the size of individual offensive linemen.

After having practiced against first-round draft picks Caleb Lomu and Spencer Fano at Utah, Vakalahi said he’s used to practicing physically the whole way through.

“The Big 12 offers a lot of physicality,” Vakalahi said. “I saw a lot of that physicality through practice as well at Utah. Just being able to have those guys (Lomu and Fano) and coming here helped me to be able to match physicality when it's needed.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses challenges of facing Michigan QB Bryce Underwood
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and Michigan will meet on Saturday in a battle between two teams who have first year coaches from the Big 12.

Matt Campbell met with the media on Wednesday ahead of the matchup to discuss losing linebacker Alex Tatsch to injury, the defensive versatility and defending Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood.

Here’s what Campbell had to say.

Losing Alex Tatsch

Campbell confirmed that Tatsch will miss the rest of the season with an injury after he had just come back a few weeks ago from a long-term injury that kept him out of Penn State’s Pinstripe Bowl win over Clemson.

“I think first and foremost is how disappointed you are for Alex,” Campbell said. “Nobody's worked harder to get himself back. I really felt like he was beginning to play the style of football that he wanted to play, and obviously it's disappointing.”

The absence of Tatsch leaves the linebacker room thin and “certainly continues to put stress” on it.

With only three linebackers playing in the Nittany Lions’ loss to USC, the room is likely going to have to rely on further depth. Luckily for them, linebacker Cam Smith has returned to practice this week, with the chance of getting back into game action.

“I think if there is a silver lining, Cam Smith's practiced the last two days, and again, I think was one of the guys coming out of fall camp that I don't know if we would have been any more impressed with where he was at,” Campbell said. “So I do think that's a positive right now for that room.”

Versatility on defense

Another chance to replace the depth Tatsch added is by moving different players around. While some players have already been shifted to different spots given the offenses Penn State’s facing, the plan for defensive end Caleb Bacon is to, “continue to keep him there right now,” according to Campbell.

Bacon, who was formerly a linebacker, made the transition to edge rusher to begin fall camp, and it became permanent right before the season. He adds depth to the defensive end room that’s also had injury problems in the first half of the season.

A player who could slot in at linebacker is safety Marcus Neal Jr., who didn’t play a snap against USC due to the Trojans’ passing capabilities, but could slot back in with Michigan as more of a run-first team.

“I think for Marcus, and again, a guy that's moved all over the place for us through fall camp, trying to put him in the best position to showcase his talent and skill,” Campbell said.

Neal’s biggest strength is in rush defense, and with a quarterback in Bryce Underwood who runs on a regular basis and three players with over 40 rushing attempts this season, he could be useful up front.

“Those are things that I don't think just happen at the snap of a finger, but I think incrementally, he's a guy that can certainly find himself more in the linebacker rotation than just that safety rotation,” Campbell said.

In Neal’s place at safety against USC was cornerback Zion Tracy, who’s another player that has the versatility to be moved around given the offensive scheme.

Tracy played nickel most of last year, but has moved outside and also played a bit of safety. That move to safety could become more permanent, given Tracy’s skillset.

“When it goes back to safety, obviously he's a guy that gives you great coverage ability,” Campbell said. “He's also a guy that has proven to be able to be an open field tackler.”

Defending Bryce Underwood

Underwood gives a different look than any quarterback has given Penn State. While the Nittany Lions have faced dual-threat quarterbacks, Underwood has more rushing tendencies.

“One with a mindset of really scramble to throw, one guy who is dynamic as a ball carrier and certainly has all the tools with a big arm to make you pay if you put everybody up to the line of scrimmage to stop the run,” Campbell said.

Underwood has a 59.3% completion percentage with 881 yards and five touchdowns through the air. On the ground, the quarterback has run 57 times, the most of any player on the team, for 212 yards and two touchdowns.

“I think a very different dynamic in terms of how you're preparing for this quarterback compared to maybe what you were comparing last week,” Campbell said. “But it's certainly a great challenge. Obviously, the respect for the athleticism, the arm talent, he's got all the traits that it takes to be an elite quarterback.”

title: Matt Campbell confirms LB Alex Tatsch is out for the season
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Another Penn State defender is out long-term.

Linebacker Alex Tatsch is out for the rest of the season with an undisclosed injury, Matt Campbell said Wednesday.

"First and foremost, just how disappointed we are for Alex," Campbell said. "Obviously, it's disappointing. Certainly continues to put stress on the linebacker room."

Tatsch was injured during practice leading up to the White Out game last week. He was initially listed as questionable on Oct. 7th's midweek availability report before he was downgraded to out on Friday.

Campbell said Tuesday during his press conference that they'd know "a little bit more this week" about Tatsch's injury.

The sophomore linebacker missed the season opener while recovering from an undisclosed injury suffered before last year's Pinstripe Bowl. He returned in Week 2 against Temple and played an increasing role in the last two nonconference games and first two Big Ten matchups this season.

Despite a short 2026 campaign, Tatsch's season will end with 11 tackles, 1.5 tackles for loss, a sack and a forced fumble.

Tatsch's injury marks a massive blow to Penn State's linebacker room, which is already struggling with Cam Smith injured and inconsistent play from Kooper Ebel. The Nittany Lions defense is now missing two major pieces for the rest of the season with defensive end Max Granville also out for the year.

Campbell said Wednesday Smith has practiced the last two days.

title: Penn State will remove Flock cameras after reviewing cost
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State University Police & Public Safety (UPPS) is opting to not renew its contract with Flock Safety, and will remove the cameras from campus.

Jacqueline Sheader, UPPS’ chief information officer, told The Daily Collegian in an email on Wednesday that the decision came “after reviewing the system’s cost, return on investment and operational value.” The decision was confirmed by Penn State Chief Financial Officer Sara Thorndike during a Penn State Faculty Senate plenary meeting on Tuesday.

Flock cameras are automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras. Over 20 Flock cameras have been sighted at Penn State’s University Park campus and logged on a map compiled by the volunteer organization DeFlock. The Daily Collegian confirmed their presence in the spring.

The cameras, which were installed in August 2025 as part of a yearlong, cost-free pilot program, have since come under fire. Several community members have said they’re instruments of mass surveillance that infringe on people’s privacy; and that UPPS has not been transparent about their use and what specific measures are in place to prevent misuse.

Because Penn State is a “state-related university,” it is partially exempt from the Pennsylvania Right-to-Know Law, so the university’s records on Flock camera usage, which would include audit logs and data collected from the cameras, can not be accessed by the public.

Sheader did not state when the Flock cameras will be removed in her Wednesday email, but did say UPPS “will continue to research and assess tools that may provide similar operational capabilities in a more cost-effective manner,” and the decision to replace Flock with another ALPR system has not yet been made.

title: Three defendants waive preliminary and arraignment hearings in alleged cocaine ring tied to Penn State fraternities
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Three defendants allegedly involved in a fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring tied to several Penn State fraternities waived their preliminary and formal arraignment hearings on Wednesday morning.

Kaden Howe, Daniel Price and Connor Hurleigh are among 14 defendants charged in the case, and were each charged with two misdemeanor counts of drug possession.

The three defendants appeared before Judge Jonathan Grine and signed their waivers for the hearings. Howe’s attorney was not present in-person, and appeared over Zoom.

The defendants were released on recognizance. The conditions of their bail include they must appear at all times required, obey bail authority, provide written notice of their address and any changes 48 hours in advance, not cause or permit witness intimidation or retaliation, refrain from criminal activity and comply with the finger print order issued by the court.

The next court date for the three defendants is Jan. 11, 2027 at the Centre County Courthouse for their criminal pretrial conferences. If the charges go to jury trial, the defendants are scheduled to appear on Feb. 7, 2027.

Two additional defendants, Michael Brogno and Charlie Weisman, were scheduled to appear for their formal arraignment hearings on Wednesday afternoon, however, according to a Centre County Courthouse official, these hearings have been waived and the defendants will not be appearing.

Five defendants waived their formal arraignment hearings on Sept. 29, and intend to plead not guilty. Their next court appearances will be Nov. 16 for pretrial conferences.

title: Satire | Super niche, easy Penn State halloween costumes
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
With Halloween right around the corner, some Penn State students might be scrambling for last-minute costume ideas to pull together.

This year, the holiday falls on a Saturday, which means more days to celebrate and, subsequently, more costumes needed for celebration. Don’t let the extended celebration fill you with anxiety and dread around what you’re going to wear. Halloween is a fun time to celebrate with friends and get out of your shell, and it’s the one day a year you can be whoever you want to be.

If you’re still in the market for some costumes, here’s a list of super easy costumes.

A campus squirrel

This costume can be easily done with a full-body squirrel costume that most students can find in their closet. Or for those students less committed to the bit, you can wear a brown bodysuit or T-shirt paired with brown pants or a brown skirt, and, of course, a bushy squirrel tail.

This costume, however, wouldn’t be complete without acorns as a much needed accessory. Whether you DIY them and attach them to your costume or simply hold them in your mouth, your costume will 100% come together in the end.

If you’re concerned about being cold in this costume, don’t worry, you can simply run across people's feet on the sidewalk and scurry up trees on the HUB-Robeson Center lawn to help you warm up.

Penn State freshman

If you are one of the few students who doesn’t keep a squirrel tail on hand, never fear, there’s more options for you.

There’s no better time to show your Penn State pride than on Halloween. This easy costume only requires one piece of clothing that, luckily, all Penn State students have: their convocation T-shirt.

Show off your major with pride on Oct. 31 by pairing your bright teal College of the Liberal Arts shirt with a pair of jeans or your neon orange College of Engineering shirt with a pair of leggings. If you need places to find some pants to pair with your stylish shirt, check out Connections or Pitaya for some good finds.

The Whoop (White Loop)

“Whoop whoop” — that’s the sound of a great and trendy Halloween costume. This outfit can be easily assembled with your whiteout clothes from this past weekend partnered with your phone flashlight. Just make sure you don’t forget a portable charger so your phone, just like the White Loop, doesn’t die in the middle of Shortlidge Road.

One necessary aspect of this costume includes showing up to wherever you’re celebrating Halloween 20-30 minutes after the time you said you would be there. This also presents you with a great opportunity to lead a conga line on the dance floor while still being in character.

If you’re in the market for a duo costume, this idea can double as that as well, with your friend being the Bloop (Blue Loop). What this one entails is similar — just switch the white outfit for one that’s head-to-toe blue, and you’ve found yourself a costume you just can’t beat.

Benny Leone’s Pizza Slice

This is arguably the biggest slice of pizza in State College, so this costume will make you hard to miss.

The basic pizza slice costume is available at Spirit Halloween located at 507 Benner Pike in State College. With that costume as the base, you can add the signature Benny’s flair by adding the toppings from their monthly specials: The Soprano, with bacon mac and cheese, or Bobby Bruschetta, with tomatoes, onions, basil and, of course, the balsamic glaze drizzle.

If you’re not interested in being the slice itself, you can just cut a hole in the top and bottom of one of their boxes, and it would likely fit your whole body.

Grilled stickies creamery ice cream

A fan favorite at the creamery is the Grilled Stickies flavor that is served year-round. So why not make it part of your Halloween costume rotation?

This costume presents you with a couple of different paths to take. You can choose to go the classic route and just DIY a life sized cone to walk around in with a pint of ice cream in hand for those you pass by. Or, if you’re feeling especially creative, you can just put the Grilled Stickies directly on your clothing, and, if they’re true to the name, they should stay there the whole night.

The HUB Starbucks line

If you have too many friends for just a solo costume, this is a great group costume idea that anyone can participate in.

As students who have passed the Starbucks line in the HUB can tell you, there are never less than 50 people there, so you don’t have to worry about leaving anyone out. For this costume, you can stay nice and warm in your sweatpants, hoodie and backpack with that signature look of impatience on your face.

Unfortunately, you can’t have any accessories for this outfit, since your drink won’t be out for another 45-55 minutes, somehow, right when your next class starts.

title: Series history | Penn State vs. Michigan rivalry a tale of win streaks
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Penn State and Michigan played nearly every single year from 1993 to 2023 before four new schools joined the Big Ten and eliminated the divisions within the conference.

Across that time span, the Wolverines won 17 games to the Nittany Lions’ 10, with James Franklin struggling to defeat one of Penn State’s biggest rivals on a consistent basis, holding a 3-7 record against Michigan.

Matt Campbell will get his first crack at beating the Wolverines, who are also struggling under a first-year head coach, on Saturday. It’s the first matchup between Penn State and Michigan since 2023, which ended in a 24-15 win for the Wolverines and deflated the Nittany Lions’ playoff hopes.

Here are some of the most notable matchups and moments from the decadeslong conference rivalry.

Penn State dominates very early years

The Nittany Lions won three of their first four games against the Wolverines, all of which came under Joe Paterno.

Michigan was victorious in the inaugural contest between the two in 1993, with a 21-13 win at Beaver Stadium. Penn State came back and won the next three, including a pair of wins on the road.

One of the most iconic moments from the early days of the rivalry came in 1995, when wide receiver Joe Nastasi scored on a fake field goal to put the game away on a fourth-and-goal situation late in the fourth quarter. Penn State wound up winning 27-17.

The other notable play was in 1994, with the Nittany Lions looking to avenge their loss from the year prior in front of what was then the largest crowd in Michigan history. Quarterback Kerry Collins found wide receiver Bobby Engram for a 16-yard touchdown on a crucial third-and-11 with about four minutes remaining to put Penn State ahead 31-24, which would become the final score.

Michigan pulls away

After three straight Penn State wins, Michigan went on the longest winning streak in the series history with nine consecutive victories from 1996 to 2007.

Of those nine games, the Nittany Lions were held to 10 or less points five times, two of which were shutouts.

But the most soul-crushing defeat in that span came in 2005, with the Wolverines handing the Nittany Lions their only loss of the season.

Quarterback Michael Robinson scored a 9-yard rushing touchdown to give Penn State a 25-21 lead with just 53 seconds on the clock, but that was too much time for Michigan, which scored a touchdown on the final play of the game after a big kick return and two timeouts helped the Wolverines get down to the 10-yard line.

Post-Paterno iconic moments

Arguably Penn State’s most iconic win against Michigan came under Bill O’Brien in 2013.

The Nittany Lions and Wolverines hadn’t played for two seasons, and Penn State was unranked and dealing with the aftermath of NCAA sanctions. Michigan was No. 18 and undefeated.

With the Wolverines holding a 34-27 lead late, Penn State had 50 seconds and no timeouts to make some magic happen, and that it did. From the 37-yard line, Christian Hackenberg found Allen Robinson II at the goal line, setting up a rushing touchdown from Hackenberg to send the game to overtime.

The Nittany Lions wound up prevailing in four overtimes, 43-40, creating the signature win of the O’Brien era and a sliver of hope for the fanbase.

Although Penn State only beat Michigan three times under Franklin, two of those wins came in some of the most iconic White Outs ever.

In 2017, Saquon Barkley ran 69 yards to the end zone on just the second play from scrimmage as the No. 2 Nittany Lions went on to defeat the Wolverines, 42-13.

Franklin bested Jim Harbaugh in 2019 behind one of the most played White Out moments ever — the “Mo Bamba” timeout. Penn State won 28-21 and would defeat Michigan once again the following year at the Big House, marking the last time the Nittany Lions have defeated the Wolverines.

title: Sports Editors Weekly | Is there reason for concern after Penn State men’s hockey 0-2 start
author: Myles Hannak & Gianna Dowling | Sports Editors
description:
Editor’s Note: Sports Editors Weekly is a dueling column written by Collegian Sports Editors Gianna Dowling and Myles Hannak. It aims to provide timely debate on Penn State sports performance and news each week.

A year ago, Penn State fell short of expectations after a highly anticipated men’s hockey season highlighted by the addition of then-future No. 1 overall NHL Draft pick Gavin McKenna. Despite lower expectations this season, the Nittany Lions entered the year ranked No. 17 in Division I.

However, the start to the blue and white’s season looked similar to the end of its last, as it dropped its first two games to then-No. 16 UConn and Sacred Heart.

Following its 0-2 start, Penn State has dropped out of the USCHO rankings for the first time since Nov. 18, 2024. This raises the question — should there be concern for Guy Gadowsky and his squad?

Gianna Dowling: No need to fret yet

The most memorable season to date for the Nittany Lions was the 2024-25 campaign, when they reached the Frozen Four for the first time in program history. However, fans may also remember that this season was far from perfect for Gadowsky’s squad, especially at the beginning.

This historic blue and white season included a six-game losing streak through November, so considering how this campaign ended, Penn State’s 0-2 start doesn’t provide any reason for panic.

Another reason for fans to remain calm is that the season is long. It’s only October and the regular season runs until March. 5, so the Nittany Lions have 20 weeks and three days before it's safe for them to get booed off the ice. This being said, the blue and white’s showing in two games doesn’t tell the full story of what’s to come. The squad has plenty of time to prove its full potential.

Penn State has a big opportunity to answer its forgettable weekend when they host No. 8 Quinnipiac on Friday. It only takes one game to find momentum and if Gadowsky's squad can find theirs before starting Big Ten play at the end of the month, I believe they’ll be in good shape.

Myles Hannak: Long road ahead

The pieces of Gadosky’s squad are great. There’s defenseman Jackson Smith and a solid freshman core on attack, giving reason to have optimism that the squad is better than the results it’s put up.

Penn State will show flashes of talent. (Did you see that SportsCenter highlight from Justin Larose?) But it won’t have the depth of talent or experience to compete in a hockey world that’s become increasingly competitive at the collegiate level.

It’ll be hard for this group to not get bounced in the first round of the Big Ten’s postseason, but it’ll still be great regardless. The bar for overachievement is low for this group, given the departure of personnel to the professional level.

Given the NHL recruits already on the table for the future, I’m looking ahead past this year to next year, when the Nittany Lions may field a notable squad that could make a real push. If Sacred Heart is beating you this handily, it ain’t your year.

Let the young guys go through the pain, get the hunger, learn what Hockey Valley is about and get better with age. It'll pan out — this season's start has shown that’ll be the fate of this group.

The approach of snagging No. 1 overall level talent didn’t pay off. Now it’s time to build from the ground up.

title: Weekly Recap | No. 15 Penn State women’s volleyball adds two wins after 2 weekend sweeps
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State women’s volleyball swept Northwestern on Friday and then swept Washington on Sunday, improving their record to 12-4.

The blue and white kicked off its weekend sweep against the Northwestern Wildcats. Penn State won the first set 25-18, the second set 25-17 and the third 25-19.

Kendall Northern contributed five kills and Kennedy Martin added four of her own in the first set. The Nittany Lions were tested early on in the second, adding four errors to start off the set.

The match saw a tighter back-and-forth, but Penn State stayed on top. The third set saw a different performance, as Penn State took an early five-point lead.

New Northern heights

This match against Northwestern was a breakout performance for freshman Kendall Northern. The 6-foot-1 middle blocker from Cincinnati totaled 12 kills on 13 total attacks, marking a .923 hitting percentage. Northern also added two block assists, bringing her point total to 14.

“She’s here for a reason, and I think that she’s just showing the world why,” Gabrielle Nichols said after Penn State's 3-1 win against Iowa on Oct. 3.

Aside from her offensive totals, Northern had a perfect performance in set one. The 6-foot-1 middle blocker gathered five kills on five attacks. Her fifth attack gave Penn State its 23rd point, which Martin soon followed up to earn set point.

“She challenges me and Ryla in practice all the time. Like, she’s supposed to be in this conference,” Nichols said after the Iowa match.

Game of errors

While Penn State defeated No. 20 Washington in a sweep, both teams committed a plethora of errors. To open the first set, Alexis Stucky contributed an ace, then picked up another immediately after.

This error didn’t affect the blue and white much, as it reached a lengthy lead at the midpoint.

By contrast, Washington’s Huskies started set two with a pair of attack errors, which dug them into a hole as Penn State took a 5-0 lead.

While Washington was able to get back into the set and even the score, the Huskies committed another trio of errors. This gave Penn State a six-point differential at 18-12, and it eventually took the set after a service error from the purple and gold.

While a Husky attack error again gave Penn State a lead in the third set, the Nittany Lions didn’t escape unscathed. At the halfway point, Penn State led, but the margin in which they did shortened more and more with the errors it picked up.

At 15-11, service and attack errors by the Nittany Lions gave them a risky one-point lead. While it came close, the blue and white refused to give up the upper hand, and a similar energy from Northern in the Northwestern match reappeared to take the match.

Penn State will end its four-match home stretch and head to Los Angeles to take on UCLA on Friday. Due to the time zone difference, the game will be streamed on Big Ten Plus at 10 p.m. EST.

title: Penn State Interfraternity Council releases statement in response to alleged gang-rape involving Cornell University fraternity members
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Content Warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

The Penn State Interfraternity Council (IFC) posted a statement on Thursday saying they were “deeply troubled” by reports of the alleged gang-rape involving fraternity members at Cornell University that occurred in Oct. 2024.

The statement, posted on their website and Instagram, comes after The Cornell Daily Sun reported on Sept. 18 that a former Cornell student filed a lawsuit against the university, Cornell’s Chi Phi chapter, seven current and former students and others alleging she was gang-raped and coerced into consuming drugs at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house.

“Sexual violence and sexual misconduct have no place in fraternity and sorority life, on Penn State’s campus, or in our community,” the statement read.

Penn State IFC wrote that it condemns “sexual violence in all forms” and that a fraternity’s brotherhood should not be used to “excuse harm, shield wrongdoing, or justify standing by when others are at risk.”

Penn State’s Chi Phi chapter posted their own statement to Instagram on Sept. 30, saying “behavior like this stands in opposition to everything our fraternity stands for.”

Chi Phi is a member of the IFC, which includes 34 other fraternities, according to the council’s website. The council is affiliated with and recognized by Penn State University.

The statement also mentioned Penn State IFC’s involvement in community initiatives, such as its “growing partnership” with the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education Center, and its Men Against Violence walk.

It wrote that it will “continue to stand with survivors,” and highlighted a number of reporting methods in the community, including Penn State’s Office of Sexual Misconduct Reporting and Response and anonymous reporting hotline, along with campus and local law enforcement.

“We encourage all members of the fraternity and sorority community to speak up and take action when someone’s safety and wellbeing may be at risk,” the IFC wrote. “We remain committed to fostering a fraternity community rooted in respect, accountability, and safety.”

As of Oct. 13, The State College Interfraternity Council, which was founded in 2025 by three disaffiliated universities, has not released a statement.

title: Penn State still in search of ‘the perfect match’ in struggling run game
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s longest rush on Saturday against USC was a 10-yard run by Rocco Becht on fourth down to get the Nittany Lions into field goal range right before halftime.

Despite using only two of the four running backs that it has used in the past to try to get more rhythm from those specific backs, Penn State averaged 2.2 yards per rush, struggling to consistently run the ball well.

“We mixed up who the running backs have been and the scheme has been, and we haven't been able to just find the perfect match yet,” Taylor Mouser said Tuesday. “And it's something that we're desperate to find.”

Penn State has only found real consistency in the running game against its worst opponent, Buffalo, where it ran for 304 yards. In that game, the staff utilized all four running backs, some of which was because of the score.

However, the usage of less backs in a game is something Matt Campbell wants to see more of.

“I thought that rotation with (Carson Hansen) and James (Peoples) was probably closer to where we would like to be, in terms of what's going on,” Campbell said.

Campbell and Mouser have a lot of experience with a bell-cow running back or a two-back system from their time at Iowa State. However, they had the talent of Breece Hall and David Montgomery, both of which have carved out strong NFL careers, to utilize in the run game.

The Nittany Lions don’t have a running back to the level of Hall or Montgomery, or if they do, it hasn’t been shown yet through the first six weeks.

“Last couple years, it's been duo,” Mouser said. “We've been able to create great chemistry up front and hammer double teams and things like that, and for us, I think that you would say it's probably been a wide zone and a gap emphasis for us to be able to allow those guys to be able to stay on combos.”

Penn State has run outside the tackles this season, but hasn’t been able to find open ground despite trying to get its running backs into space.

A player who hasn’t gotten significant time since the Nittany Lions’ blowout win over Buffalo would likely be the biggest threat in wide zone runs. Running back Quinton Martin Jr. ended up bouncing a run outside and taking it for 61 yards against the Bulls, showcasing his speed in open space.

Mouser knows the explosive capabilities that Martin can bring, and despite the restriction that Penn State has gone with at the position, he still believes the former 4-star could make an impact this season.

“I love Quinton. I think he's a great kid and does all the right stuff,” Mouser said. “So for us, putting him in a spot to be able to execute well at practice and then go out and do what he does well, and he did that today in practice.”

While the run game hasn’t consistently had big plays, it did make progress in short yardage situations. Penn State went with heavier sets on short fourth down plays, which helped Hansen get the yards he needed, which included a 3-yard rushing touchdown.

“I do feel like there were some things even in that game that showed up as positives for us that I think we can build off of, and I think there's some other things that continue to show we have to figure out what we do well, and then have the ability to adjust when people take that away,” Campbell said.

title: Penn State men’s hockey notebook | Guy Gadowsky talks slow season start
author: Chase Fisher | The Daily Collegian
description:
Guy Gadowsky met with the media Tuesday evening after his team dropped its first two games of the season to No. 17 UConn and Sacred Heart over the weekend. The losses resulted in the Nittany Lions falling out of the USCHO poll for the first time since Nov. 18, 2024.

So what did Gadowsky have to say after the program's first 0-2 start since 2020? Here's what we learned from his midweek press conference, starting with a tough, season-ending injury to one of its bottom-six forwards.

Keaton Peters will miss the rest of the season; what now?

Peters missed the entire 2025-26 season after ACL reconstructive surgery. Friday, on his first shift back from his injury, he tore his ACL, MCL and sustained medial and lateral meniscus injuries after a knee-on-knee collision. The injuries will sideline him for the remainder of the 2026-27 season, a tough blow to a roster already short one player.

"The whole team is still crushed for him because it's so hard for 13 months (to rehab), and really, really hard to get back into playing shape," Gadowsky said.

Peters was key for Penn State in its Frozen Four run two years ago, specifically in a bottom-six center role. He was one of the best on the Nittany Lions at the faceoff dot (54.9 percent) and a stout defensive forward. Gadowsky said Tuesday that the team lost its best faceoff guy on the right-hand side of the dot.

So how will the staff and the team fill that role? "In my mind, it has to be collectively," he said.

Gadowsky also mentioned the team, which is one player short at 25 instead of 26 skaters, cannot add somebody yet; it would have to be later in the season.

"It's really hard to see that after the first shift," Gadowsky said. "We really, really feel for him, A. And then B, we were really excited to have his mentality back on the bench, on the ice. … A huge part of our Frozen Four run with his mentality — we need guys to step up and fill that void."

'We were not ready to play'

Gadowsky was not pleased with the latter of Penn State's two weekend games. He was blunt and up front Tuesday when asked about the second period against Sacred Heart, when the Nittany Lions were outscored 3-0 and outshot 16-8. "We learned a lesson," he said.

"We didn't necessarily act like a mature team," Gadowsky said, "(we didn't) turn the page really quickly when the puck started going in against us."

Gadowsky did say, however, that he was happy with how captains Dane Dowiak and Reese Laubach handled it when the team had a chance to regroup. He said once they got the team refocused, which led to them playing "some of our best hockey of the weekend."

Regardless, slow starts have been a problems for Penn State early in the season over the past few years, and it has to be fixed, especially after a winless first weekend.

"We were not ready to compete at the level we had to be, and that's why the chances, the shots, etc. were going against us," Gadowsky said. "We had great goaltending — we didn't paint on the scoreboard, but it caught up to us."

Gadowsky still curious about his team

Penn State lost 3-1 to UConn in the season-opening game Friday, but Gadowsky was pleased with how his team played. The Nittany Lions outshot the Huskies 43-25 and looked like a team that had it all figured out.

If you asked Gadowsky right then and there, "Do you fully know what you have with your team?" he would've said, "This is happening a lot quicker than we thought." But as of Tuesday, he's unsure.

"I don't think we've ever put a date or a number on it," Gadowsky said in terms of knowing what he has with his team. "As we say often here for Penn State hockey — consistency is better than greatness. So if that's the battle, what's the timeline? I think that's a really tough question to answer. It really is. I think you can put that into another curiosity category. We're obviously going to do all we can to make the transition as quick as possible, but I think that's hard. It's hard to get at."

title: Penn State men's hockey forward Keaton Peters suffers season-ending injury
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State forward Keaton Peters announced via X that he'll miss the remainder of the season after suffering an injury in the team's season opener on Friday.

After missing the entire 2025-26 season with an ACL tear, Peters sustained another ACL tear, along with an MCL tear and medial and lateral meniscus injuries in the first shift of his first game back on the ice this weekend.

"I'm incredibly grateful for the support I've received from my family, friends, teammates and all the fans who have been there for me throughout this process," Peters wrote in his message on X. "I vow to attack this hardship head-on and come back stronger than ever!"

During his freshman season in 2024-25, Peters played 35 games for a Nittany Lions' unit that went to the Frozen Four, earning an assist in the game against UConn that propelled the blue and white to that berth. Throughout his Penn State tenure, the Sussex, Wisconsin, native posted six points with two goals.

title: Penn State women’s soccer notebook | Erica Dambach talks recent results, how to get over the hump
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s six-match unbeaten streak came to an end against No. 13 Washington on Sunday. Before the 1-0 defeat, the blue and white bested Minnesota, Maryland, USC and Oregon and tied Iowa and Purdue.

This week, the Nittany Lions are off until Saturday when Rutgers comes to town. Coach Erica Dambach spoke to the media Tuesday about the unbeaten streak, her team’s adaptive athletics experience and goals for the quiet week.

Recent results

Penn State has shown it can win at home and on the road against all manner of opponents. Dambach has also utilized a variety of lineup combinations, and she cited that as a strength throughout conference play.

“The biggest asset of this team is our adaptability, and our ability to use different players in different situations in order to get at our opponents in different ways,” Dambach said. “I think that's our greatest strength. I haven't had a team in a long time who's been able to take a game plan, put it in, and own it, and that to me, that's the sign of a really good team. Now, how do we turn that into being an elite team?”

Dambach’s squad has consistently fallen short against that elite competition in 2026. Beyond the Washington defeat, the Nittany Lions have suffered narrow losses to No. 3 Ohio State and No. 13 West Virginia, gave up a 2-0 lead to tie then-No. 2 Notre Dame, and gone all season without a ranked win.

“The final step in all of this for this team is, as a coaching staff, we need to turn things over to this team now, and they need to understand just how good they are because they have these qualities and make plays to win these games like a Washington game, because it's all there for them,” the national champion coach said. “This team is as elite as a team as I've coached in years, and now it's just that belief and ability and confidence to make the plays to win these games.”

Adaptive Athletics crossover

In the middle of its unbeaten streak, the team was visited by four adaptive athletes. World-class competitors Jack Cunningham, Lucas Resch, Esther-Faith Henn and Angel Guzman came to the practice grounds surrounding Jeffrey Field and spent time with the women’s soccer squad.

“One of the things I took is just their mental strength to look at things through a different lens of, ‘sure, these physical challenges that I face are barriers at times, but mentally, I can be tougher and I can work my way through it, and I can achieve my goals of being a champion.’ And I thought that they were incredibly impressive,” Dambach said.

Cunningham, Resch and Guzman are all collegiate gold medalists in their respective sports, and Henn is a double silver medalist. Cunningham is a quadruple gold medalist on his own and won the 400-meter national championship at the 2026 Toyota USATF Nationals.

“For them to come and share their experience with us was just really cool for all of us, coaches and players alike. I think we gained an appreciation for elite athletes doing it at the highest level,” Dambach said. “These are national champions, so just to hear from their words what it takes to be a national champion.”

Practice week

Dambach’s team is spending this week on the home front before facing Rutgers on Saturday. After taking a red-eye flight back from the West Coast, Dambach hasn’t taken much of a look at the 4-5-4 Scarlet Knights and is instead focusing on her own team.

“It’s just finishing,” she said. “We're creating all sorts of chances, and that goes on the whole team, whether that's set pieces, and that's both defenders and attackers. It’s just getting repetition. It's no different than a basketballer on the free throw line or shooting layups. It's just repetition to build confidence.”

Penn State will put that practice in action at 4 p.m. Saturday when its game against Rutgers kicks off from Jeffrey Field.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell shares update on WR Koby Howard's return
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn State’s third straight loss in the White Out against USC, Matt Campbell met with the media at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday.

Campbell discussed the team’s injury updates, recruiting success at the White Out and more ahead of the Nittany Lions' trip to Michigan this week.

Here’s a look at what Campbell had to say.

Injury updates

Both Koby Howard and defensive end LaVar Arrington II have been out for multiple weeks, while linebacker Alex Tatsch was sidelined on Saturday.

Campbell said both Howard and Arrington’s returns will be a “post-bye week conversation.” He’s especially looking forward to Howard’s return, saying “if anybody's going to get back sooner than later, it'll be Koby Howard just because of how he works.”

On the other hand, Tatsch’s injury came last week during practice, and the significance and duration is unknown.

“Hopefully, we'll know a little bit more this week,” Campbell said. “I think you guys all know what Alex means to that linebacker room.”

Tatsch was out for the season opener against Marshall while recovering from an undisclosed injury in 2025. He played a depth role at linebacker for four weeks, but missed his second game of the season last week.

White Out recruiting

Penn State welcomed over 100 recruits to campus for its White Out game against USC on Saturday, with commits from the Class of 2027, prospects from the 2028 class and others inside Beaver Stadium.

Despite the loss, Campbell emphasized the success of the weekend and the impact of the program on the recruits outside of just the game itself.

“I think from our end of it, our recruiting staff did an incredible job,” Campbell said. “It was great to have so many great families here Friday, Saturday, even Sunday, Sunday night. Thought it was huge for us, so I thought a really positive weekend from that standpoint.”

Campbell had a very small recruiting class this year after joining the program after National Signing Day in December. Over the last 10 months, he’s put together the No. 24 recruiting class in 2027, per 247sports composite, and the No. 9 group in the Class of 2028.

Saturday’s White Out game showcased the atmosphere inside Beaver Stadium and what Penn State has to offer, which is a big recruiting piece for Campbell and the Nittany Lions.

“It was a great recruiting weekend in terms of the number of humans here that we've been able to identify over the last six months, them, their families,” Campbell said. “I think absolutely seeing that environment, watching that environment, watching our football team grow, I think are all things that were positive.”

Run-game responsibilities

Penn State’s run game has yet to develop six weeks into the season. Carson Hansen and James Peoples have battled for the starting role, but neither has performed well enough to become the bell cow.

At the same time, redshirt sophomore Quinton Martin Jr. has showcased signs of flashes, including a team-best 61-yard rush against Buffalo. Despite his success, he’s had significantly less carries than Hansen and Peoples and didn’t record a snap against USC.

“I thought that rotation with (Carson) and James was probably closer to where we would like to be in terms of what's going on,” Campbell said. “Obviously, we still have great faith in Quinton and Cam (Wallace).”

Hansen had 14 carries against USC, the most he’s had since Week 2, and was seen as more of a short-yardage back. Meanwhile, Peoples had his fewest number of carries this year, while Campbell noted his potential explosiveness.

The Nittany Lions rushed for just 68 yards, as Campbell said the run game needs to keep improving and create more success.

“There was growth there,” Campbell said. “Are we where we want to be? No, but I certainly think those two right now catching the ball in the backfield, some of the protection things, I think those things started to show itself, and we'll need to continue to grow in those areas.”

title: Penn State notebook | OC Taylor Mouser speaks on the usage of TE Benjamin Brahmer
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser took the podium at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday following Penn State’s third-consecutive Big Ten loss.

Mouser touched on the Nittany Lions’ offensive identity, shared his disappointment regarding not fully utilizing tight end Benjamin Brahmer and shared his philosophy with third and fourth down situations.

Here’s more on what he said.

Offensive identity

Matt Campbell said last week Penn State “lacks an identity.” Against USC, the Nittany Lions began to find their footing in the passing game, but Mouser said the run game continues to desperately search for identity.

“We have to find a way to get better,” Mouser said. “It's been our biggest focus and talking with our head coach, (Ryan) Clanton, myself and (Savon) Huggins. We have to continue to stress and have urgency to grow there.”

Mouser said he still has complete faith in Rocco Becht and the passing game, but the team can’t throw the ball “50 times a game.” He noted the team needs to improve in the run game to complement the pass game by controlling the time of possession.

Seeing success from the running backs would be paramount to helping the rest of the offense find consistency. Mouser added with Michigan’s pass rush on the horizon, Becht may be under a lot of pressure, so getting the run game involved is important.

“We're always trying to lean into the best parts of our offense, and we feel really good about the pass catchers that we have,” Mouser said. “There's got to be a great balance between the two to be able to stay on schedule and help the quarterback and help the offensive line.”

Benjamin Brahmer

Despite Brahmer only having one catch on Saturday for four yards, Mouser said he specifically called plays to get him more involved, so he left Beaver Stadium “confused” as to why Brahmer didn’t have more of a contribution.

“I certainly have a checklist on my call sheet of, these are the best ways to get Ben the ball,” Mouser said. “Obviously it doesn't guarantee anything, but for him to have one catch isn't right in my mind.”

Mouser noted USC took away a lot of Brahmer’s opportunities to get touches, and it allowed tight ends Andrew Rappleyea and Gabe Burkle to step up in a meaningful way.

Regardless, Mouser said Brahmer is one of the best players on the team, stressing how important it’s going to be to get him more involved as the season continues.

Brahmer was crucial to Iowa State’s offensive success last season and was brought to Penn State to be the leader of an elite tight end room. The production hasn’t been up to that standard despite Brahmer being a “focal point” of the offensive preparation.

Third and fourth downs

Penn State converted just two third downs, but moved the chains on all five fourth down opportunities. Mouser said this trend is primarily due to the distance of the first down marker, as the Nittany Lions have seen numerous third-and-long situations this season.

“You don't want to be in fourth-and-long, you don't want to be in third-and-long,” Mouser said. “We just have to be able to stay on track in the pass game to be able to be efficient to help our offensive line out.”

Mouser said he felt the team got into a rhythm in fourth-down situations, and the offense began to treat third down like a second down to create “manageable” fourth downs.

He mentioned how throwing the ball on second and third down is a tendency of the offense due to the struggles in the run game.

“You can’t run the ball for no yards on second-and-10,” Mouser said. “So from my standpoint it’s being able to call stuff that you can execute well and putting our guys in places to be successful and throw stuff that we're good at.”

title: Penn State field hockey's Cam Standish earns Big Ten weekly honors
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s Cam Standish was named the Big Ten Defensive Player of the Week, the conference announced Monday.

The Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, native anchored the Nittany Lion defense to two shutouts in last week’s games against Michigan State and Kent State. Hannah Prince’s squad took down the Spartans 1-0 in overtime, then beat the Golden Flashes 3-0.

The blue and white allowed eight total shots on the week, and none were shots on goal. Standish, a graduate student, also played an instrumental role in Penn State winning the penalty corner battle by seven in both games.

The Nittany Lions are back in action at 5 p.m. on Friday when Ohio State comes to town.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | Parker Washington scores twice, Pat Freiermuth, Tyler Warren face off
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
It was a touchdown-filled weekend for several former Penn Staters as Week 5 of the NFL season wrapped up on Monday night.

Wide receiver Parker Washington and tight end Pat Freiermuth each scored a pair of touchdowns, while a Penn State reunion took place at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh.

Here’s a look at which former Nittany Lions stood out this week.

Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Indianapolis Colts

Four Nittany Lions were rostered between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Indianapolis Colts during Sunday’s matchup, with the three Steelers players earning the 34-22 victory.

Freiermuth was the go-to guy for quarterback Aaron Rodgers, hauling in five receptions for 44 yards and two touchdowns,marking his third and fourth scores of the season.

Freiermuth’s first grab came early in the second quarter when he ran a 1-yard stutter-step route into the end zone. Rodgers found him practically unguarded for another 17-yard touchdown pass in the fourth quarter.

On the other side of the field, Warren also found success for the Colts. He finished the day with seven receptions for 83 yards and a 1-yard rushing touchdown.

Just inches from the goal line, Warren lined up in a fullback position behind Daniel Jones, took the handoff and jumped forward for the score. This wasn’t new for him, as he recorded six rushing touchdowns while at Penn State.

Safety Jaquan Brisker also played a big role in Pittsburgh’s win, with seven tackles and two passes defended.

Parker Washington, wide receiver, Jacksonville Jaguars

While Washington didn’t receive the contract extension he was pushing for before the season, he’s shown through five weeks why he’s deserving of it.

Washington was a crucial part of the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 19-17 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles in London on Sunday. He recorded six receptions for 124 yards and two touchdowns.

His first score came off a 1-yard pass from quarterback Trevor Lawrence, followed by 50 yards after the catch as he weaved past multiple defenders. With minutes left in the fourth quarter, he reeled in his second touchdown off a 27-yard, one-handed grab, falling backwards into the end zone.

Washington has 22 receptions for 352 yards and four touchdowns so far this season. His yardage ranks 14th among receivers, while his touchdowns are the fourth-best in the league.

Injuries sideline Nittany Lions

Former Offensive Player of the Year Saquon Barkley missed a majority of the Eagles’ Week 2 contest with an injury, and after playing the following week, is out again.

Barkley sustained a hamstring injury on Oct. 4 against the Los Angeles Rams, forcing him to the sideline after just one quarter. He didn’t practice leading up to Sunday morning’s contest, and was ruled out for the first time this year. There’s no update on his return.

Green Bay Packers defensive end Micah Parsons has been out since tearing his ACL on Dec. 14, 2025. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Parsons is unlikely to return to practice this week, but the Packers are hoping he’ll begin football activities sometime this month.

Mike Gesicki, tight end, Cincinnati Bengals

Tight end Mike Gesicki had a quiet week for the Cincinnati Bengals, recording just one reception for four yards.

However, his catch found him in the back of the end zone against his former team, the Miami Dolphins, contributing to the Bengals’ 31-24 victory.

Gesicki now has four touchdowns this year, marking his third straight week with a score.

Pass rushers wreak havoc

Penn State’s been known for its success in developing linebackers and pass rushers, and that was on display Sunday.

Packers defensive end Dani Dennis-Sutton earned his first career solo sack against the Chicago Bears. He burst through the B-gap past left tackle Theo Benedet, wrapped his arms around quarterback Case Keenum and brought him to the ground.

New York Giants linebacker Abdul Carter also recorded a sack, chasing Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels out of the pocket for a loss of yards.

title: Column | Penn State can be a basketball school if we let it
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State Athletics is in disarray, as I’m sure you’ve all noticed. Don’t worry, though. Its savior is here.

Blue and white basketball is back this weekend, with an exhibition against St. Bonaventure and Mike Rhoades’ magic is just what not-so Happy Valley needs right now.

I won’t sugarcoat it: The Nittany Lions are the laughing stock of the Big Ten. The results have upheld that notion and this year’s fate is hard to shake as another season of it. Only three wins in conference play last season, and there were some bad moments. A blowout at the GIANT Center by rival Pitt. Disappointment on Senior Night. The Return to the Rec and the Big Ten Tournament. Overall, the program stagnated to a forgettable 44-52 record under Rhoades.

The next generation of hoopers sees the state where Pittsburgh and Villanova are both in a transitional period. And then there’s Penn State: A program that was starting to soar at the start of the decade, but can’t seem to capitalize on the trends.

Picked at the bottom in the Big Ten again in the unofficial Media Poll and trailed only by Northwestern in the first KenPom rankings of the year, it’s hard not to anticipate another gloomy season for Penn State.

But this offseason has been different, filled with reporters and fans who have their eyes on the hardwood for once.

The dialogue actually feels aware of the position of the program, and it almost feels synonymous to the movie “Rudy.” Campus has embraced both the need to punch up and the underdog mantra. The social media buzz has fans joking about themselves, acknowledging the difficulties head on.

The justification for the program's stagnation has been the notion that Penn State just “isn’t a basketball school.” However, this summer proved that notion wrong. People do care. As much as that phrase has been thrown around by Athletics and isn’t pushed back on by those who have reported on basketball, it’s short-sighted.

The care has tapered because AD Pat Kraft doesn’t believe in the product or the investment; the people do. College basketball will always make waves and capture hearts; the charm of Rhoades and Co. should make that an easy sell. They love Penn State more than any hoops coach would.

Last year’s team was one of the worst in recent history. The overall win percentage was the 15th all-time worst at Penn State, and Big Ten production was the seventh worst. But through it all, fans still showed up for any game and brought in a crowd that only showed flashes of what the Bryce Jordan Center has to offer. Home attendance actually averaged higher once the team imploded in Big Ten play than during a light nonconference slate.

Athletics needs to invest, bring a winner and add prestige, and the Penn State fandom will reflect that generosity by revealing the love for hoops that exists. Check the Purdue upset in 2024; the pandemonium was a brief glimpse of what’s possible. Let’s build off those moments instead of reliving glory days.

The women’s squad has hit an even stiffer wall, but the connection to blue and white was enough to bring program legends back to the sidelines and woo top recruits into visits.

Past groups of players haven’t shown the same care for the program, as evidenced by the mass transfer portal exodus in recent seasons of Rhoades’ tenure. This group of players, contrarily, perfectly reflects where the people are at — passionate and seasoned through the wringer.

Rhoades’ emotion for the program always shone through. Now that there’s a group of players where a majority arguably feel the same way, it’s time to put up the results.

Miami (OH) transfer forward Brant Byers, one of the leading acts on a nationally prominent RedHawks squad, had a grocery list of suitors in the portal but landed at the bottom of the Big Ten. Why? Because he loved the program and he knew what it stood for.

Despite what happens, watch it all. The sidelines, the players, coaches and environment — the energy is there; it’s just a matter of finally acknowledging it, and for once embracing it.
