title: Off the Record | Penn State guy starter pack
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer writing under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic are invited to do so through this anonymous form.

Imagine walking in the library and passing a 6-foot-something brunette. Not even five minutes later, you’re walking near Old Main and you pass a 6-foot-something brunette. Naturally, you think, “Wait, I just saw that guy going in the other direction.”

Have you just experienced a space and time disruption, an overlap between two worlds? Was this confirmation that we live in a simulation, and everyone is a nonplayer character under mind control by the government? You wonder if the planet would combust should you introduce these two men.

Unfortunately, you have not, in fact, made a groundbreaking scientific discovery. You've just experienced the Penn State man phenomenon: They’re all different people, yet somehow exactly the same.

If you’re a 6-foot-something brunette reading this wondering why you’ve been mistaken for another man three times already today, you’re in the right place. There’s so many other basic uniforms you can try on to look exactly the same as everyone else, just in a different genre!

Blue suit

If you’ve got “Frat Formal Friday” or a career fair in the Business Building, this staple piece is a must. Nothing screams “a man putting on their best look” like a blue suit with a white button-down underneath.

Bonus points if you walk with your friends in the same drip, taking up the whole sidewalk, annoying everyone else who’s just trying to get to class.

Comfy, nonchalant ensemble

While the blue suit is a crucial wardrobe item for Penn State men, it can’t be worn every day — that would violate Penn State man-code. (I think.) For class or a stroll downtown, you’ll want to strategically put together an outfit consisting of gray sweatpants, white socks and slides.

It’s comfortable, but the level of nonchalance it takes to pull off slides and socks is one you must be able to achieve. Plus, you get to show off the slides while keeping the toes toasty. It’s nonchalant, yet practical.

Elevated backwards hat

The design doesn’t really matter. A Penn State, sports team or branded hat will suffice.

What it’s really about is placement. You’ll want your baseball cap resting on your head backwards without being fully worn. This way, you have space to store all of your aura.

You don’t want it to fall off your head, but be careful, because you also don’t want to be seen wearing a hat correctly. The baseball cap placement is a little bit of an advanced technique, but once you master it, you’ll be unstoppable.

“The Wolf of Wall Street” ball knowledge

This one is really important. The past few have revolved around appearance, but this one will help you develop your character. If you’re ever asked your favorite movie, it’s “The Wolf of Wall Street.” Even if you have a different movie in mind, no, you don’t.

If a woman wants to have a movie night with you, suggest “The Wolf of Wall Street.” Just remember your line: “Leonardo DiCaprio is just so good in this.” If you memorize that, you’re golden. She’ll want to rip that baseball cap right off you.

Vocabulary skills

There are certain words you need to have in your repertoire in order to truly live up to being a Penn State guy. Luckily, I’ve prepared a short lesson for you on some of the most essential words to get you started.

“Type” or “bet” can be used verbally or via text message. It makes most sense as a substitution for “yes” or “OK,” but you can really use it whenever. Just make sure you say it with a slight head nod up and a frat boy accent. Nobody will question the context if you say it with enough confidence.

“My boy” or “my boys” is how you’ll want to refer to your friends. You can even say “the boy” if he’s really something special.

Lack of emotional vulnerability

When it comes to being a Penn State man, you want to leave any emotional vulnerability at the door. It’s important to forget people have feelings in order to thrive in this persona. It’s equally as important to say “type” and move on with your day instead of ruminating on any emotion that happens to win the race in percolating through your mind.

Set your calendar for your 25th birthday, though. That’ll be the day you discover empathy. The feelings you’ll soon discover are compassion and, stay with me now, the ability to love.

Now that I’ve equipped you with the only starter pack you’ll ever need, I wish you the best of luck on your journey, however you choose to use this information.

You can take the man out of Penn State, but you can never take the Penn State out of the man.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: Recruiting roundup | Penn State brings in top talent for White Out weekend
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The White Out is annually Penn State’s biggest recruiting weekend of the season, something Matt Campbell acknowledged the Wednesday before.

This year was no different, with the Nittany Lions bringing in over 100 recruits from all over the country, including a majority of its 2027 class. Penn State invited a plethora of highly rated 2028 recruits, while also handing out offers to players who could be targets down the line.

Here’s a roundup of the recruits from White Out weekend.

2027 reunion

The largest group of 2027 commits since Penn State’s official visit weekend on June 5 were in attendance on Saturday.

Eighteen of the now-22 committed players in the 2027 class were in attendance for the Nittany Lions’ biggest home game of the year.

The class currently ranks No. 20 in the country, according to 247Sports composite, and is No. 8 in the Big Ten. It features seven 4-star recruits, six of which were in Happy Valley on Saturday.

Of the four players who weren’t in attendance, 3-star running back Chukwuma Odoh continued to make a name for himself on Saturday. He faced off against New Jersey’s top-ranked team, Bergen Catholic, tallying three rushing touchdowns in the second half to help Paramus Catholic pull off the upset, 31-17.

The class is mostly filled out, with the potential to add another player or two with flips. Campbell’s first recruiting class at Penn State will likely remain in the top 25.

Pipeline

Penn State continues to focus on the 2028 class, with only three players committed so far. However, it’s currently ranked No. 9 in the country, with two 4-star commits in quarterback James Armstrong and cornerback Deonte Flemings Jr., both of whom were in Happy Valley over the weekend.

Alongside the commits were some of the nation’s top players in the 2028 class.

4-star wide receiver Jaden Jones, 4-star athlete Brandon Murphy and 4-star offensive lineman Nick Anderson all visited from the Pittsburgh area. Anderson is a legacy recruit, with his dad, Bill Anderson playing for the Nittany Lions from 1992-95. His son, Nick, is the No. 8 player in Pennsylvania in 2028.

Penn State’s push for the top talent in the state has been consistent in the 2028 class. Jones ranks as the No. 7 player in the state and No. 26 player at his position, while Murphy is the No. 4 player in Pennsylvania. Both players have visited Penn State more than any other school so far, but they still have over a year to decide on where to play in college.

On the other side of the state, offensive lineman Ty Winn was back in town for the White Out. Winn is the prototypical offensive lineman that offensive line coach Ryan Clanton would target, given his 6-foot-8 stature. Winn is the No. 6 player in the state, and he has visits lined up with other top schools for each weekend until the end of the regular season.

Penn State has a clear pipeline in the New Jersey and New York area, as Director of Recruiting Naz Oliver coached at Malcolm X Shabazz High School in New Jersey prior to being hired in his role with the Nittany Lions on Feb. 25, 2025.

4-star edge rusher Cam Toomey is the No. 1 player in New York, and has been one of Penn State’s most sought after targets. Toomey has also visited Ole Miss and Virginia Tech this season.

4-star wide receiver Mekhi Parker is a top-100 player in 2028 and the No. 3 player in New Jersey. Parker stands at 6-foot-4, which would be the second-tallest receiver on the Nittany Lions’ 2026 roster. Parker holds offers from the top teams in the country, including Georgia, Ohio State, Texas and Alabama.

Latest offers

Penn State dished out a handful of offers over the weekend in the 2028, 2029 and 2030 classes.

4-star cornerback Zayden Williams received an offer Saturday while on his visit. The Tennessee native is the No. 33 cornerback in the 2028 class and holds offers from Georgia, Auburn, Florida State and others.

Penn State added offers to many players in the southern part of the country. 4-star receiver Carson LaCombe made the trip from San Antonio, Texas, and received an offer from the Nittany Lions. The No. 21 wide receiver in the 2028 class visited LSU at the beginning of September and received an offer from the Tigers, as well. He also holds offers from Oklahoma, Ohio State and Texas Tech.

Penn State also offered 2028 3-star tight end AJ Henley out of Harper Woods, Michigan. Henley stands at 6-foot-3 and has offers from Michigan, Louisville, Indiana and Iowa State. He was joined by fellow Michigan native, safety Jayden Evans, who is a 3-star recruit and the No. 9 player in Michigan.

While the Nittany Lions didn’t pull out a victory in front of its biggest visiting group of the season, it showcased one of the best environments in the country and a record-setting 114,419 fans at Beaver Stadium.

title: Review | On ‘The Life of a Showgirl: Encore,’ Taylor Swift reminds us to find joy in life
author: Rebecca Fein | The Daily Collegian
description:
Pop princess Taylor Swift released a four-song vault track album titled “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore,” a follow-up to her October 2025 release “The Life of a Showgirl.”

Fans were skeptical of Swift’s songwriting capabilities after she married Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce. Many “Swifties,” the title of her fanbase, claimed she needed struggles and heartache to create a chart-topping album.

Much to the dismay of her naysayers, these four new songs sent “The Life of a Showgirl” back to the No. 1 spot on the Billboard 200 albums chart. Although some fans (and haters) think the new editions fell short to their ears, the numbers don’t lie.

“The Life of a Showgirl” was one of Swift’s happier albums. With upbeat songs like “Opalite,” “Wood” and “Honey,” the album laid the foundation for these new tracks by setting up the specific tone for the new melodies.

"The Encore" starts with “Patient Zero,” a song with minor scale tones and haunting melody that alludes to the idea of bonding with someone over a shared toxic ex-boyfriend.

Swift sings, “When the toxins take their hold, you'd rather die than let it go/But if you’re sick of him, I got you, I was patient zero.”

These words tell us that when your dream boyfriend begins turning into more of a nightmare, and you still feel drawn to him, Swift understands. She’s “been there, done that.”

The next song is “Cleveland!,” named after the city Kelce grew up in. The lyrics reflect her joy in finding someone who loves her, despite all of her haters and pressure from her global stardom: “You only need to find one person in this entire world who doesn't find you completely insufferable/and I have an important announcement to make: I found mine.” Listeners can experience and empathize with Swift’s delight that she found her best friend and lover wrapped into one person.

The third track is “Pink Clouding.” Here, Swift apologizes to past lovers for using their romance as an emotional escape, and she admits to being the problem in the relationship. Although many fans were left disappointed that the online speculation about a surprise feature from Grammy-winning singer and actress, Ariana Grande, was false, the song still sent listeners to the clouds.

Pink cloud is a phrase used in addiction recovery to describe the euphoric feeling after the first few weeks of sobriety — a possible connection to the song, as Swift sings of the misleading bliss in the first few weeks of a relationship that belies darker problems.

The happy honeymoon phase isn’t built to last, she tells us, singing, “But I was pink clouding from the thrill of it/Skydiving as you wrapped your arms around my body/Gray rocking where the arrow hit/Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry.”

It can be easy to use romantic connections to hide from the stress of school and hurt the people involved, especially in early college relationships. Since Swift was so trapped in ecstasy, she didn’t realize the damage she was causing. She reminds fans constantly through her lyricism that everyone — even successful, blonde popstars — make mistakes.

The last new edition to the album is “Babylon.” The song quickly became a fan favorite due to its catchy rhythm and the deeper message “Swifties” tend to search for in her music.

Swift sings, “You're using nostalgia as a weapon to hurt yourself/but darling, you end up hurting everybody else/The self-harm of never being where you are/It's bedtime, but you're sitting in your car/You're missing all the best parts.”

These lyrics implore us to be present in the moment; if you spend all of your time focused on the past or looking for the next best thing, one day you’ll turn around to find you never actually lived.

This is especially relevant to Penn Staters approaching graduation day. It can be easy to start dreading finals and graduation, or wishing the semester away to get to Christmas break. But it's important to appreciate Happy Valley, while you’re still in it.

“The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” brought us the optimistic energy we need to push through midterms. Now, we'll all just have to sit and wait until she gives us our next album.

title: ‘Everybody just loves each other’ | Penn State women’s basketball finds team culture despite new faces
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
New faces fill the roster, new voices lead from the sidelines, and a new identity soon blossoms.

For Penn State, the upcoming season is less about building on what came before and more about discovering what comes next.

First-year coach Tanisha Wright's 11-player squad features 10 faces that are new to the Lady Lions uniform.

In the unique situation that presents the blue and white ahead of the season, the question remains of how a nearly entirely new team fits into a new place, but more importantly, how they do it together.

"Ultimately, when you're building a team, right, you want to be player-centric, where the players decide who they want to be and the identity that they want to be and the culture that they want to be," Wright said. "I got lucky with the athletes that we have, that they've decided that they want to be a close-knit team.'

The Lady Lions had less time than most to figure out their culture and who they were as a team. Wright and her staff added four-star freshman Kamrah Banks as their first addition on April. 21. Before Vitória Santana announced her return on Sept. 29, Penn State didn't have a full 10-player squad until Aug. 11, when graduate transfer Savannah White announced her pledge to Happy Valley.

With signings and additions scattered through May and June, the blue and white had limited time to bond as a full team. However, the Lady Lions used the summer to build chemistry.

"You're building a whole new program and building the new foundation for everything, but so far it's been really exciting, and I feel like we did a pretty good job," Nebraska transfer Petra Božan said. "Especially during the summer of bonding and building that chemistry off the court. We were hanging out all the time and like making sure that we're on the same page and that reflects when we were playing on the court."

Božan was one of the bigger additions for Wright in the portal and brings Big Ten experience to the table. The 6-foot-4 junior forward appeared in all 32 games for the Cornhuskers last season, averaging 6.6 points and 3.4 rebounds per game. Božan also started two NCAA Tournament games in which she averaged five points and three rebounds.

Another strong addition for Wright's squad with Power Four experience is junior guard Devyn Quigley from NC State. The Manchester, New Jersey, native started six games for the Wolfpack last season, averaging 4.3 points and 2.4 rebounds per game.

Quigley said having former Lady Lions at the helm has helped build a strong culture, as one of Wright's newest assistants is all-time leading scorer Kelly Mazzante.

"That was a huge factor as to why I decided to come here," Quigley said. "As soon as I got here and started working out with coach Kelly, (she) has been my main position coach. Sometimes I even worked out with coach (Wright). I have grown so much as a player, and not even just physically and on the court, that will show."

Growth reflects a larger theme for Penn State as it brings together players from different backgrounds. The Lady Lions will look for a way to turn their varied experiences into a shared identity on the court.

Despite being new to Happy Valley, White, along with fellow graduate transfer Enjulina Gonzalez, brings plenty of college experience as Penn State marks the fourth school for both players.

"I think it has its pros and its cons, but it's definitely shaped who I am as a player now," White said. "But we're here now, so focused on being Penn State players."

With players arriving from different programs, the Lady Lions bring a variety of experiences, personalities and perspectives into the locker room. The blue and white are looking to turn those differences into a strength and hold each other to high expectations.

"I think the biggest thing for us that's gonna translate off the court to on the court is being able to hold each other accountable," White said. "We all have the same goal. We all want the same things, and I think holding each other accountable is going to be huge for us, especially when it comes to the season."

While the different paths each player took to Penn State helped shape them individually, bringing the experiences together presents a different challenge. In a team sport, one of the biggest keys to success is chemistry and how well a team bonds, both on and off the court.

"It's been seamless for us to just being together. Just it's been easy, and I think we have great people on the team," Gonzalez said. "Everybody just loves each other, so it's easy for us to just hang out."

title: 'I love Penn State' | Vitória Santana talks return to Penn State women’s basketball for fifth year
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Out of 12 players who suited up for Penn State last season, only one is back for Tanisha Wright’s first season at the helm.

On Sept. 29, the Lady Lions announced that Vitória Santana would return for her third season with the program and fifth year in college basketball.

“It’s nice to be back,” Santana said. “I love Penn State. I graduated from here, and I like the energy, the whole new staff, everything’s going great.”

Santana, a Sao Paulo, Brazil, native, transferred to Happy Valley in 2024 after two years at Eastern Arizona, where she averaged 15.9 points and 8.1 rebounds in her final season.

The guard started five games in her first season at Penn State, then appeared in 28 games last year. This summer, she traveled the world with the Brazilian national team on the FIBA 3x3 Women's Series.

On the circuit, Santana competed in Chengdu, China; Baku, Azerbaijan; Bangkok, Thailand and Singapore. She led the team in scoring with nine points in its 19-9 victory over Azerbaijan in Baku.

The international stage taught Santana how to play basketball at a different level of intensity, and her experience is now showing itself in Penn State practices. Wright mentioned how “her veteranness has definitely showed out” in the preseason.

While Santana is under a new coach, years of basketball experience inside and outside the Bryce Jordan Center allowed her to slip into a leadership role right away.

“I think she has a great voice,” Savannah White said. “Even just when she came in learning, whether it's the offense or learning the drills, she hasn't let that cripple her from being a leader and having a voice and making sure that we're all on our P's and Q's, so I think she's done a really good job since she's been here for sure.”

White, a graduate student from St. Paul, Minnesota, has been around plenty of leaders over the past four years. The 6-foot-2 forward played at Wisconsin, Indiana State and Xavier and is now making her final stop in State College.

Someone with far less collegiate experience, Ashlee Brown, agreed with White’s assessment.

“I think it's been really good for her having the experience,” the freshman guard said. “She's done really well with communicating, like even just little things. Maybe she might not know much of what coach T may want specifically right now, but she knows how it is as a college athlete, and I think she's been really good at relaying that back to us.”

Santana was all smiles as she talked about her teammates. She made it clear that “everybody has a good positive mindset, good energy, so everything is going great.”

While the faces and methods around the program are new, the mindset is not. Penn State replaced Carolyn Kieger, a fiery leader, with someone who has just as much competitive gas in the tank in Wright.

“I don’t have (a) really big difference,” Santana said. “They are both a great coach, great intensity and we all have the same goal to win and do great for Penn State.”

By returning to Penn State, Santana created another unique chance to make good on that goal.

“I love Penn State; I love State College,” she said. “I love the community, the fans. So when I heard that I have (the) opportunity to (spend) another year playing basketball in the States and being in school, I took the chance.”

title: Penn State women’s basketball notebook | Wright “got really lucky” as season-opener approaches
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s almost Tanisha time.

With less than a month to go until the Lady Lions’ season opener against Cleveland State on Nov. 2, Penn State took to the podium for local media day on Monday to set the stage for the upcoming season.

Here’s what first-year coach Tanisha Wright had to say as her debut draws closer.

Building the culture

Carolyn Kieger’s departure after last season led to a mass exodus of players from the program, and it looked as if Penn State would sport an entirely new roster until Vitoria Santana announced her return on Sept. 29.

With ten newcomers and a fresh coaching staff, Wright was tasked with rebuilding the culture from the ground up. According to her, she hasn’t needed to do much to foster chemistry.

“I got really lucky, to be honest with you,” Wright said. “They've taken the initiative to do things on their own and build the culture that they want. Ultimately, when you're building a team, you want to be player-centric, where the players decide who they want to be and the identity that they want to (have).”

Wright noted that the players have made an effort to attend volleyball games together, have group dinners and spend time together off the court.

Savannah White, who transferred from Xavier in the offseason, saw the team start to gel in the short time it’s been together.

“Coach T did a really good job of recruiting good people,” White said. "It's been easy to get here and be able to be focused. We all came here believing Coach T's goal, and we all have our own goal of being successful. It's been seamless translating that.”

Post play

Last season, Gracie Merkle held down the paint for the Lady Lions. With her off to Minnesota, Wright is looking to a new group of bigs to be powerful near the basket.

Merkle was an elite finisher and efficient from close range, but was lacking defensively and as a facilitator. This year’s group won’t be as physically imposing as the 6-foot-6 center, but Wright expects them to be more well-rounded.

“We want all players on the court to be playmakers,” Wright said. “That's the skill set of the players that we brought in. So we certainly want to use their skill set. I think our players have done a great job of showing that they could be trustworthy with the ball in their hands, so we're going to put it in their hands and allow them to make plays.”

Petra Bozan and Cristen Carter are the tallest Lady Lions this season, each standing 6-foot-4, and Wright said that they could end up sharing the court in certain situations, especially with Penn State’s short bench.

“Anything's possible,” Wright said. “We have 11 players, so we're going to take advantage and take the opportunities that present themselves. “There might be opportunities [where] they need to play together, so we're going to take advantage of our full bench and use it to the best of our ability.”

Backcourt ballers

Penn State will likely start two young guards in the season-opener against the Vikings.

Skylar Durley came east after earning Mountain West Freshman of the Year honors last season at Nevada. With the Wolf Pack, she averaged 11.8 points per game while starting all 31 games.

She’ll face higher competition at Penn State, but Wright is looking forward to watching her seize that opportunity.

“I'm really excited about her being at this level and showing that she can compete [in the] Big Ten, which, as we know, is the best conference in the country,” Wright said.

Kamrah Banks, a freshman, was ranked as a four-star prospect coming out of high school, having averaged 20.4 points per game as a senior and received a McDonald's All-American nomination.

“From day one to now, Kam has grown so much,” Wright said. “Penn State used to be called Point Guard U; some great point guards have come out of this university, so I'm really excited for her opportunity to continue to grow and become one of the next great point guards out of this place.”

title: Penn State recommends closure of 47 academic programs, including 11 at University Park
author: Fabiola González-Cruz | The Daily Collegian
description:
Correction: A previous version of the article listed the geosciences, multidisciplinary studies programs and the information sciences and technology programs as recommended for closure. This article has been updated to reflect that geosciences (BA) information sciences and technology (BS) and multidisciplinary studies (AA and BA) have been recommended for closure, while the geosciences (BS) and information sciences and technology (AS) programs will be maintained. The Daily Collegian apologizes for this error.

Penn State announced 47 academic programs, including 11 at University Park, have been recommended for closure, according to a press release. The announcement follows a university-wide review of 403 associate and bachelor’s degree programs, as well as months of community feedback and discussions with university leadership.

The programs recommended for closure at University Park campus include professional photography (BDES), geobiology (BS), geosciences (BA), elementary and kindergarten education (BS), middle level education (BS), world languages education (BS), information sciences and technology (BS), security and risk analysis (BS), multidisciplinary studies (BA and AA) and planetary science and astronomy (BS).

The number of programs recommended for closure decreased from 49 in the preliminary recommendation released this spring to 47 in the final recommendations. Of those 47 programs, 24 would continue to be offered through another college within the university.

Additionally, 71 programs will undergo further evaluation over the following year, while 55 have been already identified for potential additional investment due to opportunities of growth and expansion.

According to the university, 784 students, approximately 1.1% of Penn State's undergraduate community, are enrolled in programs recommended for closure. Nine of the programs currently have no enrolled students, while 15 have already submitted formal plans to phase out their programs or suspend enrollment.

The recommendations are not official closure decisions. Programs must first undergo faculty senate review before receiving final approval from Executive Vice President and Provost Fotis Sotiropoulos. Penn State said affected students will receive support in order to complete their degrees.

The review is part of the university’s broader effort to adjust its academic offerings in response to changing enrollment patterns, workforce demand and rising costs, according to the release.

title: Big Ten roundup | Indiana survives Nebraska, UCLA gets signature win in Week 6
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
In a week where upsets happened all around the country, the Big Ten was relatively chalk in the conference’s eight games.

The top of the Big Ten became a bit more clear, while two other ranked teams ran away with blowout victories to remain at the top of the conference standings.

Here’s what happened in the Big Ten in Week 6.

Close wins keep teams atop Big Ten standings

While Nebraska led for a majority of the game, a late comeback helped Indiana remain unbeaten and keep their longest active winning streak in the country, which now stands at 22.

Wide receiver Nick Marsh put Indiana’s offense on his back in the fourth quarter. After Nebraska quarterback Anthony Colandrea extended the lead to 11, Indiana quarterback Josh Hoover found Marsh on the first play of the Hoosiers’ next drive, and he ran it all the way for a 75-yard touchdown.

On the following offensive possession, Marsh found paydirt again, this time on a 44-yard receiving touchdown to give Indiana its first lead of the game. The Hoosiers held onto the lead, escaping Lincoln with a 20-17 win.

The biggest game of the Big Ten weekend, meanwhile, took place between Oregon and UCLA. It was a chance for the Bruins to have their maiden major win under first-year head coach Bob Chesney.

It also was an opportunity for Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola to make a name for himself as the Ducks’ quarterback for the near future.

Chesney’s squad ended up coming out on top, with a total of four quarterbacks playing in the game. UCLA quarterback Nico Iamaleava had to leave the game with a lower-body injury, which opened the door for Cal Poly transfer Ty Dieffenbach.

Dieffenbach didn’t have to do much, throwing a touchdown pass on six passing attempts, with a majority of the offense coming from running back Wayne Knight, who eclipsed 100 yards on the ground for the third straight game.

On the other side, Raiola was benched after underperforming, going 6-of-19 for 43 yards and two interceptions. Backup Brock Thomas entered and was much more efficient, but couldn’t lead enough of a comeback against the Bruins, who took down Oregon 17-15.

Ohio State, Iowa dominate

While Maryland kept it close through the first quarter, Ohio State pulled away on the back of its Heisman Trophy favorite receiver.

Jeremiah Smith only had 93 yards receiving, but scored two touchdowns on his first two receptions of the game. He also made a highlight-reel grab, reaching behind him and snagging it out of the air with one hand to move the chains near the end of the second quarter.

Ohio State cruised in the second half after carrying a 31-10 lead into the final two quarters. While quarterback Julian Sayin turned the ball over twice, it didn’t make a difference, and the Buckeyes defeated the Terrapins, 45-16.

On Friday night, Iowa had to roll with backup quarterback Jeremy Hecklinski after starter Hank Brown suffered a shoulder injury against Ohio State the weekend prior. But no matter the quarterback, the Hawkeyes may finally have an offense.

Hecklinski played safe football, throwing three touchdown passes while not turning the ball over. This allowed running back Kamari Moulton to run wild on Washington’s defense, running it 26 times for 208 yards and two touchdowns, including a 56-yard rushing touchdown to end the first quarter.

Washington played a lot of the game without starting quarterback Demond Williams Jr., who left the game in the first half with a rib injury. Despite a third-quarter comeback effort led by Stanford transfer quarterback Elijah Brown, Iowa’s 24-point lead at the half was too much and the Hawkeyes ran away with the contest, 41-24, to stay in College Football Playoff contention.

Illinois, Purdue win middle of the pack battles

Illinois wide receiver Collin Dixon caught a touchdown pass at the start of the fourth quarter that gave the Fighting Illini a 31-17 lead. However, Michigan State scored two touchdowns, including a rushing touchdown from running back Jaziun Patterson with 1:17 left in regulation, to tie the game at 31 and sent it to overtime.

Illinois scored a touchdown on the first play of overtime and kicked the extra point to take a seven-point lead.

Michigan State responded with another touchdown from Patterson and opted to go for the win. Quarterback Alessio Milivojevic’s pass went incomplete and Illinois held on to defeat the Spartans, 38-37.

Purdue hosted a Minnesota team that was coming off one of its biggest home wins in recent history. However, the Golden Gophers’ momentum was completely halted in West Lafayette, Indiana.

The Boilermakers’ leading rusher, Fame Ijeboi, ran all over Minnesota’s defense, accounting for more points than the Golden Gophers scored in total. He ran it 31 times for 195 yards and three touchdowns, while the Boilermakers’ defense held star running back Darius Taylor to 15 yards rushing on seven carries.

Purdue’s 41-13 win over Minnesota keeps it near the top of the Big Ten standings with a 2-1 record in the conference.

title: Penn State women's soccer falls short against No. 13 Washington in scrappy matchup
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Battling in Seattle, Washington, at the Husky Soccer Stadium, Penn State and No.13 Washington faced off in a tough conference matchup.

The Huskies took a 1-0 victory over the Nittany Lions, pushing them to 11-1-2 for the season and 8-0-1 on their home field.

Both programs came into the matchup with immense momentum from previous gameplay. The blue and white came in at a steady seven games unbeaten, with the purple and gold maintaining a six-game win streak over their total seven games played at home.

Penn State and Washington both started in a 4-3-3 formation and came in hot with offensive pressure. The Nittany Lions notched three shots within the first five minutes of gameplay compared to the Huskies’ one.

Kayleigh Herr saw a lot of action within the first 15 minutes, continuously battling against the purple and gold front line and deflecting any attacking opportunities. The redshirt senior defender has seen 1,057 minutes of gameplay out of 1,080 in the season, leading not just within the blue and white backline but across the entire team.

Whistles were continuously blown as the physicality level began picking up in the first half of the match. Washington was called for three fouls to Penn State's two.

Coach Dambach tried challenging a play involving Bella Ayscue inside the Huskies’ 18 in the 23rd minute, hoping to be awarded a penalty but was rejected by the official.

In the 25th minute, Aubrey Kulpa created a dangerous scoring opportunity for the Nittany Lions in the first breakaway of the game, where the junior forward was ultimately challenged and stopped by Huskies’ Anna Menti just inside the 18-yard-box.

Washington orchestrated its first shot on goal in the 27th minute. Samiah Shell placed the ball in the bottom center of the net, but it was easily saved by Mackenzie Gress.

Penn State regained possession in the Huskies’ half, leading to Lily Boyden placing a dangerous cross into the box from the left side of Washington’s final third during the 36th minute. The ball bobbled around the six-yard box until Tanner Ijams gained control.

The tightly contested nature of the match continued up until the final whistle of the first half. Outside of the Nittany Lions’ 18, Taylor Thomas placed a rocket in the top left corner of the net that was punched over the crossbar by Gress.

Gress’ save ended the hard-fought half, leaving the blue and white and Washington equal heading into the last 45 minutes of gameplay at 0-0.

The blue and white opened up the second half fast, quickly making its way into the Huskies’ final third, creating their fifth corner kick opportunity of the game.

Washington regained possession of the ball and found Lucy Newlin in the center of the field. Emma Johnson pressured up on Newlin and the two got into a physical altercation in the 47th minute. A foul was called on Johnson, and both players received yellow cards for unsporting.

In the 55th minute, Newlin gained possession of the ball in Penn State’s final third and played a ball to Alex Buck. The junior forward took one touch to settle the ball down with her chest, turned to open up towards the net and shot a low-placed ball to the bottom left corner of the goal that Gress couldn’t get her hands on.

A VAR review was initiated for Buck’s goal, but the call ultimately remained the same, pushing the Huskies up 1-0 on the Nittany Lions.

The blue and white quickly responded to the Washington goal in the 58th minute with a shot on goal from Lily Boyden that was deflected by Ijams and found Kulpa’s feet. Kulpa placed the rebound in the back of the net but was called offside, erasing the goal.

As the end of the match approached, both squads fell into a back-and-forth rhythm as neither team created a clear advantage.

It wasn’t until the 77th minute that the second half saw more intense action after Herr and Buck made contact in the blue and white’s final third while battling for the ball, prompting Buck to appeal the collision for a penalty kick. The appeal was eventually denied.

The Nittany Lions made last-minute efforts in Washington’s final third but nothing stuck. The Huskies took the game 1-0.

title: Week 6 report card | Secondary silent, passing game renewed in Penn State’s loss to USC
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s first White Out game under Matt Campbell is in the books, and it didn’t go the way the Nittany Lions wanted it to.

While some aspects of Penn State’s game showed meaningful improvement, others completely unraveled as USC beat the Nittany Lions, 31-23, on Saturday night.

Here’s how I’d grade Penn State’s offensive and defensive performances in the White Out game.

Overall: C

Coaching staff: F

Throughout the game, Penn State’s coaching staff mismanaged the clock, and it led to using timeouts at inopportune times.

The Nittany Lions were slow to get set on offense, and Campbell was forced to use two timeouts in the first half to avoid delay of game penalties after late substitutions allowed USC to change out.

Additionally, Campbell was outcoached by Lincoln Riley at the turn of the half. He didn’t make the necessary adjustments needed to stay competitive in the football game, and it showed as the Trojans pulled away with two touchdowns in the second half compared to Penn State’s two field goals.

Offense: C+

Penn State was tied with USC, 17-17, at halftime behind a passing touchdown, rushing touchdown and a field goal. Rocco Becht returned to form with poise and more consistency in the passing game, but running backs Carson Hansen and James Peoples simply couldn’t generate meaningful yardage.

Passing game: B+

Becht said Matt Campbell didn’t truly know whether Penn State was a pass-first or run-first offense, and it contributed to the team's lack of identity cited in the wake of its loss to Northwestern.

Becht put in his best performance of the conference slate so far on Saturday, going 21-for-32 for 289 yards and a touchdown pass to tight end Andrew Rappleyea. He was more consistent, accurate with his deep throws and got his tight ends involved.

Becht started to skid in the second half, particularly on short passes, but it’s a step in the right direction, and he has the potential to continue improving as the Nittany Lions hunt for their first Big Ten win.

Run game: D-

Hansen and Peoples were the only two running backs to see the field, and while both showed flashes of what they’re capable of, there was very little to show for it.

The run game only averaged 2.2 yards per carry, with Hansen’s 28 yards on 14 carries the highest mark. Becht had three more carries than Peoples, and both each only gained 20 yards after a late sack took off yardage from the quarterback’s rushing statline.

Hansen’s gritty 3-yard touchdown is the only reason this grade isn’t an “F.”

Offensive line: C

The offensive line had better protection of Becht for most of the game, allowing him to get into a rhythm. However, Trevor Buhr allowed a sack on third-and-10 in the fourth quarter, and the offensive line as a whole couldn’t carve a path for the running backs.

Defense: D

Last week, Northwestern posterized Penn State’s run defense. However, USC flipped the script and exploited wide-open gaps in the secondary as quarterback Jayden Maiava threw for 301 yards and three touchdowns.

Penn State’s run defense limited the Trojans to only 4.4 yards per carry, which was a better showing, but still not ideal.

Pass rush: F

Penn State’s pass rush has been a problem all season, and things weren’t any different against USC.

Tony Rojas had the Nittany Lions’ only sack, and the defensive ends couldn’t make Maiava feel much discomfort despite cornerback Josiah Zayas and defensive end Yvan Kemajou posting quarterback hurries.

Maiava had all the time in the world to go through his progressions and air it out to his receivers. He distributed the ball extremely well, too, as six receivers made catches.

D’Anton Lynn only sent three pass rushers at times because he knew the ball would get out anyways, but that didn’t work either.

Defensive backfield: F

There’d been a lot of talk about how Penn State’s secondary is the best unit on the team, especially with Terry Smith’s cornerbacks playing at an elite level so far this year. For such a highly-touted group, it came as a shock to see them get lit up by USC’s offense.

When wide receiver Tanook Hines said he wasn’t worried about the secondary this week, he meant it. He and wide receiver Trent Mosley were wide open the entire game, as they consistently punished blown coverages and maneuvered well in space for big gains.

Penn State’s tackling problems resurfaced, as the Nittany Lions allowed 86 yards after catch.

Linebackers: C-

Rojas alone bumped this grade up from a “D.” He led the team with 10 tackles, a sack, a tackle for loss and a forced fumble that USC recovered regardless. By comparison, Kooper Ebel and Cael Brezina combined for only six tackles.

Lynn said he put a bigger emphasis on tackling in practice, but it didn’t show on Saturday.

Special teams: B

Kicker Ryan Barker was a perfect three-for-three on field goals with a long of 48 yards to tie the game, 17-17, at the end of the first half.

Punter Nathan Tiyce had two punts downed inside the 20-yard line, including one at the 10-yard line, but he missed an opportunity to pin the Trojans even closer to the goal line when he landed a boot in the end zone for touchback.

Wide receiver Amarion Jackson made a heads-up play on USC’s on-side kick to secure possession of the football, but it only amounted to a field goal as Penn State’s offense didn’t capitalize on the quality field position.

title: Stock up, stock down | Rocco Becht improves, secondary falls apart against USC
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State put up a stronger fight against USC in Saturday’s White Out than it did against Northwestern the week prior, but the result was the same as the Nittany Lions fell 31-23.

The Nittany Lions improved several aspects of their game, with better consistency from Rocco Becht to wide receiver Chase Sowell and tight end Andrew Rappleyea becoming reliable targets. However, the secondary fell apart and there were a few questionable coaching decisions.

Here’s whose stock went up and whose stock continued to fall in Week 6.

Stock up: Rocco Becht

Last week, Becht’s stock fell after he threw two interceptions against Northwestern, had several passes batted down at the line and was inconsistent with his throws, but Saturday’s game was a step in the right direction.

Becht threw for 289 yards with 65.6% accuracy, his best since Week 2 at Temple. He had just one touchdown, but recorded his first interception-free game in conference play and his deep ball was near-perfect throughout the contest.

Despite his much-needed improvement, Becht is still looking to grow, rightfully so. In Penn State’s second-to-last drive of the day, his throws to Sowell and Rappleyea were off-target, leading to a punt two plays later.

“Not good enough. I think for me, I’m a perfectionist, and I need to be better,” Becht said postgame. “I felt like we took a small step today, but we just got to be able to finish. We’re not there yet.”

Stock down: Secondary

USC wide receiver Tanook Hines was asked four days before the game what stood out about Penn State’s secondary. His response: “Nothing much for real.”

That was right on cue as Penn State’s elite secondary, who came into the game giving up the third-fewest yards in the nation, allowed quarterback Jayden Maiava to throw for 301 yards and three touchdowns.

Hines had the longest reception against Penn State, hauling in a 40-yard catch in part of his 82-yard, one-touchdown outing. Freshman wide receiver Trent Mosley tallied the most yardage for the Trojans, recording nine catches for 111 yards and a score.

Stock up: Chase Sowell, Andrew Rappleyea

Both Sowell and Rappleyea had their best performances of the season against USC.

In the absence of Koby Howard, Sowell has stepped up, and Becht found him on a pair of deep throws against USC. He picked up 47 yards on the second play of Penn State’s opening drive and had another 36-yard reception in the second quarter — both of which set up Nittany Lion touchdowns.

“He’s been amazing,” Becht said. “He’s always been that type of guy.”

While tight end Benjamin Brahmer has been Becht’s go-to receiving tight end through the first few weeks, Rappleyea was the one who contributed most on Saturday, leading the Nittany Lions with seven receptions for 63 yards and the team’s only receiving touchdown.

Stock down: Marcus Neal Jr.

While Penn State’s secondary as a whole struggled against USC, safety Marcus Neal Jr. never had the opportunity to see the field on defense.

“I think today was such a unique football game, and as we went into it, coverage was at a premium in terms of what was going to go on,” Matt Campbell said in response to Neal’s absence. “I think collectively, as we’re continuing to put this defense together, Marcus is a critical piece.”

Neal started the first four games of the year, but was the fourth safety to play against Northwestern, the first sign things were trending in the wrong direction for the Iowa State transfer.

Cornerback Zion Tracy played his first snaps this season as a safety. Campbell discussed his multiplicity earlier this year, but as a result, the cornerback room was short depth as well.

Stock down: Coaching decisions

Campbell faced a lot of backlash through the first two games of Big Ten play regarding his aggressiveness, but that was fixed as the Nittany Lions went five-for-five on fourth down against USC.

This time around, it was his poor time management decisions that came under scrutiny.

Twice Campbell was forced to use a timeout due to late substitution, allowing USC to wind down the rest of the play clock with its own substitution. Later in the game on fourth down, Campbell ushered his punt return squad on the field while the Trojans left Maiava and the offense on the line of scrimmage, resulting in another timeout

“I just didn't want to screw around with it,” Campbell said. “To be honest with you, I wanted to make sure we secured the football if we had the opportunity to do it at the end of the football game.”

There was another moment where Campbell didn’t realize the officials started the play clock, ultimately taking a timeout to avoid a delay of game.

title: Penn State pass rush still ‘a hair off’ after underwhelming performance against USC
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Tony Rojas sacked Jayden Maiava on the first drive, it seemed Penn State may have found a way to pressure the quarterback against USC.

However, the Nittany Lions didn’t tally another sack the rest of the game and only had two quarterback hurries on one of the Big Ten’s premier passers.

“I think it starts with looking at each person, looking at yourself, seeing where you can be better each week in practice,” defensive end Caleb Bacon said.

Defensive end Yvan Kemajou was the only defensive end to record a hurry. Cornerback Josiah Zayas was the other player to tally a hurry.

USC’s offense gave looks that Penn State’s defense hadn’t seen this season. With the skill at the receiver position, the Trojans used mostly passing packages, with the receivers spread out wide, forcing the Nittany Lions to switch up their defensive alignment.

“They got good skill guys out there, and we knew that,” Bacon said. “We really knew that coming in like this could be the best group of outside skill receivers that we were going to see.”

Even without an impactful pass rush, the defense still managed to put the Trojans into third-and-long situations, but it couldn’t put any pressure on Maiava and allowed the quarterback to sit in the pocket and let his talented receivers get open.

This included a third-and-7 play in the third quarter, where after multiple seconds in the pocket, Maiava rolled out and found wide receiver Tanook Hines for a 40-yard reception and a first down.

“I thought the biggest killers were some of the third down opportunities that we weren't able to finish on, and I think you're talking third-and-10, third-and-12, third-and-13 opportunities,” Matt Campbell said. “Getting them to those points and not finishing, those were the killers.”

Penn State tried to change things up to trick Maiava’s eyes, but it was to no avail, with the Trojan totaling 301 yards and three touchdowns on a 64% completion percentage.

It brought more guys up to the line, but didn’t send every defender in attempts to confuse the offensive line, with some edges dropping back into coverage. Campbell knows the defense will have to continue to find creativity, with the general pass rush unable to get home on a consistent basis.

“We're going to have to continue to find ways to get creative,” Campbell said. “I think that's an area for us, especially in those third-down situations. They had time to be able to make the plays and extend the play.”

The defense chose to rush three more often than the typical four in hopes of giving USC’s offense different looks to try to throw off momentum, but it rarely resulted in any pressure on Maiava, giving one of the best quarterbacks in the Big Ten ample time to throw.

“How many different ways could we disguise coverage, especially post snap, especially when it got under 15 seconds on the shot clock?” Campbell said. “I think there was some thought process for us to be able to do that. There were moments where it put us in some advantageous situations.”

Bacon feels the defense is “a hair off in a lot of different places,” which gives the unit some hope that it can start to find more success.

“Football's a game of inches, so you've got to just find that inch that you're just a little bit off, and just a little tweak there could make the whole entire change,” Bacon said.

The defensive line will continue to go back to the film room, and find ways to create pressure in the more conventional way, while D’Anton Lynn and Campbell look to find more creativity in other ways.

“There's so much to pass rush that I think you gotta look at,” Bacon said. “So I think this week for sure, as an edge and our group of edges and DTs, I think we definitely just look at the film, look where we're missing the mark.”

title: No. 18 Penn State women’s volleyball completes sweep of No. 20 Washington
author: Jimmy Blair | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 18 Penn State wrapped up its weekend slate with a home matchup against the No. 20 Washington Huskies on Sunday.

The Nittany Lions continued their strong form, sweeping the ranked Huskies at home.

Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley opened the first set with an alignment consisting of blockers Kendall Northern and Gabrielle Nichols, Kennedy Martin, and Whitney Launstein, Alexis Stucky, and defensive specialist Ava Falduto.

Stucky got the match started with a service ace, but committed a service error right after. Nichols then got a pair of kills off of Launstein serves, as the blue and white established control of the net early.

Both sides continued to trade blows until Penn State went on a 13-of-15-point run in the middle of the first set to take a commanding lead. The run was highlighted by blocks from Martin and Nichols, with Haley Burgdorf adding a pair of kills.

Launstein capped off a strong first-set performance with a powerful shot from the left-hand side that was deflected out by the Huskies, giving the blue and white a win in the first set, 25-14.

To begin the second set, Launstein picked right where she left off, taking a commanding opening point. The Nittany Lions kept the momentum going, with Washington committing two attack errors and putting Penn State up 5-0 early in the second set.

The Huskies responded by taking the next three points, with Hayden Connor recording two block assists. Washington slowly started regaining their presence in front of the net, as Penn State began having more trouble getting shots past Washington blockers.

With the second set tied at eight, both squads began trading blows, not giving the other side an inch. Northern got a kill off a Stucky assist, which began a run for the Nittany Lions again, highlighted by a pair of kills from Nichols.

A trio of attack errors committed by Huskies gave the blue and white an 18-12 lead, and the Nittany Lions looked to close out the set and take a two-set lead.

Julia Hunt got three kills for the Huskies late in the set to keep the Huskies in it. Northern did it all for the blue and white late in the set, getting a kill and a block assist to put the squad within a point of claiming set two.

A service error by Andrea Fabikovicová ended the second set, giving the blue and white a commanding two-set cushion heading into the third.

Penn State wanted to come into the third set swinging, not giving Washington any hope of a comeback. A Husky attack error followed by Martin and Launstein kills gave the squad a quick 3-0 start. Martin didn't stop there and added another kill, followed by two service aces from Launstein.

The Huskies showed no quit as the third set continued, but the Nittany Lions kept the pressure up, consistently protecting their early lead. A kill from Nichols put the blue and white up 15-11 halfway through.

As the third set continued, the blue and white kept shooting itself in the foot with service errors and attack errors. However, they stayed in front of the net and managed a 20-19 lead near the end of the set.

Kennedy Martin sent a beautiful lob over the net past the Huskies, giving Penn State a crucial two-point cushion. Martin answered right back with a laser over the net, making it her 14th kill of the match and pushing the score to 23-20.

Julia Hunt responded for the Huskies with a kill in a long rally. Burgdorf's kill gave Penn State a match point. Launstein almost dotted the Huskies on the back left corner but went barely out-of-bounds.

Kendall Northern denied the Huskies at the net, closing out the sweep for the Nittany Lions.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will travel across the country for a matchup against UCLA at 10 p.m. Friday.

title: Penn State field hockey defeats Kent State, dominates with penalty corners
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 1-0 overtime win over the Michigan State Spartans on Friday, Penn State field hockey looked to extend its winning streak to five games when it faced the Kent State Golden Flashes in Ohio on Sunday.

Excluding their matchup with Kent State, the Nittany Lions will play every remaining regular season game in 2026 against a Big Ten conference opponent. The Nittany Lions closed out the nonconference slate with a strong 3-0 win.

After two straight extra-time contests, the blue and white needed to find ways to gain the advantage in regulation.

In the opening minutes, Penn State played several balls into the Golden Flashes' half, already pressuring the opposing defense.

The Nittany Lions earned their first penalty corner six minutes into the first half. Sophomore forward Joji Purdy's shot was blocked wide by Kent State graduate goalkeeper Michaela Skinner.

The next several plays for both teams were full of back-and-forth interplay and solid ball movement.

Sophomore forward Laura Pyle's shot was blocked wide nine minutes into the contest and the score remained 0-0.

The Golden Flashes were given their first penalty corner soon after. Graduate midfielder Sienna Dunn blocked the shot from Kent State and the score remained even.

The second blue and white penalty corner resulted in sophomore defensive back Cooper Cutchin's shot being blocked again by Skinner to end the first quarter.

Both teams were locked in a 0-0 draw after the opening period.

Penn State began the second quarter with a quick strike into the Kent State circle, and Skinner came up big with another save.

The Nittany Lions were given another penalty corner within the first minute of the second quarter. Cutchins was unable to convert and another corner was awarded.

The Golden Flashes' defense held firm, and officials awarded a fifth corner.

Skinner made another save, earning a sixth corner.

After four straight corners, Penn State took the early 1-0 lead from a goal by junior forward Ella Gaitan just over two minutes into the second period, assisted by Dunn and senior midfielder Natalie Freeman.

Kent State began to put tighter pressure on the blue and white backline as they looked to tie it up in the minutes that followed.

However, the Golden Flash attack was to no avail as Penn State took the 2-0 first-half lead from a goal by sophomore midfielder Olivia Marthins just over five minutes into the second quarter, assisted by freshman forward Chloe D'Hage.

Kent State continued their offensive pressure, but the Nittany Lions were able to keep the Golden Flashes at bay with key backline positioning.

With just under two minutes remaining in the first half, Penn State maintained its defensive pressure and limited Kent State to minimal scoring chances, keeping the 2-0 lead going into halftime.

Graduate midfielder Camryn Standish's shot proved unsuccessful, but it earned a seventh penalty corner two minutes into the third quarter.

The Golden Flashes defense held firm and stopped the Nittany Lions from extending their lead.

The Penn State pressure forced an eighth penalty corner four minutes in, but Skinner's eighth save stopped the blue and white attack once again.

Kent State earned its second penalty corner with 9 minutes remaining in the third quarter. Penn State's solid defense continued, and they kept the two-score lead.

The Nittany Lions kept up the pressure in the Golden Flash defensive half, forcing Kent State to play on the back foot.

Kent State began to ramp up the aggressiveness as its need to make it a one-score game increased late in the third period.

Redshirt freshman forward Hope Russo's shot proved unsuccessful and the Nittany Lion advantage remained at two goals.

The third quarter ended with Penn State still up 2-0 heading into the final 15 minutes of regulation.

Pyle's shot to start the fourth was blocked, as the Golden Flashes held firm.

Penn State earned a ninth penalty corner opportunity with just over three minutes left in the final quarter.

Kent State came up with another key stop, keeping their penalty corner defense strong, a continuous theme for them all game long.

Marthin's shot was deflected wide, forcing the game's 10th penalty opportunity for the Nittany Lions with 11 minutes remaining in regulation.

Skinner's two key saves kept the score 2-0, and Penn State couldn't convert yet again.

Freshman forward Chloe D'Hage scored Penn State's third goal of the afternoon off a shot from just inside the scoring circle with just under 9 minutes remaining.

Both teams traded positions over the next several minutes, with ball movement and offensive intensity increasing exponentially.

Ultimately, Penn State came away with a 3-0 win over the Golden Flashes in regulation.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will now prepare to face the Ohio State Buckeyes on Friday at 5 p.m. in Happy Valley.

title: 'He’s been amazing' | WR Chase Sowell provides spark for Penn State's offense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
On Penn State’s second offensive play of the day, Rocco Becht connected with wide receiver Chase Sowell for a 47-yard catch, helping set up an early touchdown.

Sowell went on to have the best performance among Penn State’s wide receivers against USC, recording four receptions for 95 yards.

“Having explosive plays in the passing game is huge, and we haven’t had those in a while,” Becht said postgame. “It was great to see that tonight.”

Over the past three weeks, Sowell has been one of the players stepping up in the wake of Koby Howard’s absence with his three best games coming in the last three Big Ten contests.

Although he failed to find the end zone, Sowell’s recent stretch has seen him emerge as Penn State’s most reliable receiving option at the moment.

“He’s been amazing,” Becht said. “He’s always been that type of guy. He’s made huge steps since last year in a leadership role, in the player role, and he’s matured so much. I’m excited for that connection to get better.”

That leadership has become increasingly important for Penn State’s receiving corps as it looks to find consistency amid the team’s offensive struggles.

Following wide receiver Brett Eskildsen’s costly late-game fumble, Sowell drew on his own experiences to encourage his teammate, recalling a similar play during his time at East Carolina.

“Just got to tell them like ‘Hey, got to keep going,’” Sowell said. “You’re doing what you need to be doing, and sometimes they make a good play, and sometimes it’s just football.”

For Sowell, maintaining that confidence requires a consistent approach, regardless of the outcome on the field. He emphasized that preparation throughout the week is essential to building the confidence needed to make plays in critical moments.

“You have to rep it. You have to practice it. You gotta put yourself in those positions to have the confidence to make the plays,” Sowell said.

While Sowell’s leadership has grown, his contributions on the field were most evident early in the game. His production slowed considerably after he briefly exited with an apparent lower-leg injury with a minute remaining in the half.

Sowell described the injury as “nothing crazy,” saying he banged his shin off an opposing player.

“It’s almost like you get hit with a scooter, like you get hit with Razor scooters,” Sowell said. “But yeah, I was fine. Got to halftime, checked it out, made the series. I was good.”

After halftime, Sowell was targeted just once, but Becht’s pass was batted down before reaching him.

Despite the loss, Sowell’s explosive plays provided a bright spot for Penn State's offense. For the redshirt senior, the opportunity to contribute in front of a record-breaking White Out crowd made the night even more memorable.

Growing up outside of Houston, Sowell was accustomed to big crowds from baseball. After stops at Colorado, East Carolina and Iowa State, Sowell had never experienced an atmosphere quite like the White Out.

“I didn't even think about playing in games like this,” Sowell said. “Just being able to represent a university this great and fans that come out and show that much support is amazing.”

title: Penn State’s record-setting White Out was ‘the most crazy feeling’ despite loss to USC
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When “Mo Bamba” by Sheck Wes blared over the loudspeaker, a record-setting crowd shook Beaver Stadium to its core. A hostile choir of eager Penn State fans screamed the song before ditching words to make as much noise as possible in an attempt to throw USC off its game.

That’s the expected volume of a White Out game, but this iteration saw its fair share of firsts on Saturday despite the Trojans defeating the Nittany Lions 31-23.

It was the first White Out game under Campbell, who brought a host of players with him from Iowa State, all of whom got to debut playing in the conditions. 114,419 fans piled into Beaver Stadium, setting the program attendance record, aided by the additional seats offered by the newly constructed west side bleachers.

“It was an unbelievable atmosphere,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “It was one of the most impressive environments that I've been able to coach in or be a part of.”

Campbell voiced his frustration with not being able to deliver a favorable result to the crowd.

He made a similar statement after Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin in the Homecoming game, but the energy brought by the fans had him even more disappointed his team couldn’t get the job done.

“I think the most disappointing part for me is that we can't give this incredible fan base that has shown out,” Campbell said. “We can't give them the result that they deserve, but the reality is we will, and we will find a pathway forward.”

Penn State had been on a two-game skid heading into the White Out game, and Rocco Becht was overjoyed how the fans showed up to support the team in such a manner despite how the season has gone so far.

“Props to all those people, and I appreciate them,” Becht said. “We need all their support as much as we can get for this rest of the season because I know this team's not done. God works in mysterious ways, and that's what we're telling each other right now. We're going to continue to go to work.”

For wide receiver Chase Sowell, he never imagined himself playing in a game like this. He said the crowd noise created the “most crazy feeling.”

“That first snap, first play, the ground was literally shaking,” Sowell said postgame. “Water bottles were shaking.”

Sowell has compared Beaver Stadium to its video game counterpart in EA College Football 27 on multiple occasions, and he said the White Out atmosphere lived up to the expectations.

“Stadium Pulse was on 100,” Sowell said. “It's literally just like the video game. We’ve got a great fanbase. They give us that extra oomph, especially going into like the fourth quarter, third quarter, seeing them around is just like an extra energy bar. The White Out was just different, so it was definitely fun.”

Kicker Ryan Barker said the best part about this particular White Out was seeing the transfers and freshmen experience the atmosphere for the first time.

He and other returning Nittany Lions briefed the newcomers on what to expect Saturday, and Barker said it was great to see them finally experience it, bringing back fond memories.

“I was kind of reliving my first White Out again through the eyes of everyone else,” Barker said.

title: Penn State sees growth offensively, but couldn’t finish in loss to USC
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The result didn’t change from the first two Big Ten games, but the growth in Saturday’s loss to USC pushed the Nittany Lions in a forward direction for the second half of the season.

The Nittany Lions made significant strides in most facets of the game, playing in a much more competitive game compared to its blowout loss to Northwestern in the previous week.

“I would just say tonight, I think we made the right growth,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “I thought we played in a much different rhythm tonight in the football game.”

Rhythm is something Campbell has harped on the last two weeks, saying his team hadn’t fully found it in the first two Big Ten games. Saturday’s loss was different, as the offense kept up with USC’s through a majority of the game.

Despite the loss, the unit garnered the momentum it had been looking for in the past six quarters, scoring more points in the first half than it had in either of the last two games.

“I think we definitely found a rhythm, and that's credit to coach (Taylor Mouser) and credit to Rocco,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “I think they did a great job of staying within the game plan, not trying to force anything, taking what they give us. So yeah, I definitely think we took a step forward.”

Although the run game didn’t generate much with only 2.2 yards per carry, it was utilized to set up the pass game, which Penn State had a lot more success with than the previous week.

The ability to use the run game to find success through the air added to the complexity of Penn State’s offense and kept it in the flow of the game.

“When you talk about the ability to use the run game to set up the pass game, play action passing, movement passing, I think all those things were realities tonight,” Campbell said.

Rocco Becht recognized the team’s ability to show fight in a game where the Trojans continued to throw punches in their pass game.

The offensive response to USC’s scores was part of the growth Campbell saw, as it kept the Nittany Lions in contention throughout the duration of the game.

“I felt like we just kept playing no matter what happened,” Becht said. “We went down 7-0 early and we were able to drive the ball right down the field and we did it again.”

Becht led the offense to three scoring drives in the first half, matching USC en route to a 17-17 halftime score. That in itself was an improvement from the week prior, where Northwestern led 24-7 at the half and the offense couldn’t respond to the Wildcats’ punches.

“I think the tenacity and the conviction that we had today was a lot better,” Becht said. “But we just got to be able to finish the games and we're not doing that right now.”

The strides the Nittany Lions made didn’t change the result of the game, however, with the team coming up short in the fourth quarter on both sides of the ball. That part of the game is what stood out to the players.

The Nittany Lions made progress but couldn’t put it all together to come out victorious.

“Still got a long way to go,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said. “I honestly feel like we had a great week of preparation. Just came up short.”

Penn State took a step it hadn’t taken in almost two games, finding momentum and competing with the No. 19 team in the country. It didn’t get the result it wanted on the scoreboard, but the play on the field was more of the production from the first three games of the season rather than the first two games of conference play.

“I did think there were some moments tonight where we grew a lot closer to the team that we want to be than where we were, especially last week,” Campbell said.

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's loss to USC
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A record-setting crowd of 114,419 fans packed in Beaver Stadium on Saturday night as Penn State returned home to face No. 19 USC in the Nittany Lions’ first White Out game under Matt Campbell.

While the game was tied, 17-17, at halftime, the Trojans continued to exploit Penn State’s failing secondary and ran away with a 31-23 victory. The Nittany Lions fell to 3-3 overall and 0-3 in the Big Ten while USC improved to 6-1 overall and 3-1 in the conference.

Here are three takeaways from Penn State’s loss to USC.

Penn State’s identity is a pass-first team

Campbell said Tuesday he felt his team “lacked an identity.” Rocco Becht said Campbell didn’t quite know whether the offense was pass-first or run-first.

That question was answered on Saturday, as Becht came out of the gates swinging with an offense closely mirroring how the team played in the nonconference schedule. Becht went 21-for-32 for 289 passing yards with a touchdown.

“I thought Rocco certainly gave us every opportunity in the football game to be successful,” Campbell said postgame. “He found a rhythm that we want to play in, and that we need to continue to move forward in for sure.”

Penn State’s second play of the game was a 47-yard completion to wide receiver Chase Sowell. But unlike his poor performance against Northwestern, Becht continued to find success in the passing game, particularly utilizing his deep ball and looked like his early-season self, showing poise in the pocket and delivering accurate and timely passes.

A few of the incompletions weren’t on him, either, as both running back James Peoples and Rappleyea dropped open checkdown passes. Becht did sail a throw through the back of the end zone that was intended for tight end Benjamin Brahmer in the fourth quarter, so it wasn’t all perfect through the air.

“Not good enough. I think for me, like I've always said, I'm a perfectionist, and I need to be better,” Becht said. “I felt like we took a small step today, but we just got to be able to finish.”

There was a bigger emphasis on the tight end room as well, primarily coming from Rappleyea, who had the most targets and Penn State’s only receiving touchdown.

Saturday’s offensive performance showed Penn State can be explosive even without star wide receiver Koby Howard, as Sowell finished with 95 yards while seven players had a catch.

Becht’s legs open new possibilities

Becht’s ability to run the football was nowhere to be found through the first five weeks of the season. But he unlocked that piece of his game in front of the largest crowd in Beaver Stadium history, finishing the game with 20 yards on 10 carries.

Penn State’s offensive line gave Becht the time and space to rush up the middle, and his brief instances of success were crucial on fourth down specifically, as he twice called his own number to move the chains.

“He is a good runner and he can make plays with his legs,” running back Carson Hansen said. “We have seen him do it in the past.”

One such run was a 10-yard gain on a fourth-and-3 in the dying moments of the second quarter. He recognized the advancing Trojan defense and sprinted to the right for the first down, running out of bounds with three seconds on the clock. The gain paved the way for kicker Ryan Barker to tie the game before the half with a 48-yard field goal.

He wasn’t just mobile beyond the line of scrimmage. Becht demonstrated a key ability to throw on the run on play action, headlined by an impressive 37-yard completion to Sowell in the second quarter.

Utilizing Becht’s legs in the offense proved how effective Penn State’s ground game can be when it’s not just the running backs carrying the ball. Should the running backs establish a stronger run game, Becht’s mobility adds an extra layer for opposing defenses to consider when scouting the Nittany Lions.

Secondary falls apart

Penn State’s secondary — particularly the cornerbacks — have been the team’s best unit so far this season. USC broke that trend as quarterback Jayden Maiava threw for 301 yards and three touchdowns.

The run defense, which was the problem against Northwestern, only allowed 129 yards by comparison.

Wide receivers Trent Mosley and Tanook Hines were left wide open on nearly every play, despite Penn State’s pass rush sometimes only sending three rushers. Additionally, the Trojans had 86 yards after catch as the Nittany Lions once again struggled to tackle at an elite level.

“(Maiava’s) a super talented passer,” defensive end Caleb Bacon said. “Struggled a little bit there to keep (the passing game) contained because we knew he can make those throws outside the pocket on the move and hit open receivers. We really knew that coming in. This could be the best group of outside skill receivers that we were going to see.”

D’Anton Lynn spoke extensively about Penn State’s poor tackling at Northwestern, and he increased the number of tackling drills at practice this week in hopes of fixing that. However, the Nittany Lions, except for Tony Rojas, once again struggled to tackle at some points.

Penn State’s tackling is a serious issue, more now than ever, as the secondary wasn’t able to threaten USC’s receivers.
