title: ‘Get our swagger back’ | Penn State battles with adversity after 2 straight losses
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht has lost many football games throughout his career. He had back-to-back losses in 2024 and four straight losses in 2025, and now, he’s fallen short in this year’s first two Big Ten games.

But in the past, Becht has bounced back from these losing stretches, winning the remaining games each season. He’s carrying that same mindset right now.

“For me, it's digging back to that 2024 season,” Becht said Tuesday. “What did I do? What did I change to get out of that slump? And I think for me, it was coming to work every single day with a positive attitude.”

Penn State’s next chance to right the ship is the White Out game against No. 19 USC, which is the fourth-highest ranked Big Ten team. On the other hand, the Nittany Lions are coming off a 34-13 loss to Northwestern and are one of the seven teams with an 0-2 record in conference play.

Over the last six quarters of play, the Nittany Lions have struggled in all aspects. The offense has failed to generate significant yardage, specifically on the ground, the defense gave up 413 rushing yards against Northwestern and even kicker Ryan Barker missed a field goal.

While the team isn’t where it wants to be performance-wise, it’s stayed true to its core philosophies and is attempting to grow each week with a positive mindset.

“I went in there with positive vibes throughout the whole facility, and I think that just brings everybody up,” Becht said. “Whatever I’m doing, that’s what the whole team is going to be doing, and so that’s how I carry myself every single day. I’m just going to continue to do what I do and believe what I believe.”

But Becht isn’t the only one who’s faced adversity before. The Nittany Lions lost six straight games last year before ending the year winning five straight. More than 50 of those players are back on this year’s squad and facing similar adversity.

“(I’ve) definitely learned some things about our team last year and about myself individually,” right guard Cooper Cousins said. “I see the capabilities that this squad has. I see how hard everybody works. I see everybody attacking. This team’s hungry to go out there and compete for the best fans.”

Following last week’s loss to Northwestern, several players talked about how the practices were less physical due to the short week. That may not have been the best option, as they then said the game wasn’t as physical as they hoped with several players missing tackles.

This Tuesday, the players said they had one of the most physical practices in a long time, flushing the loss and moving forward.

“No matter what adversity you’re going through, whatever hard times you’re going through, you can’t have a poor me mentality,” Cousins said. “You have to grab your lunch pail and go back to work.”

While the Nittany Lions are facing their first sustained bout of adversity this year, it hasn’t shocked them. They knew before the season this would happen at some point, but they’re now working to fight through it.

“There’s going to be adversity that happens every season, it’s not going to be a Cinderella story,” Cousins said. “I think Rocco has done a really great job and phenomenal job getting us all together.”

With seven more conference games on the horizon, Becht knows the team needs to gain its confidence back from earlier this season because they have the potential to be great.

“I think we just have to get our swagger back and walk around like we're the best person at that position,” Becht said. “We just got to be able to have fun and bring that swagger back.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell says his team 'lacks an identity'
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Matt Campbell took the podium at Beaver Stadium on Tuesday after Penn State’s loss to Northwestern. The Nittany Lions are headed into their first White Out game under Campbell at 7:30 p.m. Saturday.

Campbell discussed the team’s lack of a real identity, offensive struggles across the board and gave an update on wide receiver Koby Howard.

Here’s more of what he said.

Team identity

Campbell expressed his frustration regarding the lack of a team identity. He noted Penn State has gone through difficult times in the past and has managed to come back stronger, and while he has confidence in his players and coaching staff, the team “isn’t where it needs to be.”

“The reality of it is, we lack an identity,” Campbell said. “We lack who we want to be and where we need to be.”

He said the team lacks identity on offense, defense and in special teams while not playing to the standard they set for themselves. To improve the culture, he said facing adversity is crucial, something they’re going through right now.

Campbell said the team wasn’t where it needed to be after the Buffalo game, so he’s not surprised by the void in identity at this point because the program is newly growing into it in the first season under his leadership.

“You're trying to mold the culture together, and it's a growth process,” Campbell said. “We have to be better, and it starts with my leadership of making sure we get better. But I have great belief in the humans that we have, and we're just not there right now.”

Rocco Becht, offensive concerns

Rocco Becht has been inconsistent in Big Ten action with just one passing touchdown and three interceptions the past two contests. Campbell noted how when the offense struggles, it can “put a spotlight” on the quarterback’s mistakes.

Although Campbell said Becht needs to be better, he was quick to defend his quarterback and said the entire offensive unit around him needs to be more consistent.

“We need to be better with the other 10 people around him too,” Campbell said. “We need to be better in our pass protection at times, we certainly need to be better in terms of our run game. So we can get him into a rhythm, so he can play with great consistency. We haven't been able to do that, and obviously that is frustrating.”

Campbell noted how the Big Ten is a physical conference, but downplayed the switch from the Big 12. He’s played against Big Ten opponents during his time at Iowa State, and said the physicality of the conference is not the primary concern at this stage.

“Where we're at is trying to build a culture, schemes and foundations, “ Campbell said. “So I think the easy thing to say is, ‘is it a physical problem? Is it a lack of physicality?’ I think some of that shows up when you're so inconsistent in some of the detailed things it takes to play good football.”

Update on Howard

Campbell said Howard is still “a couple weeks away” from his return to the field despite Howard implying he’d be back against Michigan on Oct. 17 via his Instagram story a few weeks ago.

Not having him has added to the difficulties in the passing game, as Campbell said Howard was the player who executed against opponents’ top defenders, a role Chase Sowell is charged with in Howard’s absence.

“One thing that Koby brought was consistency,” Campbell said. “He was the guy that was consistently executing. Koby was the guy that was creating matchups.”

Campbell alluded to how many other players were dealing with offseason surgeries, which could be affecting their play now, and the team needs to have a next-man-up mentality in the wake of injuries such as Howard’s. He said this applies across the board, not limited to the wide receiver room.

“There is a little bit of a process of those guys getting back to where we need them to play with the physicality and the detail we need them to play,” Campbell said. “Those aren't excuses, and that happens in every team in the country. We have to make sure simplicity equals velocity.”

title: Penn State notebook | DC D'Anton Lynn reflects on poor performance from his run defense
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Three days after Penn State’s defense allowed 506 yards to Northwestern, D’Anton Lynn took the podium in Beaver Stadium ahead of the Nittany Lions’ White Out against USC.

Lynn discussed the team’s struggles against the Wildcats on Friday night, the upcoming matchup against his former team and more.

Here’s a look at what he had to say.

Struggles in Evanston

The run game was the most glaring issue in the loss to Northwestern, as Penn State allowed 413 yards on the ground. After watching the film, Lynn said the line of scrimmage was the biggest weakness.

“I don’t know if we won the line of scrimmage once,” Lynn said. “We didn't lose every time, but we didn't win at all.”

As the run defense struggled, Penn State gave up multiple runs of over 30 yards. Several of those came as the result of missed tackles.

Despite those misses, Lynn expressed his confidence in his defense and his linebackers, saying “everyone has done a lot of good things.”

“I would just say the biggest thing is just consistency,” Lynn said. “Consistency in our fits and tackling.”

While the Nittany Lions couldn’t come back and find an answer against the Wildcats, Lynn focused on what it takes to move forward and build success.

“If we have to move guys around, we have to get the different looks,” Lynn said. “We have to put guys in different spots, getting different looks, but put those guys in position to win.”

USC reunion

Lynn spent the 2024-25 seasons at USC before coming to Happy Valley, where he coached against starting quarterback Jayden Maiava during practice.

With the Trojans coming to Beaver Stadium on Saturday, Lynn has experience against Maiava and what he presents offensively. However, coach Lincoln Riley’s playstyle has its difficulties as well.

“He doesn’t have a playbook, he just has plays, and he’s gonna do what his guys do best,” Lynn said. “There's times where he'll present things, and it's like, man, you just don't have an answer for us. You have to keep them guessing.”

The Trojans are coming off a close victory against Washington and are the first top-25 team the Nittany Lions will face this year. Playing against one of the top programs in the Big Ten, Lynn prioritized going back to some of the basics to compete against USC.

“We need to be great on third down,” Lynn said. “We need to be great in the red zone, and we need to stop the run and then don't give them chunk plays.”

Coaching location

Through the first four games of the season, Lynn coached from the booth — a decision that faced a lot of contemplation during fall camp. Against the Wildcats, Lynn started the game in the booth, but moved onto the sidelines after halftime.

“It was just hard to watch from up top,” Lynn said. “Just not being down there with the guys and being able to talk to them, look them in the eye. You don't know what's going on down there, so it just felt better being down there while all that was going on.”

While he made that switch in the second half of Friday’s game, he hasn’t made a decision yet on this weekend’s location, but recognized the benefits of being on the field.

“I just felt better being down there, just making sure, regardless of what the circumstances are, regardless of what's going on on defense, regardless of what's going on on offense,” Lynn said. “When we go out there we have to have the same mentality.”

title: Penn State professors examine concerns about AI's rapid development
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has grown by leaps since ChatGPT’s 2022 launch, leading to concerns that its development is beginning to outpace people’s ability to control it.

These concerns are often exemplified by incidents where AI models break out of their test environments and hack parts of the internet after gaining access to it. This was the case in July, when OpenAI’s models escaped containment during a security test and managed to hack into the AI startup Hugging Face.

This incident has been followed by a series of other hacks by AI models, including successful and unsuccessful breaches into government websites belonging to Canada, Australia and the United States. The Federal Trade Commission has since launched an investigation into the matter.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier,” focused on the Hugging Face hack and its ramifications for global AI development. He presented a plan in the essay to slow its progress both in the U.S. and potentially throughout the world.

He wrote that actions need to be taken to verify safety practices and report incidents within AI companies, including embedding evaluators with “employee-like access.” And he wrote about the need to limit AI’s ability to create the next generation of itself in a phenomenon called recursive self-improvement.

Alan Wagner, an aerospace engineering associate professor whose research and interests include AI and machine learning, said he had heard “bits and pieces” of some of the ideas presented in Amodei’s essay. Amodei’s position as Anthropic’s CEO, Wagner said, also makes him well-suited to speak on concerns within the industry.

Wagner is skeptical about whether some of the actions Amodei presented warrant a complete pause at all. He also said he was not convinced a pause of American AI development will cause other countries, like China, to follow suit, out of fear they will be outcompeted in the race for more powerful AI models.

“There's no way, really, to pause AI research globally. And it sort of leaves us in a situation where these things are gonna advance until something bad does happen because of both national competition and international competition,” Wagner said.

Wagner said he is also concerned having evaluators be treated as employees within the companies they are meant to keep in check will cause them to eventually work to protect a company’s interests with AI development over ensuring it is being done safely and in compliance with established policies.

He also said he viewed Amodei’s description of the threats posed by recursive self-improvement in his essay as being too vague and expressed a desire to learn more about why Amodei focused on this aspect of the dangers of rogue AI.

“Presumably, the development of super intelligent AI is not just a matter of having the agent write code: it’s algorithmic development; it's mathematical advances; possibly, it's just scaling, but recursive self-improvement is really not going to improve those things,” Wagner said. “An agent's not gonna go to the Library of Congress and copy books physically, so I'm not sure that these agents are going to be able to scale or improve.”

Wagner also said he predicts AI companies will form an agreement among them to set the terms of a development pause before one ever takes place.

Such negotiations between American AI companies may be possible as Sam Altman and Elon Musk, the CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX respectively, have been reported to have joined Amodei in calling for a “coordinated slowdown” of artificial intelligence development.

Brian Lennon, a professor of English and comparative literature who specializes in topics related to AI, said he found it hard for him to determine whether Altman and Musk’s statements are completely genuine, given the investments both have made into artificial intelligence infrastructure, such as data centers.

He also said some may interpret Altman and Musk’s comments more cynically by believing they are attempting to convince the U.S. government to enact regulations that would allow their companies to dominate the AI industry by putting them in a position where they are considered “too big to fail.”

Amodei’s own calls for the pacing of AI development also come at a time when Anthropic is expected to go public sometime in November, with investors expecting the company to be valued at between $1.8 to $2 trillion.

“I don't take the entirely cynical position that this is all purely self interest. THAT’S likely to be a strong ingredient of anything involving as much wealth as this industry right now,” Lennon, 55, of State College, Pa. said. “Whatever you think of (Altman and Musk) as people, they're both in charge of an intellectually very challenging situation, so you have to assume that there's some good faith in there somewhere as well.”

Though government action will be required for regulating the long-term development of artificial intelligence, he said, he’s unsure whether this will be enacted under the Trump administration, since its policy on the matter so far has been inconsistent.

Several members of Congress have joined with tech leaders in calling for enacting AI regulations. President Donald Trump has remained resistant to these demands and said all that’s needed to regulate AI development is a “strong and smart president.”

This statement stands in contrast to Trump’s Saturday appointment of National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to become the administration’s “AI Czar;” he’ll develop regulations and safety standards for AI development.

Lennon also pointed to the declaration of Anthropic as a supply chain risk following the collapse of a 2025 contract with the Department of Defense for use of the company’s AI models as another instance when the Trump administration was unusually hands-on in regulating the industry.

Patrick Plaisance, the Don W. Davis professor in ethics for the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, said concerns of human control over AI do deserve attention, but they shouldn’t distract from issues stemming from the social, mental and cognitive health impacts of prolonged chatbot usage — which Plaisance has spent some time researching.

Plaisance said AI’s impact on peoples' health, especially socially and mentally, mirrors those seen with the extended use of social media, another industry which received little government regulation in its early stages.

He said the only way to prevent this from happening again with artificial intelligence is through the pressuring of AI companies to enact guardrails. This could be a similar path to what led Meta agree to pay a $17 billion settlement and implement stronger child safety features on Instagram and Facebook after a federal lawsuit filed for these platforms’ addictive effects on children, Plaisance added.

“The single metric of success for chatbots really comes down to engagement. That's all the companies care about, is keeping your eyeballs there,” Plaisance said. “That was the same thing that we allowed to be the metric of success for social media platforms, and we now know the harms that stem from that kind of mindset. It took us 15 to 20 years, and I hope it doesn't take us another 15 or 20 years to realize that we have to grapple with these similar moral questions with AI assistants.”

title: 23 cases of sexual misconduct have been reported to university police since Aug. 19. Penn State has sent no Timely Warnings
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Content warning: This article contains mention of sexual assault. Resources and support are available through Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services.

Since Aug. 19, 23 cases of sexual misconduct have been reported to University Police and Public Safety (UPPS), according to its Daily Crime Log. These reports include incidents of sexual assault and harassment listed under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA).

These reports occurred during the “Red Zone,” a period from the start of the fall semester to Thanksgiving break where more than 50% of sexual assaults are reported on college campuses.

In the past, Penn State has issued Timely Warnings to alert the community of certain crimes reported to UPPS, especially for cases involving sexual misconduct and sexual assault.

However, the university has not issued a Timely Warning for University Park since Feb. 19, 2025, which was for two separate hazing incidents at both on and off-campus student organizations.

The last Timely Warning for a sexual offense was Nov. 19, 2024.

In 2024, 10 Timely Warnings were sent, eight of which were sexual offenses.

In 2023, 11 Timely warnings were sent, six of which were for sexual offenses and one for stalking under the VAWA.

In 2022, 15 Timely Warnings were sent, 13 of which were for sexual offenses and one for stalking under the VAWA.

Cases of sexual misconduct reported to UPPS in fall 2026

Aug. 19

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall on Aug. 7 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is not cleared.

Aug. 24

A student reported being harassed at an on-campus property. The case is not cleared.

Aug. 29

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

Sept. 3

A visitor reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall between June 4 and 6 in an unknown residence hall. The case is open.

Sept. 4

A student reported being harassed on Sept. 4 in the Blue Band Building. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 6

A student reported being harassed between Sept. 5 and 6 at an on-campus property. The case is open.

Sept. 8

An employee reported indecent offenses at the Chambers Building between March 2025 and Sept. 8, 2026. The case was cleared by adult arrest.

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by an unknown person in a residence hall on Sept. 5 in Porter Hall. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 11

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person at a parking lot outside Beaver Stadium between Aug. 30 and Sept. 11. The case is open.

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 21 and Sept. 11 in Nittany Apartments. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 14

A student reported being harassed at the Intramural Building. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 22

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 24 and Sept. 22 in Pollock Hall. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 23

A student reported being harassed between Sept. 1 and 23 on campus. The case is not cleared.

Sept. 24

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall between Sept. 17 and 18 at an on-campus residence hall. The case is open.

Sept. 27

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall on Sept. 25 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

A student reported being harassed on Sept. 25 in East Halls Residence Complex. The case is open.

Sept. 28

A student reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in a residence hall between Sept. 24 and 25 in West Halls Residence Complex. The case is not cleared.

A student reported being harassed between Aug. 17 and Sept. 26 on campus. The case is open.

Sept. 30

Campus police assisted an outside law agency with a reported Clery crime sexual assault at an off-campus fraternity occurring between Sept. 5 and 12. The case is closed.

Oct. 1

Campus police assisted an outside agency with a reported sexual assault at an off-campus fraternity occurring on Sept. 25. The case is closed.

Campus police assisted an outside agency with a reported sexual assault at an off-campus apartment between Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 on West College Avenue. The case is closed.

Oct. 2

A student reported being physically assaulted by a known person on campus between Sept. 21 and 26. The case is not cleared.

Oct. 3

A visitor reported they were sexually assaulted by a known person in an unknown location between Oct. 2 and 3. The case is not cleared.

What are Timely Warnings?

In Penn State’s annual security and fire safety report published on Sept. 30, the university described the purpose of Timely Warnings as “an effort to provide timely notice to the campus community in the event of a Clery Act Crime that may pose an ongoing threat.”

UPPS may distribute these warnings through emails, posters, web postings and media, and it has the discretion to determine whether a Timely Warning is required, according to the report. UPPS may issue Timely Warnings for events occurring off campus if the location is frequented by the university population.

The definition says they may issue a Timely Warning for the following crimes: criminal homicide, aggravated assault, sexual assault, burglary, robbery, motor vehicle theft, arson, certain hate crimes, dating violence, dometic violence, stalking and hazing.

The warnings are issued on a “case-by-case basis” based on the following criteria: One of the above listed crimes are reported; the perpetrator has not been apprehended; continuing threat risk

to the safety of other members of the campus community because of this crime; and possible risk of compromising law enforcement effort.

Timely warnings are required by the Jeanne Clery Campus Safety Act, a federal statute governing how colleges and universities that receive federal funding report crimes on and near campus. After a Clery Act crime occurs, campus officials are required to “evaluate if there is a serious or ongoing threat to the campus community,” according to the Clery Center.

In an email to The Daily Collegian, UPPS Public Information Officer Jacqueline Sheader wrote that all reports to UPPS are individually evaluated to determine if they meet Timely Warning criteria.

“Factors that may support a decision not to issue a Timely Warning include situations where the suspect has been identified and apprehended or law enforcement has determined that there is no ongoing danger. University Police also assess the nature of the crime, the circumstances surrounding the incident, the likelihood of recurrence, and the amount of information available to provide a meaningful warning,” Sheader wrote.

Resources

Medical services include Mount Nittany Medical Center; Penn Highlands State College; and University Health Services.

On-campus resources include Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS); the Office of Sexual Misconduct Reporting & Response; the Relationship Violence Outreach, Intervention, and Community Education (R-VOICE) Center; and The Center for Sexual and Gender Diversity (CSGD).

Off-campus resources include Centre Safe.

title: A look at No. 17 Penn State men’s hockey’s new defensive core
author: Maggie Hardy | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 17 Penn State will have a new look to its defensive core as it opens the season against No. 15 UConn on Friday.

After losing sophomore Cade Christenson to the transfer portal and both Jarod Crespo and Carter Schade to graduation, the Nittany Lions have a new blueline group debuting this weekend.

Between new additions and key returners, here’s a preview of the blue and white’s 2026-27 defenders.

New Additions

One of Penn State’s biggest offseason additions was former Vermont defender Caeden Herrington. The 6-foot-2 sophomore is a skilled two-way defenseman with offensive upside that has the potential to drive production for the Nittany Lions.

The Los Angeles Kings selected Herrington in the fourth round of the 2025 NHL draft, and he played in 34 games at Vermont, tallying one goal and seven assists. Previously, Herrington skated with the Lincoln Stars of the USHL, serving as an alternate captain and recording 16 goals, the second most in a single season by a Lincoln defenseman.

Another transfer portal addition was former Miami University blueliner, Charlie Michaud.

Michaud brought depth to the RedHawks, appearing in six games before finishing out the 2025-26 season with the Penticton Vees of the WHL. In 35 games, the Denver native tallied 15 assists.

Freshman Ethan Weber is the only Penn State defender new to NCAA play this year. Weber is coming off a productive season in the WHL, playing alongside Michaud with the Vees, where he put up 51 points in 68 games and led the team in scoring among defensemen.

The 6-foot-1 Manhattan Beach, California, native has the potential to add more scoring to Penn State’s blueliners as he develops alongside NCAA veterans.

Key Returners

Sophomore Jackson Smith has built a solid case for one of the best defenders in the Big Ten.

The Calgary, Alberta, native wrapped up his freshman season with an impressive resume — breaking two program records for the most single-season goals by a defenseman (11) and most power-play goals by a defenseman (7), as well as being named to the All-Big Ten Second Team and All-Freshman Team.

Smith, the No. 14 overall pick in the 2025 NHL Draft by the Columbus Blue Jackets, is poised for another big season after being named to the Preseason All-Big Ten Second Team.

Senior Mac Gadowsky is another key returner to Penn State’s defense. Gadowsky, son of Penn State coach Guy Gadowsky, transferred from Army last season.

After leading all defensemen in the country in points and goals during the 2024-25 season and becoming the Black Knights’ first-ever Hobey Baker Award Top-10 Finalist, Gadowsky fell significantly short of his previous offensive production this past season, waiting until the Big Ten Tournament to score his first, and only, goal with the program so far.

Despite the State College, Pennsylvania, native’s pure scoring struggles, he managed 17 assists and finished second for the defensemen on the team in both scoring and blocked shots, with 42.

Both Casey Aman and Nolan Collins are also solid returners for the Nittany Lions.

Aman, entering his senior season, has the ability to slot in almost anywhere in the lineup, used in a range of defensive pairs, as the extra skater, and sometimes even as a forward last season while the blue and white battled an extensive injury bug.

Collins begins his sophomore season after spending most of last year alongside Christenson, and while not the flashiest of scorers, he can generate creative offensive plays while using his 6-foot-4 frame to take a more physical edge.

To round out the defensive group, Nick Fascia’s return will add more depth to the blue and white’s roster.

The sophomore appeared in 25 games last year, registering a goal and three assists before suffering a season-ending injury in February.

title: Nittany Lions in the NFL | Joey Porter Jr. debuts, Chop Robinson records 1st sack of season
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Week 4 of the NFL season has come and gone, and former Penn Staters were involved all weekend.

The tight ends were once again heavily featured, while a former Penn State cornerback made his season debut with his new team following a mid-week trade.

Here’s what former Nittany Lions stood out on the first weekend of October.

Battle of cats

The Cincinnati Bengals and the Jacksonville Jaguars met in Cincinnati for a matchup that featured four former Penn State offensive players.

Tight end Brenton Strange led the Jaguars in receiving with seven catches for 95 yards, including a failed attempt at a hurdle in which he fumbled, but the ball went out of bounds and no damage was done.

The Jaguars’ leading receiver on the season, Parker Washington, was relatively quiet in Sunday’s game. Washington had one catch for seven yards and a rush for three yards, but he still leads the team with 228 receiving yards on the season. Strange and Washington are the top two receivers on the 3-1 Jaguars.

On the other side, Mike Gesicki found himself in the end zone for the third time this season. In games this season where he’s caught a pass, the former Penn Stater has also scored a touchdown, proving to be a reliable red zone target for Joe Burrow.

The Bengals signed Mitchall Tinsley off the Houston Texans’ practice squad on Sept. 29, and he made his season debut on Sunday. Tinsley caught three passes for 49 yards, including a 29-yard reception down the sideline to push the Bengals into Jaguars’ territory.

With some uncertainty at the position due to injuries to star wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, Tinsley could be a reliable and familiar target for Burrow.

Joey Porter Jr., cornerback, Dallas Cowboys

Former Penn State cornerback Joey Porter Jr. made his Dallas Cowboys debut after being traded from the Pittsburgh Steelers following lengthy contract disputes.

Porter proved once again he’s one of the league’s premier cornerbacks against the Houston Texans.

In the game, Porter played 24 snaps and was targeted just one time on his primary receiver. He has already shown to be a big boost to what was a struggling Cowboys’ defense.

Vega Ioane, offensive lineman, Baltimore Ravens

For the Ravens, Vega Ioane shifted from guard to center after they put both centers on injured reserve.

The move didn’t make a difference for Ioane, who proved to be a dominant force in the run game and pass protection against the Titans. In one rep, he took on defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons one-on-one, neutralizing one of the league’s top defensive tackles.

In just four games, Ioane has already proven to be a valuable pick at No. 14 for the Ravens, showcasing his dominance like he did at Penn State, but also having the versatility to switch positions when the Ravens needed a center.

Firsts of the season

A former Penn State tight end reached the end zone for the first time on Sunday, with New York Giants’ Theo Johnson scoring on his only catch of the game.

Johnson made the catch through a defender to record his second grab of the season. After being the starter last season at tight end, Johnson has taken a step back with the addition of Isaiah Likely. However, he still has played a good amount this season with the Giants using a lot of 12-personnel on offense.

On the defensive side of the ball, former Penn State edge rusher Chop Robinson recorded his first sack of the season against the Minnesota Vikings. Robinson’s presence on the edge was felt all game, tallying eight pressures, three quarterback hits and a 32.3% pressure rate against the Vikings.

His first sack of 2026 was a pure bull rush, pushing the right tackle right into Kyler Murray to end the Vikings’ drive.

title: Penn State softball adds 3 class of 2028 recruits
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Coach Crowell’s unit has been busy on the trail.

After a season in Happy Valley in which key freshman Breanna Hanik and Allison Oneacre helped the Nittany Lions finish 33-21, Crowell has already begun adding new talent to Penn State’s ranks.

After Crowell had a busy Monday on social media, posting that her squad added four recruits to its 2028 class, fans finally got clarity on three of those names, as those players announced commitments via social media.

A week prior, shortstop and infielder Demi Lotus announced her commitment to the Nittany Lions, following in her family’s footsteps as the third of her sisters to play Division I softball.

The class of 2028 lefty bat currently plays for the Premier Conroy 16U team in Illinois and for St. Laurence High School. In her varsity career, Lotus already started with a bang, earning honors to the Southtown Sports All-Area team, GCAC-Red All-Conference Team, and All-State Third Team.

A day before Crowell posted the four additions, fellow class of 2028 prospect catcher Audrey Riley announced her pledge to join the blue and white.

Riley spends her club time with EC Bullets Gold Ellis, which sent multiple prospects to collegiate programs this cycle, and her high school career with Glenelg. The righty also plays third base and has spent time with the U15 Women’s National Team.

The final recruit to make a public social media pledge was class of 2028 middle infielder Lily Kwis, who primarily plays shortstop. Kwis announced her commitment that same Monday night, when Crowell made her posts.

The gem of Crowell’s recruiting efforts announced her decision in a lengthy post, fitting for the hard work she’s put on the diamond in her young career. The righty was voted the top high school sophomore in the sport in her home state of New Jersey last year by NJ.com following a season where she posted a .633 batting average at the plate. Kwis plays for Eastern Regional High School and with Pennsbury Gems as her travel squad.

For now, that’s all the known names with public pledges to Penn State, though more are expected to be revealed soon based on Crowell’s posts.

title: Centre County man pleads guilty in case connected to child sex abuse ring
author: Mia Debelevich | Managing Editor
description:
A Centre County man pleaded guilty on Monday to trafficking and sexually exploiting two minors in a sex abuse ring, according to a press release from District Attorney Bernie Cantorna.

Samuel C. Friday, 68, of Tyrone, Pennsylvania, pleaded guilty to five felony charges, including two counts of trafficking of minors, two counts of production of child sexual abuse material and one count of sexual assault, according to the release.

Between 2021 and 2025, Friday “paid juvenile victims to engage in sexual acts with him and others and subjected them to sexual servitude. He also admitted photographing and recording juvenile victims engaged in sexual acts,” the release read.

The conduct occurred for one of the victims through the ages of 14 to 17, the release read, and hundreds of images and videos were found by investigators depicting the conduct. He was also charged for one other victim.

Under the plea deal, Friday and prosecutors agreed on a prison term of 30 to 60 years, which judge approval is still required to impose. The agreement also requires him to register as a sex offender, complete treatment, stay away from the victims and minors, forfeit seized property and pay restitution.

His sentencing is set for Jan. 19, 2027.

Three others were charged in connection with the child sex abuse ring, according to court documents:

Morris W. Reese, 65, of Tyrone, Pennsylvania, has been denied bail for being a threat to the community and being a flight risk, according to court documents.

Michael H. Woomer, 67, of Tyrone, Pennsylvania, has bail set at $2 million.

James Kobuck, 62, of Tyrone, Pennsylvania, has posted bail at $50,000 through a professional bondsman.

title: Penn State women’s hockey skaters Sofia Ismael and Sophie Morrow earn AHA weekly awards
author: Noah Radio | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is well-represented in the Atlantic Hockey America weekly awards. Freshman Sofia Ismael was named AHA Forward of the Week, and sophomore Sophie Morrow earned Defender of the Week honors, the conference announced Monday.

Ismael scored four goals this weekend, including a hat trick Saturday against Robert Morris. She scored or assisted on every goal in the victory.

Morrow, a defenseman, racked up more shots on goal than the entire Robert Morris team on Saturday. She fired eight while the Nittany Lions allowed just four.

Penn State is back in action Friday on the road against Syracuse at 6 p.m.

title: Art talks, football | Here’s what’s happening in the valley
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State Football is back in Happy Valley, but there are many other events to take part in this week.

Although the anticipation for White Out will be felt all week, there are plenty of options to captivate your attention before the big game. Here’s what’s happening in the valley this week.

Monday, Oct. 5

Lion Country Line Dancing

Get ready to kick off your dancing shoes. Lion Country Line Dancing is back at Bellefonte Moose Lodge from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. this Monday with tunes and dances for beginner- and improver-level dancers.

The event is $5, cash only, for non-members, and it’s for any dancer ages 18 and older. You must show ID to enter.

Tuesday, Oct. 6

Nature Sketching at The Arboretum

Some Penn State students definitely need to reconnect with nature after many arrived back in the Valley after quick trips to Las Vegas and Montreal this weekend.

Penn State’s Arboretum invites adults of all skill levels to this free, drop-in class to connect with art and nature. They invite attendees to bring their own materials or use those available at the arboretum.

Class begins at 10 a.m. at the H.O. Smith Botanic Gardens, and it will end with a small art showcase.

Good Times Line Dancing & PSU Meetings & Events Fundraiser Night

Can’t make the line dancing on Monday? Don’t worry because Good Times Line Dancing has you covered.

The Marriott Foundation Building is hosting Good Times Line Dancing from 7 to 9 p.m. on Tuesday. Tickets are $10 and should be purchased beforehand here. Proceeds from the night benefit THON.

Wednesday, Oct. 7

Artist Talk: Wonjung Choi

As part of the Palmer Museum’s series of artist talks, the art museum will be hosting Wonjung Choi. During this free event, at 11:30 a.m., Choi will discuss her work, which focuses on identity in a globalized world.

Thursday, Oct. 8

Artist Talk: Ryan RedCorn

This week is full of opportunities to connect with the arts. The Palmer Museum is also hosting Ryan RedCorn for an artist talk.

This Thursday, the artist – who is best known for his film, graphic design and comedy work – will be speaking at 5:30 p.m. Admission to this event is free.

The Best of The Second City!

In need of a good laugh? The comedy troupe, The Second City, is coming to the State Theatre this Thursday at 8 p.m. The group, which launched stars like Tina Fey and Steve Carrell, has tickets for sale on State Theatre’s website.

Price varies by seat but ranges from about $40 to about $60.

Friday, Oct. 9

Discovery Drop-In

This free, drop-in event in the Arboretum’s botanical garden encourages children of all ages to explore Pennsylvania’s ecosystems. Registration is not required for this event, and it may be canceled due to weather.

The Arboretum asks that all minors are accompanied by a parent or legal guardian.

Harvest Moon Bingo with Beth

What better excuse to dress up with friends, taste wines and meet new people?

Mount Nittany Winery is hosting bingo this Friday from 5 to 7 p.m. The $12 entrance fee covers a glass of wine and two bingo cards. Bingo winners get $5 vouchers towards an additional glass or bottle of wine.

Attendees can bring their own snacks, and charcuterie is available for purchase.

Alabama: Live in concert

If live music is more your thing, the class country band ALABAMA, known for songs like “Born Country,” is bringing their “Mountain Music” to the BJC on Friday at 7 p.m. Tickets are available for purchase through Ticketmaster.

The Band Memo

The Band Memo, a New York City-based rock band, will also be performing Friday night. Their performance will be at State Theatre at 8 p.m. Tickets, which are available on State Theatre’s website, range from $19.60 to $21.70.

Saturday, Oct. 10

Billy Price Band

Billy Price Band will take the stage on Saturday at 7 p.m. at Pine Grove Hall. The Blues Music Awards nominee is one of Pine Grove Hall’s touring artists for this season. Reservations are encouraged.

Although this week may have been a disappointing time for Penn State and Philadelphia sports fans alike, as Penn Staters, it’s in our blood to go big or go home for the White Out.

The Penn State Nittany Lions football team will take on the USC Trojans on Saturday at 7:30 p.m. at Beaver Stadium. This game marks Penn State’s annual White Out, so don’t get caught blue-handed.

Boalsburg Renaissance Faire

After a harrowing first month of the semester, it may be time to enter a distant land.

The Boalsburg Renaissance Faire, which is hosted on the grounds of the Boal Estate, is from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. this Sunday. For a $10 admission fee, be transported to medieval times with a day filled with historic entertainment and hands-on activities.

To prepare for the Arboretum’s annual pumpkin fest, head to the Overlook Pavillion between 2 and 4 p.m. this Sunday to pick up a pumpkin to carve for the annual jack-o-lantern contest. Those who preregistered by Wednesday Oct. 7, can begin picking up their pumpkins from 1 to 2 p.m.

Drop in Tour: Indigenous People’s Day

This drop-in event to celebrate Indigenous People’s Day encourages visitors to explore the Palmer Museum with a guide. The event runs from 2 to 3 p.m., and tours begin in the Dr. Keiko Miwa Ross Lobby.

SCAC Harvest Fest

This free event, hosted by State College Alliance Church from 4 to 7 p.m., is a celebration of fall and community connection. The congregation invites all to join them for cider, live music, games, inflatables and more.

“Weird Al” Yankovic

Weird Al is coming to the BJC at 7:30 p.m. this Sunday. Known for his parodies and outrageous acts, Weird Al is bringing his BIGGER & WEIRDED 2026 tour to Happy Valley, and tickets are available for purchase through Ticketmaster.

Have another great week in Happy Valley.

title: Big Ten roundup | Ohio State wins top-15 matchup over Iowa, USC survives Washington
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Big Ten’s elite competition this year was on display this week, as Penn State fell to Northwestern on Friday, Minnesota took down Michigan and Washington’s loss to USC was decided in the final minute of the fourth quarter.

Five teams remain undefeated in the conference — Ohio State, Indiana, Minnesota, Nebraska and Wisconsin. Beyond that, many who the nation believed were going to have strong seasons have fallen from grace, such as the Nittany Lions and Wolverines.

Here’s how Penn State’s fellow Big Ten programs performed in Week 5.

Top-10 programs stay golden

No. 5 Ohio State traveled to Kinnick Stadium to face then-No. 14 Iowa in the only Big Ten game this week featuring two ranked opponents. The Buckeyes rolled past the Hawkeyes, 31-14, led by star quarterback Julian Sayin and a record-setting performance by the nation’s top wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.

Smith had 11 receptions for 206 yards and two touchdowns, breaking Ohio State records in career receptions and receiving touchdowns.

The nation’s top Heisman Trophy candidate struck the iconic pose in the end zone after his second touchdown of the game, a 57-yard reception that broke Chris Olave’s record for most receiving touchdowns.

Then-No. 6 Indiana was also on the road this week, and the Hoosiers were all gas when they faced Rutgers at SHI Stadium. The defending national champions sprinted to a 23-0 lead by halftime and finished the game with a 47-15 victory to stay undefeated.

Both the pass and run games dismantled the Scarlet Knights on their home turf, as quarterback Josh Hoover threw for 251 yards and four touchdowns while the Hoosiers rushed for 329 yards.

Running back Turbo Richard was another offensive standout, accumulating 204 rushing yards and a touchdown on 13 carries.

Rutgers quarterback Dylan Lonergan left the game late in the first half after getting hit hard on a failed quarterback sneak on fourth-and-inches. He was replaced by AJ Surace, who was efficient in the second half, throwing for 128 yards and a touchdown.

Fumble recovery pushes USC past Washington

The most unlikely hero scored USC’s game-winning touchdown on Saturday. After Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. fumbled the ball, defensive tackle Jahkeem Stewart recovered it and trudged 48 yards into the end zone for a scoop-and-score.

Previously, Washington was firmly in the driver’s seat when tight end Decker DeGraaf caught a short pass and ran down the sideline for a 42-yard touchdown to make it 21-10 in the third quarter.

However, the Trojans’ offense and defense woke up to win 25-21. USC improved to 5-1 on the season and 2-1 in the Big Ten while Washington fell to 3-2 overall and 0-2 in the conference.

USC quarterback Jayden Maiava finished the game with 245 passing yards and a touchdown.

Kicker Caden Chittenden’s 39-yard field goal in the fourth quarter forced the Huskies to try the end zone, but USC’s defense stood tall with a sack and a stop on fourth down to win the game.

Minnesota wins the midwestern battle

Minnesota and Michigan had a defensive battle, and the Golden Gophers got the job done at home with a 20-14 win.

Minnesota scored 10 points at the beginning of the fourth quarter and held on for the rest of the game.

Quarterbacks Drake Lindsey and Bryce Underwood threw two interceptions each in the contest. Lindsey finished the game with 136 yards and a touchdown while Underwood had 101 yards.

The Wolverines struggled greatly on offense, with the only offensive touchdown on a 5-yard rush from Jordan Marshall. Michigan’s other score was a 79-yard pick six from Nathaniel Staehling, which gave the Wolverines a 14-7 lead in the second quarter.

Underwood threw an interception on the first play of the fourth quarter before Lindsey threw the game-winning touchdown pass to running back Darius Taylor three plays later.

title: Letter to the Editor: Penn State pick a side, justice or genocide?
author: Letter by Students for Justice in Palestine at Penn State
description:
This letter was written by Students for Justice in Palestine, an organization at Penn State dedicated to fighting for the liberation of Palestine and the freedom and self-determination of the Palestinian people. Anyone interested in submitting a letter to the editor may do so here.

This week marks three years of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. For the past three years, Penn State Students for Justice in Palestine has organized several weeks of action to raise consciousness about Israel’s brutality against Palestinians and counteract the university’s silence on the genocide.

This silence is a disturbing truth: By failing to condemn Israel’s genocide and take actions that prevent further violence, Penn State is actively enabling the system that upholds Palestinians’ suffering.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza is the issue of our time, and Penn Staters have a duty and choice to make: fight for justice or be complicit in genocide.

Penn State has a vested interest in perpetuating the genocide of Palestinians through its direct ties to Israel, weapons manufacturers, and the US military industrial complex. Through this genocidal network of U.S.-funded weapons research and development, the Israeli Occupation Forces have destroyed every university in Gaza, incapacitated their medical system, and strangled major aid routes that Palestinians depend upon.

All of this is in greater service of Israel’s zionist settler colonial project, which ultimately seeks the total annihilation of every Palestinian.

The connection between Penn State, top weapons manufacturers, and the U.S. Department of Defense is directly linked through their Applied Research Laboratory and the university’s position as a Land Grant Institution.

Penn State is connected to weapons manufacturers like RTX, formerly known as Raytheon, through its Applied Research Laboratory: a company that has a $1.25 Billion contract with Israel.

The Palestinian struggle is materially connected to our experiences on this campus. Weapons research at Penn State is prioritized as 30% of Penn State’s $1.45 billion research budget comes directly from the Department of Defense, and so far in 2026, the funding from DoD has reached $500 million. This not only implicates Penn State as an institution, but also those of us who are recruited to contribute to the genocidal war machine through internships, career prospects, and research.

It is indefensible to prioritize weapons research that has enabled Israel to murder over 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, wound over 175,000, displace over 2 million, and end 2700 family lineages forever.

The U.S. government, weapons corporations and universities, including Penn State, are complicit in the military industrial complex and contribute to legitimizing Israel’s zionist settler colonial violence and occupation of Palestine.

Knowing how our university is linked to genocide, we have a responsibility to show solidarity with Palestinians and demand an end to Penn State’s complicity with weapons manufacturing. Join Penn State Students for Justice in Palestine for our week of action from October 5-9th.

title: College of IST hears from ‘a variety of perspectives’ during its first ever AI in Research symposium
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Dozens of Penn State students and faculty filled the lobby of the Graduate Hotel on Friday to attend the College of Information Science and Technology’s (IST) first ever AI in Research symposium.

Opening at 9:30 a.m., attendees were able to view and ask about presentations featuring several student projects exploring the benefits and risks of involving artificial intelligence in research. Attendees were also able to vote on which projects they believe should receive awards later in the symposium.

College of IST Associate Dean of Research and Graduate Affairs Carleen Maitland said the symposium’s organization is meant to allow faculty and students to come together and consider how to create AI use policies that both groups agree with.

“In our college, we have a variety of perspectives,” Maitland of Guilford, Connecticut, said. “Some faculty are opposed to AI use in research; some are okay, but want it staggered where students in their first two years of the doctoral program use it less and then start to use it more in the later years; or, third, that there are people who are fine using it throughout their graduate program. And so the idea that the faculty and students understand one another is really important at this point.”

She said the symposium also represents a larger reckoning within research communities on how to respond to the proliferation of artificial intelligence. She referenced a change the Association for Computing Machinery’s made to their AI policy in May to no longer require the disclosure of AI-assisted writing as an example of how quickly this debate can change.

Shuhua Yang, 28, of Anhui province, China, said she was told about the symposium two weeks in advance by one of her faculty advisors, Dongwon Lee, and used the event to present her work on finding ways to optimize AI “to do the job properly” by making prompts more concise.

“The takeaway of this project is how we can potentially enhance our experience when interacting with AI and how we can make AI more efficient and more accurate to help with our work,” Yang, a PhD student studying informatics, said.

Yang also said her research into AI prompting has offered her three insights into how to best leverage artificial intelligence: never completely trust the results that are generated, try to solve some problems without AI assistance and to be “polite” with an AI and to not send prompts as part of an emotional reaction.

“Sometimes I become really angry and I prompt the AI using some sentence like ‘what is wrong with you?’ but it doesn't help,” Yang said. “You have to stay not that emotional because emotion doesn't help you.”

Yang said the high level of attendance made the symposium “a meaningful experience” for her by allowing for everyone to contribute, regardless of if they had extensive experience with using AI or not.

Following the conclusion of project presentations at 11 a.m., attendees packed into the Graduate Hotel’s Coaly Ballroom to listen to a discussion and Q&A panel moderated by IST informatics and intelligent systems professor Sarah Rajtmajer and featured the heads of all three of the College’s academic departments: Dongwon Lee, Sharon Huang and Guoray Cai.

The panel also included comments from Penn State Research Integrity Officer Courtney Karmelita and AI Vice Provost Vasant Honavar.

Following the panel, three of the students who presented projects earlier in the symposium — Stephanie TianYa Jen, Rishvanth Amsaraj and Hillmer Chona — were awarded with grants of up to $1,000 based on the votes cast by attendees earlier in the symposium.

Maitland said, based on the success of the AI research symposium, there is a potential for other colleges to follow suit with their own conferences to promote more debates on the subject within Penn State.

In an interview, Honavar said this is a position he agrees with because of how research policies developed by IST professors might not work for a project in another college or department whose views on how artificial intelligence can be used for research may differ drastically.

He also said while Penn State already has policies concerning AI use in research, they represent a “minimal bar” which he stressed needs to be pushed past through the creation of more “nuanced” policies that, when taken together, meet a diverse range of requirements from researchers both at the university and in other research circles.

“Each discipline has different needs; the type of education people are getting in philosophy is very different from computer science, or mathematics or experimental science, so each of those fields has to grapple with this topic and come up with what works for them,” Honavar said. “It has to happen at Penn State, it has to happen in other institutions and eventually research communities have to come together to define what it is for them.”

title: Stock up, stock down | Rocco Becht’s inaccuracies continue, Tony Rojas shines
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The losing ways continued for Penn State as it opened up the newly built Ryan Field against Northwestern, falling 34-13.

While there weren’t many positives to come out of a game that was mostly dominated by the Wildcats, Tony Rojas and wide receiver Chase Sowell were bright spots.

Here’s whose stock went up and whose stock continued to fall in Week 5.

Stock down: Rocco Becht

Rocco Becht’s first two games in the Big Ten as Penn State’s quarterback could have gone significantly better.

While his numbers look slightly better after some garbage time boosting, he still missed throws he was making in the first three weeks.

Some of the throws aren’t because of any rise in talent from the opposing defenses, he’s just missing passes. On a throw that appeared to be to tight end Andrew Rappleyea, he sailed it far enough over his head that it looked to be an underthrown pass to Sowell.

Becht threw for 241 yards and a touchdown, but also threw two interceptions as the passes batted at the line continued to haunt him.

Stock up: Tony Rojas

Despite the defense’s inability to slow down Northwestern, Tony Rojas was one of the bright spots in the unit.

Rojas led the team in tackles with 12, but also was all over the field making plays. With the pass rush still struggling to get home, albeit against 14 pass attempts, Rojas was the lone player to record a sack.

The linebacker tallied 3.5 tackles for loss and a pass breakup, showcasing his ability to do it all.

Rojas is arguably the most athletic player on the team, and his ability to continue to make plays has been a bright spot in the defense’s collapses in the past two weeks. If the defense starts to make more plays around Rojas, it’ll quickly take a rise with its superstar in the center of the unit.

Stock down: Run defense

Penn State’s run defense gave up some bigger plays against Wisconsin, but not enough for it to be too worrying heading into Week 5. However, Northwestern’s entire offense revolved around its run game, and the Wildcats ran all over the Nittany Lions.

The defense gave up 413 rushing yards in comparison to 93 passing yards against a team who ran for just 32 yards against Indiana last weekend.

The mix of Caleb Komolafe and Joseph Himon II created gashes in Penn State’s defense as they ran the ball at will. The defensive line was mauled by Northwestern’s offensive line, allowing it to successfully run the wing T formation to perfection, giving different looks each time.

The biggest dagger was following Penn State’s first touchdown. The score was just 10-7 and a stop could’ve completely shifted the game. Instead, two rushes from Himon put the ball right back in the end zone in a total of three plays. He ran twice for 36 and 38 yards, with massive holes open for him from the offensive line.

Stock up: Chase Sowell

One of the bright spots of Penn State’s offense was Sowell, who led the team with 68 receiving yards and a touchdown.

Sowell has been the Nittany Lions’ most consistent receiver after Koby Howard went down with an injury, but his production hasn’t been enough to get the offense scoring points.

The receiver was targeted 12 times, and despite it coming late in the game, he found the end zone on a 16-yard touchdown reception.

Sowell’s production as a reliable target for Becht has been there in lieu of the absence of Howard. His catch to start the game on offense was a perfect representation of his ability to get open, as Becht rolled out of the pocket and found his top healthy receiver.

Stock down: Offensive line

There was a lot of hype on the offensive line entering the season, with Anthony Donkoh moving back outside to tackle and former 4-star Malachi Goodman slotting in at left tackle. However, the line hasn’t been as dominant as expected and was lacking physicality against Northwestern.

Penn State’s run game hasn’t been able to get going for a multitude of reasons, but one of the main ones is because of the lack of push the line is getting in the trenches.

The interior of the line is a big part of that, as the two transfers — center Brock Riker and left guard Trevor Buhr — haven’t appeared to adapt to Big Ten defensive lines.

If Penn State wants to get the run game going and protect Becht more, it’s going to have to win in the trenches with the way the offensive line is playing.

title: Mojofest Happy Valley came, conquered and revived Penn State local music fans
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming just six months after its debut in State College, Mojofest Happy Valley returned to Tussey Mountain on Saturday, for another round of heavy jams and good times in the sunshine.

That morning, the board and crew of Local Mojo’s Penn State branch had a much more relaxed set up. There was no panic in their efforts as they already had one major festival under their belt from last semester. A general feeling of gratitude and excitement was all that loomed around the open festival grounds.

After the soundcheck of the headlining band, The Dirty Turkeys, lead singer of the band, Bradley Hansen, 25, from Boulder, Colorado, talked admiringly about the growth and attraction local music has gained from the East to West Coasts, saying that people want to feel something again.

“They want to dance, they want to boogie, they want to see someone rip the electric guitar and play the drums and feel it, feel it deep in their bones,” Hansen said.

After the last Mojofest Happy Valley, Local Mojo founder Charley Blacker said that Penn State’s 2026 Mojofest would be “something Happy Valley’s never seen before.” He couldn’t have been more accurate.

As the line formed outside the festival, students and local residents came dressed in their bohemian-inspired fits, while they trickled into the festival grounds with anticipation for what the day had in store. Bands and DJ’s from both State College and all around the country were lined up for eight straight hours of good music and good vibes.

One Penn State student, Asher Reno, 18, from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, said he was introduced to the festival through a few friends that had attended the semester before.

“I don’t know any of the people here today, so I’m excited to discover some more local music,” Asher, a first-year studying business, said

Kai Petrosky, 19, from Somerset, Pennsylvania, expressed how much he loved the environment that the festival created for the community.

“It’s just as great as last year,” Petroski, a second-year studying business and data analytics, said. ‘It’s good music, it’s a great atmosphere, there’s just a bunch of people here that really seem awesome.”

The show kicked off with a DJ performance from the director, Ava Plachter and marketing director, Caya Kassaraba, of Local Mojo Penn State. State College bands, Sean Thomas and the Waterfowl Festival Band, along with DJ’s, Soho, Poh and Jacob Gavin, followed the opening act and gave the crowd a reminder of what the State College scene sounds like.

Other acts like the popular Happy Valley bands Mick Mac and 3:46 Sunrise drew in more and more people to the front of the stage by the hundreds, continuing to give people that thumping, upbeat and reviving taste of the Happy Valley sound.

Masses of people swayed, hands high and smiles wide, as they sang word for word every tune that came through the monitors. Soon, the entire festival ground transformed into a sonic commune and the only things that seemed to matter were simple: listening and enjoying.

The show finished out with the headlining act, The Dirty Turkeys. The crowd, thinned out by a small margin, maintained its unyielding spirit as the band uploaded their head-bashing drums and ground-shaking bass.

Mosh pits formed in front of the stage, filled with fans wearing Garfield onesies, leather jackets and Elton John sunglasses. At one point during the band’s song "Quinceanera," Hansen departed the stage to be with the crowd as he created his own whirlpool of fans and belted out the chorus of the song.

After the show concluded, fans headed into a line, while they waited for the bus shuttles to take them back into downtown State College.

Dylan Tomb, 21, from Pittsburgh, said he couldn’t get enough of it and, at one point, couldn’t even feel his legs because he was moving so much. He praised the feeling that the festival gave not only to him but also to everyone around him.

“How could you not want to come up here on Tussey mountain, with the best view, to listen to some local music?” Tomb, a fourth-year security and risk analysis major, said. “It was just the best time.”

title: Gaitan delivers game-winner as Penn State field hockey defeats No. 19 Lafayette in second half thriller
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
Following Penn State’s 1-0 road win at Rutgers on Friday, the Nittany Lions looked to continue their winning form against Lafayette on Sunday for their senior day matchup.

The opening minutes of the first quarter saw Penn State have a slow start offensively, which caused the Nittany Lions to play on the back foot, as the Lafayette offense wasted no time getting in rhythm.

Neither team earned a penalty corner in the opening 15 minutes, this being the first time the blue and white managed that stat all season so far.

Lafayette’s first penalty corner, which was the first penalty chance for either team, came with just under 10 minutes to go in the second quarter, but a key defensive stop for the Nittany Lions kept the game scoreless.

Penn State’s first penalty chance came with 1:42 remaining in the first half, but junior forward Ella Gaitan’s shot was deflected wide, leaving no goals on the board heading into halftime.

The final two quarters and overtime were when the pressure rose to new heights.

The intensity began to rise as both the Nittany Lions and Lafayette each had three total shots and two saves at the 10-minute mark of the third frame. Penn State got another defensive stop on Lafayette’s second penalty corner of the game with 13:25 remaining, keeping the score even at zero.

Both the physical play and pace of the game increased as the third quarter wound down, yet neither team was able to strike first and earn the advantage.

The final quarter and overtime were a different story. While Penn State stole momentum back to begin the fourth, Lafayette senior forward Emma Maher scored the first points of the contest, forcing the Nittany Lions to play with their backs against the wall as they looked to earn their first ranked win of 2026 and of the Hannah Prince era.

Yet this is where the resilience of coach Prince’s team came to fruition. The Nittany Lions struck back when sophomore forward Olivia Marthins scored the first points for the blue and white with the help of an assist from senior midfielder Natalie Freeman at the 7:29 mark of regulation.

Just minutes later, that same pair worked together for another Penn State goal, showcasing how Prince’s team-focused mentality has helped the Nittany Lions cut into deficits in late-game situations. Marthins assisted Freeman with 6:43 remaining in the fourth, giving the Nittany Lions a narrow 2-1 lead.

When the game seemed to be fully in Penn State’s hands, Lafayette silenced the Happy Valley crowd with a late goal from senior defensive back Lena Thedrian at the 2:08 mark of regulation, that ultimately sent the game to overtime.

The opening minutes of the sudden-death period went back and forth. A Penn State penalty corner chance with 11:40 remaining was stopped short and the momentum seemed to shift back to Lafayette.

However, Gaitan’s game-winning shot on Penn State’s third penalty corner with 10:30 remaining on the clock sealed the deal for the Nittany Lions, giving them the 3-2 win, their first against a ranked opponent in 2026.

“I honestly had a great feeling. I felt like the girls were really prepared and had a ton of focus despite it being senior day. I also just felt they were locked in, ready to take whatever came at them,” Prince said. “We had a great scout and gameplan on Lafayette, saw what I expected to see, the girls even made some adjustments and matched up quite well, and I’m just really proud of the attack we generated and the outcomes because that’s been an area we’ve been emphasizing throughout the season, like executing when it matters.”

The Nittany Lions know they’ve been having success, but also know there is

always room for improvement.

“I think that varying our shape can help at times, but our goal was to try to get pressure on because they do play quite direct on their corners, so sending the fly and maybe they’ll line on some of that, could have been adjusted,” Prince said. “Those are really well placed shots and tough ones to get but I’m happy that the girls just kept their heads up and didn’t let it change our energy. We just stayed focused on us and trusted that what we were doing was gonna help us to get the outcome we wanted.”

Penn State returns to the pitch to take on Big Ten rival Michigan State on Oct. 9 at 3 p.m in East Lansing.

MORE FIELD HOCKEY COVERAGE

title: Penn State field hockey secures first ranked win with Hannah Prince, upsets No. 19 Lafayette in overtime
author: Annie Alberts | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions faced off against No. 19 Lafayette in a slow but rewarding game.

Penn State ultimately earned an upset 3-2 overtime win over the Leopards after trading late-game fireworks.

The first quarter was uneventful for both sides, as both teams had two shots on goal, neither of which went in. The quarter was mostly filled with substitutions.

The next quarter was still scoreless, but included a little more action. Lafayette’s Katie Gibb had a penalty corner shot in the first few minutes, but she missed the goal. Near the end of the quarter, Penn State’s Cam Standish also had a penalty corner shot. Similar to Gibb, Standish missed the opportunity to score.

To finish the half, Penn State’s Ella Gaitan made her second shot on goal. The two sides had equal possession and aggressive energy, but neither could score.

To begin the second half, Penn State challenged a Lafayette corner shot. The Leopards earned the shot, but missed. Penn State’s defense rocked the maroon and white, stealing the ball whenever they had the chance to.

Penn State forward Natalie Freeman made a shot on goal to conclude the quarter, but it went wide.

As the fourth quarter rolled around, the scoreboard was still empty. With the clock inside the last 10 minutes, Lafayette’s Emma Maher scored her first goal of the season.

A minute and a half later, Penn State forward Olivia Marthins tied the game with the midfielder’s ninth score of the season. Lafayette challenged the goal, but to Nittany Lions were given the goal.

Almost instantly, Freeman scored the go-ahead second goal, assisted by Marthins. Thankfully, Penn State took control of the scoreboard with five minutes left in the game.

Lafayette earned a penalty corner at the end, but Penn State challenged it.

When awarded the penalty corner, Lafayette managed to tie the game. The score laid 2-2, with three minutes left in the quarter.

Both teams entered overtime. They battled to get the ball in the opposing team’s goal for five minutes, until Gaitan sealed the win on her third shot of the day with a liner from the edge of the circle from a penalty corner. The goal was assisted by Standish and Marthins, who were both standout players during this long and challenging match. Both squads remained close in corners, shots, and saves at the end of the game.

With the result, the Nittany Lions improved to 6-4 in coach Hannah Prince’s debut season in Happy Valley, riding a three-game win streak. The new boss also has her first ranked win with the program.

Up next

The blue and white return to Big Ten play with a road clash against Michigan State on Friday at 3 p.m.

title: Week 5 report card | Rocco Becht's inconsistency, poor run defense in Penn State's 2nd loss
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
There was a lot at stake Friday night as Penn State, coming off Matt Campbell’s first Big Ten loss, traveled to Northwestern for the debut of Ryan Field.

Despite the pressure, the Nittany Lions faltered in every aspect of the game, between inaccurate throws from Rocco Becht, a struggling run defense and a missed field goal.

Here’s how I’d grade Penn State’s offensive and defensive units after the loss.

Overall grade: D

Coaching staff: F

After Matt Campbell's aggressiveness was a topic of discussion following the loss to Wisconsin, there were even more questions throughout Friday's game.

Campbell ultimately chose to punt the ball away from Northwestern's 44-yard line late in the game and decided not to attempt an onside kick after Penn State scored in the fourth quarter. When Becht struggled, Campbell said he didn't consider putting backup quarterback Alex Manske in.

Offense: D

Neither Becht nor the run game could establish consistency, finishing with 291 total yards. The sole bright spot was the use of different weapons, as four players recorded five or more receptions.

Passing game: C

If this grade were on quarterback performance alone, Becht would receive an “F” against Northwestern. He had a pair of interceptions, three tipped passes and numerous throws that were off target.

However, his receivers and tight ends made the most of their opportunities. Wide receivers Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen and tight ends Benjamin Brahmer and Andrew Rappleyea all had over five receptions each with Sowell adding a late-game touchdown.

Run game: F

It looked like things were getting established after one play, as James Peoples rushed for five yards and appeared to have conviction in his attack. However, he finished with just 13 yards on eight carries, while Carson Hansen had four rushes for 19 yards and a touchdown.

Penn State continued to struggle with rushing consistency and physicality as the team averaged just 2.2 yards per carry with 48 total yards.

Offensive line: C

Becht was sacked just once and faced minimal-to-average pressure against the Wildcats. In the run game, the offensive line couldn't establish any gaps for Peoples or Hansen.

Defense: D

While the Nittany Lions allowed under 100 passing yards to Aidan Chiles, the run game produced 413 yards against the non-existent Penn State defense.

Pass rush: C+

Penn State didn't have many opportunities to rush the passer as Chiles only threw the ball 14 times.

In one of the few chances, defensive end Caleb Bacon nearly took Chiles down in the backfield, helping Tony Rojas finish the play for a sack.

Secondary: B-

The secondary was by far the best aspect of the Nittany Lions’s performance, allowing just 93 passing yards from Chiles. However, Northwestern's running back duo ran past the defensive backs with multiple runs for over 30 yards.

Linebackers: C-

Linebacker Kooper Ebel pulled the unit’s grade down drastically, having missed numerous tackles that would've contained Joseph Himon II. Instead, Himon and Caleb Komolafe ran free for 350 yards.

Rojas was the lone bright spot against Northwestern, recording a sack, 3.5 tackles for loss, 12 tackles and a pass deflection.

Special teams: D

Even Penn State's special teams couldn't get things going against Northwestern. Kicker Ryan Barker misses his only field goal attempt and punt returner Zay Robinson — who’s been among the best in the conference — never attempted a return on Friday.
