title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State rebound from its first loss with a win at the Ryan Field grand-opening?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
Penn State has its first true road test of the year this Friday against Northwestern under the lights of the brand-new Ryan Field.

The Wildcats’ fresh stadium cost nearly $900 million with a student section designed similarly to a European soccer arena. No sitting. Banging on the back wall that echoes throughout the air.

It’ll be a tough environment for the Nittany Lions.

Can Penn State brave the noise and bounce back from its first loss of the year?

Andrew Deal: Penn State 24, Northwestern 20

Based on Penn State’s performance against Wisconsin and Northwestern keeping it close against Indiana, I expect this game to remain tight.

The Nittany Lions have been dealing with injuries, but nowhere to the extent of Northwestern. Wide receiver Hayden Eligon II and defensive backs Damon Walters and Braden Turner all were on the Wildcats’ availability report on Tuesday with questionable designations.

While cornerback Daryus Dixson is also questionable for Penn State, he’s the only Nittany Lion impact player who’s availability is up in the air compared to the multiple Northwestern players.

For the Nittany Lions to have success, they’re going to have to establish the run game, especially against a defense that has struggled against the run. If they can somewhat replicate the success they had against Buffalo, maybe not to the extent of 304 rushing yards, they have a good chance to come out on top.

Penn State will have difficulties containing the dual-threat talent of Aidan Chiles, but it’ll stop him enough to hold up and defeat Northwestern in the Wildcats’ first game at their new stadium.

Andrew Mercer: Northwestern 17, Penn State 14

Although Rocco Becht said he expects a “different team” against the Wildcats, it’s extremely difficult to turn an entire offense around in such a short week.

Penn State had both Sunday and Monday off from practice this week, leaving the Nittany Lions three days to execute on the lessons learned on the practice field before its showtime. If the issues presented on Saturday were truly fixable details, it’ll simply come down to showing up when the pressure’s on.

Penn State cracked under the pressure last week.

While D’Anton Lynn’s defense was strong against Wisconsin, the Badgers proved Saturday that a strong defense cannot completely win you a football game. If three interceptions, including a pick six, wasn’t enough to beat Wisconsin, it’s going to take an explosive performance on offense to get over the hump.

It’s that explosivity I believe Penn State lacks at this point. Without Koby Howard, the offense slumped, and if Becht can’t get into rhythm with Brett Eskildsen or Chase Sowell, there’s no reason why this losing streak can’t snowball.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 21, Northwestern 14

The poor offensive showing against Wisconsin was definitely not ideal for Penn State, and this Friday’s game is going to show exactly what this team and offense is truly made of.

I don’t expect Taylor Mouser’s offense to absolutely dominate now, but he and Becht likely have chips on their shoulders and want to prove they belong in the Big Ten. They’ll do that with a gritty win over the Wildcats.

The Nittany Lions’ run game has a big opportunity to have a statement performance, as Northwestern allowed 272 yards on the ground last week in its close loss to Indiana. Expect James Peoples to show why he should be Penn State’s No. 1 running back.

Even if Dixson doesn’t play, Terry Smith’s position group has loads of depth that can step up in place, such as fellow sophomore Jahmir Joseph. Northwestern’s passing attack also runs purely through two players, giving the Nittany Lions an advantage.

Penn State’s defense will ultimately step up and prevent the Wildcats from winning their debut game at Ryan Field.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 23, Northwestern 17

Penn State is coming off a rough start to Big Ten play against Wisconsin, as the offense was never able to find momentum and the defense gave up several big plays. While I expect those themes to remain this week, I think the Nittany Lions can do just enough to pull out the win.

One of the biggest struggles for Penn State this year has been the red zone offense, and as long as wide receiver Koby Howard is sidelined and the run game struggles continue, I think those red zone difficulties will continue. That’s where kicker Ryan Barker will come in clutch.

I think Barker will have one of the most productive games of his career, drilling all three field goal attempts. There could be an opportunity for more, but I think Matt Campbell will be a little more aggressive on fourth down after last week.

Defensively, Penn State’s pass rush will once again have a tough time getting to the opposing quarterback. Aidan Chiles was sacked a season-high four times last week, and while I don’t think the Nittany Lions will replicate those numbers, I think they’ll improve from their single sack against the Badgers.

Turnovers, however, will be the major turning point that gives Penn State the wins. A week after intercepting Colton Joseph three times, the Nittany Lions will record at least one turnover that results in a score and eventually the win.

title: Ways to celebrate autumn on a budget
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
Fall has always been an aesthetic season. From the early seasons of Gilmore Girls to a playlist with all the sappy classics, you probably want to enjoy all of fall’s glory as much as you can.

But fall, of course, comes right after the first month of school, which might have your bank account looking about as empty as the branches of the trees will.

If you’re at a loss, don't worry. Local events and your very own kitchen can keep you occupied this season.

Here are some ways to celebrate fall without breaking the bank.

Nature walk in the Arboretum

One of the best ways to take in those fall vibes is to experience the leaves changing colors. The Penn State Arboretum is a great place to see the beautiful nature that Centre County has to offer in autumn. It's free to walk around and open from dawn to dusk every day.

The Arboretum also has an annual Pumpkin Fest from Oct. 15-16 with free admission. Attendees can view jack-o’-lanterns carved by community members, student organizations and more. There will also be food trucks, vendors and children's activities at the festival.

Make your own pumpkin spice latte

Buying viral drinks from Starbucks might cost a pretty penny, but the ingredients are all available at local grocery stores to save you some money this fall.

Pour espresso or freshly brewed coffee into a mug or a glass over ice. Add pumpkin puree, maple syrup, pumpkin pie spice and vanilla and stir until combined. Add your milk of choice to the mixture, and you’ve got a homemade pumpkin spice latte.

You could also froth milk for cold foam or add whipped cream. Extra pumpkin pie spice or cinnamon make a good topping for extra flair.

Bake seasonal goods

Another way to celebrate fall in your kitchen is by baking some of your favorite seasonal pastries. Pumpkin bread, apple crisp and cinnamon rolls are some classics that can put you in the fall mood.

An apple crisp is simple and great for those who are new to baking. You just need to make spiced apples and the topping, then bake them. The apples need to be chopped and mixed with sugar, cinnamon and lemon juice.

Then, brown sugar, oats, flour, cinnamon, salt and cold butter need to be mixed together in a separate bowl. Spread this over the apples in a baking dish, and stick them in the oven. Serve with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream for the perfect fall dessert.

Pumpkin bread and cinnamon rolls are easy to make but can also be found pre-made at your local grocery store, if you’re looking for a fall classic without dirtying your kitchen.

Thrift and forage for decor

Whether you’re looking for an autumn aesthetic or a spooky Halloween vibe, finding cheap decorations can be difficult. One of the best ways to get great decor for cheap is heading to your local thrift or antique shop.

Thrift shops have amazing vintage decor for low prices. Some pieces to look for are brown glasses or vases, woven baskets, vintage quilts and warm-toned hardcover books. These are perfect to add to your home or apartment for that fall essence.

Another way to get decor for cheap is to search outside. Pinecones, acorns and branches are great centerpieces that are no cost to you.

You could also make a wreath with natural materials. Wreath bases are available for cheap at most craft stores, and you can use twigs and leaves to make a homemade wreath.

All of these options are also environmentally friendly which makes them great options to celebrate fall while lowering your carbon footprint.

Have a movie night

For those looking for a simple night in, a movie night is a great choice. Whether you love scary Halloween movies or feel-good autumn classics, a comfy watch-party on the couch is a fall staple.

Horror movie-lovers might want to rewatch standard scary films like “Scream” or “Friday the 13th.” Some upcoming horror releases are “Other Mommy” and “Clayface,” which both come out in October.

If you aren’t interested in horror, some classic fall movies are “Hocus Pocus” and “Halloweentown.”

Make some popcorn, grab a blanket and have yourself a chill movie night this fall.

Visit a farmer’s market

Farmer’s markets are a great way to soak in those fall vibes while also supporting local businesses. Some local markets to visit are the State College Farmer’s Market and the Boalsburg Farmer’s Market.

Both of these markets sell products that are perfect for fall, like pies, coffee, cider and more.

They’re also amazing ways to get outside and enjoy that crisp, autumn weather.

Participate in a volunteer project

Fall is the season of gratitude and giving, so it's a perfect time to get involved with something for the community. Take some time to think about the causes that mean the most to you and then research different ways you can make an impact.

Some local options are volunteering at the State College Food Bank, which provides food security to the people of Centre County, as well as Centre County PAWS, which is an animal shelter in State College.

title: Want to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month through books, music, movies? Here are some recommendations
author: Alli Satterfield | The Daily Collegian
description:
Hispanic Heritage Month is now in full swing. As we take time to celebrate the culture, it’s also important to learn about the history and importance of it through the media that represents and brings that culture to life.

If you’re looking for a piece of media to embrace Hispanic culture, here are some recommendations.

Movies, TV

Roma

This 2018 film, directed by Alfonso Cuarón, follows a year in the life of a family in Mexico City in the early 1970s. It focuses on the family’s maid, Cleo, as the film’s protagonist, and it mirrors events in the life of the director’s childhood maid. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Cuarón said he had an “emotional need” to make this film and explore the lives of the two most influential women in his childhood: his mother and his family’s maid.

The film also brings conversations about class divisions in Mexico to the big screen. The timeline of the film runs along some political turmoil there, which heightens the emotional conflicts displayed in the film.

The Spirit of the Beehive

This film is from 1973, so a bit older, but it’s still as poignant today as it was then. “The Spirit of the Beehive” follows a girl in the 1940s during Mexico’s civil war. The young woman sees a traveling show of “Frankenstein” and becomes obsessed with it.

“The Spirit of the Beehive” investigates its protagonist’s life and psyche while simultaneously being visually stunning.

Vida

“Vida” is a television show that explores multiple facets of culture and identity. It follows two sisters who return to their hometown following their mother’s death, where they learn more about each other, their mother and their family.

The show recognizes and celebrates their Hispanic heritage while also exploring queer identities through raw, developed and intricate characters.

The show’s creator, Tanya Saracho, said she created the show to “re-inject” Latinx stories into popular culture. She works alongside other Hispanic writers to create a show that she thinks is authentic, according to an interview with abcNews, and she said that having the creators and editors be “all women, all brown women, all Latinas,” makes the representation more valuable.

Elena of Avalor

Switching gears, I cannot recommend Disney’s “Elena of Avalor” highly enough. I loved this show when I was younger – and probably still too old to be watching a children’s show – and I love it now.

Elena is a fearless princess, and she defends her kingdom, Avalor, with a magical scepter. She is strong and ambitious, and I view her as an amazing role model for any girl and an especially important icon of representation for Latinx kiddos — and adults!

Music

ELLA by Ysrael Barajes and Samantha Barrón

This upbeat ballad expresses the love and longing of losing someone that you’re close to. It’s a cross-cultural and pretty universal experience for anyone who forms relationships, which is – really – all of us. The song explores love and loss, but also acceptance, as Barajes contemplates moving on from his heartbreak.

While these themes aren’t uniquely Hispanic, media like this does a great job of showcasing the things that unite us within our humanity instead of what divides us.

“Bailando” by Enrique Iglesias featuring Gente de Zona and Descemer Bueno

Ranked No. 6 on Billboard’s The 50 Best Latin Songs of All Time list, “Bailando” holds the record for the longest-running number one on the Hot Latin Songs chart.

The song was co-written by Iglesias and Bueno, though the first released version of this song actually didn’t feature Iglesias.

“Bailando” made history, crossing from Latin to pop radio stations and charts, and it even inspired its own “Spanglish” remix featuring Sean Paul.

Books

“Las Madres” by Esmerelda Santiago

This novel follows a group of female friends that have chosen to raise their daughters together and form their own type of family. It explores race, sex and family as it simultaneously navigates the identities of all of the women, Puerto Rican-Americans, living in the Bronx.

Santiago wrote this book as a nod to her Puerto Rican culture and especially to her father. She aims to bring Puerto Rican stories to life while legitimizing the longing that she said many Puerto Ricans experience for their home.

“Magical Realism for Nonbelievers: A Memoir of Finding Family” by Anika Fajardo

In her memoir, Fajardo explores the bounds of family through exploring her own journey as a young woman searching for her estranged, Columbian father.

Fajardo, who was born in Columbia but raised in Minnesota, boarded a plane to Columbia in 1995 to find her father. Her memoir follows that story while also going back in time to explore her parents’ relationship and their different places in the world.

title: No. 4 Penn State women's hockey to open AHA play against Robert Morris
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State women's hockey hops into its first conference action of the season this Friday when it welcomes Robert Morris to Pegula Ice Arena. The Nittany Lions are coming off a series against No. 2 Ohio State, where the team went 0-2 but showed some definite positives.

The blue and white kept both games with the Buckeyes close, losing the first game of the series 2-1 in overtime and losing the second 2-1 in regulation. The team looks to take the positives from a challenging opening series and improve on them heading into conference play.

Last season, the Colonials ended the season with an 8-14-2 conference record, finishing with an overall record of 13-21-2. In four games against Penn State last season, Robert Morris lost every matchup, being outscored 16-2. The Colonials have not beaten the Nittany Lions since 2020.

To start the season, the team is 1-1 after an 8-3 win and a 2-1 overtime loss in its first series against Post University.

Junior Forward Jessica Mackinnon is RMU’s biggest attacking threat; Mackinnon has tallied 16 goals and 28 assists for 44 career points. The junior was named to the AHA Preseason All-Conference Team for 2026-27 and was also tabbed to the All-AHA First Team in 2025-26.

Another threat on the RMU attack is junior forward Greta Brezenski. The transfer from Clarkson University has already made an immediate impact in her first two games, tallying four goals and two assists for six points.

Entering the season, Brezenski had only five career points to her name in 52 collegiate appearances; the Nittany Lions blueline have to keep an eye on her.

In net, the Colonials have senior goaltender Maggie Hatch. Hatch ranked second in the AHA in shutouts with six, tying the single-season program record, finishing the season with 11 wins, 755 saves, a 2.47 GAA and a .916 save percentage. Penn State will have to score on a veteran presence in net.

In its first series, the Penn State attack struggled against the Buckeyes, not getting much going outside of Grace Outwater's two goals. It’ll be important to get that sorted against a weaker RMU team.

The Nittany Lions should be able to possess the puck for most of the game, but they have to be able to get shots off and find the back of the net.

The blueline played the best it could against an explosive Ohio State offense last week. One thing that has to transfer over is the physicality. If the blue and white can bring the physicality over from the last series, it’ll be difficult for RMU to get anything going.

The goaltender situation will be further evaluated this series after a week where both Maddy Campbell and Morgan Stickney had stellar performances against the No. 2 team in the nation, having combined for 75 saves and four goals allowed. It will be interesting to see if anybody can emerge as the starter or if this will be a season-long battle.

title: ‘He’s a hard worker’ | Angel Guzman paves own path with Penn State Adaptive Athletics, makes sled hockey history
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Angel Guzman embarked on the cross-country journey from his hometown of Moreno Valley to University Park for what was the culmination of years of training and work. After 2,500 miles, 40 hours of travel, he took a jump to see if it would pay off.

Born with Spina Bifida Myelomeningocele, clubfoot, hydrocephalus and strabismus, Guzman was diagnosed with long-term restrictions to his movement. However, with his parents’ support and his own dedication racing through him, Guzman found a way to directly overcome his obstacles in the form of adaptive athletics at 5 years old, only three years after he got his first wheelchair.

With his parents driving a car packed full, Guzman was on the road to become the first in his family to attend college.

“It's not easy being the first one to go to college, especially going to such a great university like Penn State,” Guzman said. “It's still tough, but something that I wish that was told to me is that there is a lot of help; there's a lot of help around you — you just gotta look for it.”

With multiple hour-long trips to nearby facilities and limited ice time growing up, Guzman faced the odds in his development in sled hockey from the start. That didn’t stop the talent from prevailing, as Guzman quickly caught the eye of Penn State at the age of 14, when State College Coyotes coach DJ Wilson noticed his skills during a tournament.

“Having him come here, you ask a kid to move across the country quite literally for something like this, and you don't expect them to just jump on board and say yes, especially after one random encounter,” Wilson said. “We even got a bonus out of it. His dad is now living in the area, and I mean, the two of them (are a) phenomenal family.”

Wilson also detailed a story of Guzman hitting him against the boards during that tournament when going against him, which gave him stitches. While he and his wife were tending to the injury, Wilson remembers Guzman coming up to him, and the pair first broached the topic of coming to Penn State.

Guzman kept working despite the barriers of being a person of color with a disability in a predominantly white sport, joining the LA Kings sled hockey program and scoring the team’s first championship goal in 2024.

“For someone who has a Hispanic background, for us, it's a lot more difficult because we don't get looked at. I feel like we don't get looked at the same as others, but I feel like we should get that same recognition because we put in the work as much as anyone else, and there's no difference because we're all just a person,” Guzman said. “We put in a lot of dedication, and we're super stubborn.”

Guzman got his first chance with the Coyotes and Wilson when he came to Penn State, which unlocked unforeseen paths and opportunities. In January 2025, Penn State men’s hockey hosted the third annual Sled Hockey Classic, where Guzman’s Coyotes took on members from the Nittany Lions in a game for charity.

“I could just tell from the first time that I met him that we were going to get along, and it's been great ever since,” Max Malec, Angel’s teammate, said. “He's an incredibly hard worker, clearly set on his goals.”

Despite also being a part of an event that helped raise $18,000 for sled hockey athletes, Guzman had a performance in the game that would change his life. After scoring two goals, including the game-winner, he earned an academic scholarship to join the adaptive athletics program with the Nittany Lions.

“We have a kid that's from halfway across the country who adapted very well, so he's doing very well for himself athletically and academically,” Malec said. “He's thriving in a place like this — there's no reason why somebody from somewhere else can't come here and do the same.”

While sled hockey is his bread and butter, Guzman isn’t limited to just his on-ice work. The multi-sport athlete currently also participates in the 100m, 200m and 400m on the track and was a member of the Adaptive Athletics basketball team.

“For someone who's in a spectator view, they would be surprised how much we can actually do,” Guzman said. “Whether it's track, hockey or basketball, they would be surprised how competitive it is, and I feel like it's also coming up on the rise.”

On top of majoring in business management and all of his sporting ventures, Guzman’s been able to be a part of historical moments on the ice.

Last season, he was a part of a trio of Penn State Adaptive Athletics sled hockey players to help the State College Coyotes take home the program's first-ever Northeast Sled Hockey League Championship.

“It’s really a lot of ‘iron sharpens iron.’ We go into every practice, every lift, every training session, just trying to make each other better. We've both really seen the results of that, and he's made some noticeable strides since he's gotten here,” Malec said.

This effort helped restore prominence to Adaptive Athletics after a transitional period during the highs and lows of the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw the program's first-ever coach, Teri Jordan, step back. The operations side shifted to Student Affairs from Intercollegiate Athletics.

“We've already got a title under our belt, which says a lot about the group that we have — such a strong group, an incredible group, and we're all highly dedicated toward our craft, and it shows in how we play,” Guzman said.

The Coyotes work in partnership with Adaptive Athletics and were founded in 2016 by Wilson. Since then, the size of the team has grown exponentially to now have teams for all ages, as it now has over double the number of athletes.

Last season, State College went 8-3 in the regular season, as it resumed play for this season’s NESHL Champions in September and started so far this season at a perfect record over four games.

Through last year’s playoff, Guzman led the Coyotes in goals, which he’s also done for the last two seasons. Guzman said he’s planning on going international, mainly for hockey. For him, his decorated past and spectacular present is just the start.

“I've realized that as each tournament, as each practice has gone, I've realized that we're making history, and it's great. It's a great feeling to be a part of it, to be able to represent Penn State in that way, because Penn State's always been making history in every sport and so to be adding more sports to it is a great feeling,” Guzman said.

title: The Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act. Here’s what you should know
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
The Protect College Sports Act passed in the U.S. Senate with a 77-22 vote on Monday night after months of deliberation, advocacy and changes, marking a big win for the NCAA after years of lobbying for federal involvement regulating college athletics.

The bipartisan bill written by Ted Cruz (R) and Maria Cantwell (D) now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives. If it’s passed there, it will become law. But that vote could take weeks with potential additional challenges. Though Monday’s Senate vote was a big step forward, the end still remains out of sight.

Here’s what else you should know regarding the bill and its next steps.

Notable aspects

There are plenty of parts to this bill that would have huge implications on how college athletics operate.

Arguably the most notable is the transfer portal rule, which allows players one free transfer. If someone wanted to transfer a second time, they’d have to sit out a year. This is the same rule the NCAA had in effect from 2021 to 2024 before the portal became what it is now.

Graduate players remain free to transfer with no limits.

The Power Four conferences — Big Ten, SEC, ACC and Big 12 — are now limited to 20 members. The Big Ten currently has 18, while the SEC has 16.

Additionally, any Power Four institution that chooses to move to another Power Four conference must spend three years as an independent or a member of a conference earning less than $700 million annually in revenue. This rule only applies for six years, lining up with television contract expirations for different conferences and the College Football Playoff.

There is no timeline limit if a Group of Six or independent wanted to join a new conference.

Along the lines of limiting conference realignment is the bill’s prohibition of any kind of “super league,” which says no outside entity can consolidate schools to create a new association or conference.

As for paying athletes, the revenue-sharing cap is set at $21.6 million, but schools will also get a $22.5 million retention fund, used purely to help keep athletes stay where they are. A university can only use that fund, however, if it hits academic benchmarks and a graduation rate.

Those academic benchmarks are unknown, as the bill leaves it up to the NCAA and its conferences to determine them.

There is also a $5 million pool for women’s sports and nonrevenue sports.

This bill codifies the new five-for-five rule into law and prevents any professional athlete from returning to college athletics.

Coaches who opt to leave their current school for another one before the season’s end are prohibited from participating in head-coaching duties at their new destination before the end of that team’s season or their former program’s season, whichever occurs first.

What’s next?

This bill could take a while to reach a vote in the House, considering Speaker Mike Johnson sent members of the House home last week to campaign for midterm elections, so no votes on any legislation will happen until after Nov. 3 as of now.

Things can always change, but it seems unlikely for the House to reopen. If it did, the Protect College Sports Act is likely not the priority anyway, especially with midterm elections approaching.

Following those elections is when the bill could see movement in the House considering the overwhelming support it received in the Senate.

If Democrats take control of the House in the midterm elections, it could take even longer for a vote on the Protect College Sports Act due to the lame-duck session, when the current majority has to exit.

During said lame-duck session, typically there isn’t much achieved. Lawmakers who were voted out might not even return to Capitol Hill, making it hard for anything to be voted on, let alone the Protect College Sports Act.

title: Penn State men's soccer to battle Ohio State as both seek return to win column
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
After suffering a tough loss against UCLA on Monday night in its Scarf Night match, Penn State looks to reverse course and achieve its first Big Ten win of the season.

The Nittany Lions take on Ohio State this Friday at 7 p.m. in their annual White Out match.

The last time the two programs met on the pitch was Oct. 31. of last season, when the Buckeyes hosted the blue and white, taking the match 1-0. In all-time season history, Penn State just leads with a record of 23-17-6.

While the Buckeyes and Nittany Lions have both suffered against other Big Ten teams this season, the blue and white have a slight edge coming into the match, winning nine of 11 games played at Jeffrey Field against Ohio State since 1999.

What to watch for Ohio State

Like Penn State, the Buckeyes travel to Jeffrey Field with little to no fire under their boots. They haven’t notched a win since Sept. 8, when they defeated Kentucky 4-1.

The consistent, mutual struggle in conference play deems Friday as anyone’s game.

While Ohio State has struggled as a team recently, it has a few players still worthy to keep an eye on heading into the matchup. Notable players include Isaiah Chisolm, Aaron Hurge and Nyle Waugh.

Chisolm, a Yorktown, Virginia, native, has tallied 14 points via seven goals over the first four matches of the season. The senior leads the Buckeyes’ attacking force but hasn’t played since Ohio State’s matchup against Northern Kentucky on Sept. 3, when he netted three of five goals.

The Buckeyes have been struggling without their leading offensive playmaker, winning only one of their five games since Chisolm has been out of the lineup due to an unknown injury. It is unclear if he will be back for the matchup against Penn State.

Hurge, another big offensive outlet for Ohio State, has played and started in all nine games, tallying eight points via three goals and two assists in 693 minutes played, the third most playing time on the Buckeyes’ roster.

Waugh is third in points for Ohio State at seven via three goals and one assist. The sophomore from Miami has received playing time in all nine matches and started in four.

On the defensive end for the Buckeyes, senior goalkeeper Patrick McLaughlin has started and played in every game for the scarlet and gray, contributing the second most time on the field for any Ohio State player at 771 minutes and sits at a save percentage of .720.

What to watch for Penn State

The Nittany Lions come into Friday at 2-6-0, battling to get back into the win column, with their last win being a 1-0 victory over Yale 1-0 on Sept. 1.

The blue and white have struggled on the defensive end, with goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese sitting at a save percentage of .571, way below any of Penn State’s opponents, who have an average of .761.

Amadou Kone, Etienne Reck and Joe Sheridan are the Nittany Lions’ leaders on the stat sheet. Kone is number one with eight points via three goals and two assists, followed by Reck with four points via two goals and then Sheridan with three points via one goal and one assist.

Penn State has yet to find its footing under new coach Rob Dow, but looks to start a new chapter heading into Friday’s matchup.

MORE SOCCER COVERAGE

title: Penn State field hockey treks to Rutgers, hosts Senior Day against No. 19 Lafayette
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s time this week is split across a pair of games with contrasting outlooks as the Nittany Lions’ season begins to ramp up.

After getting back in the win column against Bucknell to end a stretch of three consecutive losses, the blue and white continue on the road with a trip to Rutgers on Friday to resume Big Ten Play.

That resumption of conference play is rather brief before Penn State’s major test of the week in its return to Happy Valley, hosting No. 19 Lafayette for Senior Day.

Here’s how the two games shape up.

Rutgers

Just as coach Hannah Prince’s unit heads to Piscataway with a .500 record, Rutgers is defending home turf with the same deadlocked record. Both squads remain similar in almost every statistical category, with records to close to differentiate them on paper ahead of their Friday clash.

Both teams also have top-of-the-conference goal scorers poised to deliver big nights ahead of this 35th all-time meeting between Big Ten foes (Penn State leads 20-11-3 and is 10-6-1 at Rutgers). Scarlet Knights’ leading goal scorer, forward Olivia Fraticelli, continues her form this season after leading Rutgers in goals last year, and she looks poised to post an even better year. The senior has eight goals in 10 games played after totaling 11 last season, and has scored with incredible efficiency, as she isn’t even in the top 20 in shots so far this year in the Big Ten.

Transfer forward Ella Gaitan leads the Nittany Lions’ goal-scoring this season with seven in the blue and white’s eight games so far, and has kept defenses busy all year with a top-three conference figure of 4.50 shots per game.

Despite both squads appearing rather mediocre on the surface within the conference, sitting in the middle of the pack in the opening weeks of Big Ten play, the fireworks on the pitch could appear.

Both squads have also been rather leaky on defense, as Penn State’s Aby Deverka and Rutgers’ Emily Nicholls, the primary netminders for both squads, sit in the top three of the Big Ten in shots faced, meaning both squads' playmakers may have a chance to notch some highlights this weekend.

Lafayette

Closing out the week with Senior Night, the Nittany Lions have a tall task ahead as they welcome the Leopards on a night already heightened by the pregame ceremonies.

Lafayette has been incredibly potent this season, forcing its way into the national rankings and into the spotlight through a body of work that appears daunting for Penn State. The maroon and white are 8-1 on the season, with the lone loss coming to a buzzsaw Northwestern squad that has torched everyone its faced, with the exception of Duke and Lafayette, which were both decided by only one score.

Over their last five matches, the Leopards have outscored opponents 12-1, as it’s been a team effort through such success. Goal-scoring has been spread out all season for Lafayette; Lena Thedrian leads with six, followed by Stella Malinowski’s four, yet only two other players have hit the back of the net multiple times this season, and five have scored only once.

The catalyst to that low scoring undoubtedly stems from in front of the net, where junior Addison Kahn has had a season of excellence so far this year.

The Fredericksburg, Virginia, native has amassed 28 saves and a .800 save percentage with a .778 goals-against average – a top-five figure in the entire nation. Yet with Gaitain’s potent offense, the Leopards risk the Nittany Lions spoiling that stellar season.

Penn State’s a team with just as much star power and the ability to counter the wall in goal, as midfielder Sienna Dunn currently averages the most assists per game, signaling the perfect candidate to slot passes to Gaitan to cause an upset potentially.

title: Penn State vs. Northwestern preview | Weather at grand opening of Ryan Field and more
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State and Northwestern will open up the Wildcats’ new Ryan Field in primetime on Friday night, with kickoff scheduled for 8 p.m. Friday.

It’s a series dominated by Penn State, which holds a 16-6 lead, but last year’s matchup featured a Northwestern win that culminated in the firing of James Franklin.

Here’s more information on the weather, betting odds and what to look for from both teams during the Week 5 matchup.

Forecast

Penn State and Northwestern likely won’t have to deal with any crazy weather as the fall temperatures continue to lower.

With sunset scheduled for 6:31 p.m., the temperature will take a significant dip. Around game time, the high is 57 degrees with a low of 54, according to AccuWeather.

There’s a 25% probability of precipitation, but no expected rainfall. There will be wind gusts of 16 mph during the night.

Betting, how to watch

After Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin and Northwestern keeping things close with Indiana in Week 4, the sportsbooks are expecting a tight game in Evanston.

The Nittany Lions are currently 2.5-point favorites over the Wildcats, with the over/under set at 45.5 points, according to FanDuel. This means a Penn State 24-21 victory over Northwestern could be in store based on the betting odds.

The game will air on Fox at 8 p.m., with the lowest ticket to get into the game sitting at $143.75, likely due it being the debut game in the new stadium.

About Northwestern

Northwestern is playing well to begin the season, and its coach David Braun received an extension just two weeks ago. Braun received a three-year extension on his contract which initially lasted through 2028.

The Wildcats are 2-1, with dominating wins over South Dakota State and Colorado. Their lone loss comes from Indiana, which escaped with a 29-23 victory against Northwestern.

Northwestern features former Michigan State quarterback Aidan Chiles as its starter, who didn’t play in Penn State’s victory over the Spartans last season.

He’s another quarterback who’s dangerous on the ground, totaling four rushing touchdowns this year. He only has 20 yards rushing, but has been sacked seven times.

Chiles shares the ball between two main receiving threats. Wide receiver Griffin Wilde and tight end Luke Dehnicke have 245 and 208 yards, respectively. Tight end Alex Honig is third on the team in receiving yards with 79.

On the defensive side of the ball, the Wildcats have struggled against the run game. They currently rank 128th in the country in rushing yards per game allowed, giving up an average of 199.33 yards per game. Penn State has averaged 183.5 yards per game on the ground.

If Penn State wants to get its offense into rhythm, its best chance is against Northwestern, which sits 80th in passing defense, but has allowed on average 18 points per game, which is good for 36th in the country.

About Penn State

The Nittany Lions struggled on offense against Wisconsin, totaling 233 yards on offense, and scored 13 points, with the other touchdown coming from cornerback Josiah Zayas’ pick six.

Despite the struggles, Penn State sits in the top 60 in the country in both passing and rushing offense. Rocco Becht showcased his legs more in the loss to Wisconsin, rushing for a season-high 10 carries for 23 yards and a touchdown.

If the offensive rhythm still isn’t there, Becht’s utilization of his legs could be a factor in keeping drives going.

On defense, the pass rush hasn’t been consistent. The Nittany Lions have six sacks on the season, which is 93rd in the country. Northwestern has allowed seven sacks on the year, including four times against Indiana.

If D’Anton Lynn can dial up the pressure against Chiles, the offensive line has proven to struggle to keep Chiles upright. Defensive ends Yvan Kemajou and Ike Ezeogu have found the most success of the unit in rushing the passer, albeit a low efficiency rating on the rush.

If Penn State wants success on defense, it’ll likely need to get to Chiles quick, and not let him pick apart the defense with his arm or legs.

The Nittany Lions’ first true road test will also be the opening of a new stadium, which could cause additional trouble.

title: Column | How ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ teaches us to change history
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
Memory is a tricky thing.

Surrealist painter Salvador Dalí based his most famous work, “The Persistence of Memory,” off the malleable nature of memory, likening it to a piece of soft cheese. Philosophers like John Locke theorized that your identity extends only to the boundary of your own conscious memory.

Thousands of years of exploration through our brains’ synapses and has begged the question: What is memory worth, and is it even real?

In Gabriel García Márquez’s epic, “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” the endless ferris wheel of memory spins around for a century as the Buendía family navigates the pain that remembering entails and whether it’s one worth suffering for.

The story, published in 1967, begins with a memory out of place, highlighting the violence of the world to come like a prophecy the reader cannot avoid: “Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.”

Like the Book of Genesis in the Bible, García Márquez transports the reader back to an Edenic time where the the first characters, José Arcadio Buendía and his wife Úrsula, acting as Adam and Eve, settle in a new Colombian village called Macondo without modern technology.

However, by the time they arrive, they had already sinned: they’re first cousins and know it.

Úrsula fears any children they have will be monstrous, having the “tail of a pig” or other animalistic features, and José Arcadio Buendía finally convinces her it will be fine. Their two children, José Arcadio and Aureliano, are healthy. Their names start a century-long lineage of Aurelianos and José Arcadios within the Buendía family so vast that some copies of the book have a family tree in the prologue.

The naming conventions behind carrying a family name are a type of remembrance, too. Those with a “junior” tacked onto their birth certificate, or the name of a grandparent becoming a grandchild’s middle name, is a way of keeping the memory of the deceased with us.

García Márquez experiments with naming conventions as a way of conflating the past, present and future. With no new names, there can be no new experiences to differentiate the flaws of the past with current lessons, and there can be no learning from your mistakes.

In Latin American history around the time García Márquez was writing the novel, the 20th century brought upon massive changes to the economic and governmental structures on the continent. After economic strife from the Great Depression and the outbreak of World War I, Latin America had a major economic boom that garnered attention from international companies to begin investing in local production.

This interest devolved into imperialism that derailed labor efforts, causing unrest among workers and even violent protests in Márquez’s native Colombia, directly inspiring the infiltration of the fictionalized Banana Company in Macondo with similar protests against unfair labor laws that led to a massacre that no one remembered occurring.

When we try to think back to our own lives, how many times do we repeat our mistakes? Like itches we can’t quite scratch, our memories can become inaccessible at times because of our own obsession with the moment ahead, with the fire to put out in front of us, and memory becomes another knee-jerk reaction to continue spasming.

Change is incredibly difficult, especially for the Buendías, but our pasts do not dictate the future or even the present if we don’t let them. While many adults believe who they are right now is a permanent fixture, a study done by Communication Psychology highlights that personality traits change over time.

Throughout the story, García Márquez writes the many Aurelianos and José Arcadios as having the same traits, their names like marks of Cain that slate them to the destinies of the previous Aureliano or José Arcadio.

An Aureliano, withdrawn and reflective, so starkly contrasts a José Arcadio, boisterous and impulsive, that Ursula is convinced a set of twins in the family, named accordingly, were switched at birth because of their personalities matching the other’s archetype.

“One Hundred Years of Solitude” details a journey of solitude over a century’s worth of Buendía generations because of an inability to remember. A priest says to the last Aureliano, “It's enough for me to be sure that you and I exist at this moment.”

However, the town was doomed from this ideology, since the actions of the past and present are so indistinguishable that the reader themself struggles to follow the story. Colonel Aureliano Buendía (the original Aureliano) loses all of his personal memories, only able to recall times of war. The town, after a years-long revolution, loses memory of his original cause in order to resign his name to being a political figurehead, creating a symbolic leader for new rebel groups to continue fighting wars that are impossible to win.

Simultaneously, those cursed with too much overbearing nostalgia suffer in the book, locked to be surrounded by memories that suffocate all possibilities for change and escape. By the end of the book, with no one left in Macondo to remember its genesis, an old bookseller notes: “Wherever they might be they always remember that the past was a lie, that memory has no return, that every spring gone by could never be recovered, and that the wildest and most tenacious love was an ephemeral truth in the end.”

“One Hundred Years of Solitude” makes a world from the cyclical nature of memory and how forgetting the past, or drowning in it, dooms us to repeat it. When we branch away from the pull of “destiny” as a sentence and begin to run towards it as a mere suggestion, then we break the cycle of solitude.

title: The Hispanic heritage of Penn State’s 1994 national championship through Collegian reporting
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
In 1994, Penn State made history. Tom Peterson’s final season in charge of the Nittany Lions concluded in Fort Wayne, Indiana, with Penn State facing UCLA with a national title on the line.

The blue and white bested the Bruins in five sets to claim its first-ever national title and become the first non-Californian college to claim an NCAA men’s volleyball championship.

Three Hispanic players — outside hitter Ramón Hernández, middle blocker Iván Contreras and setter Carlos Ortiz — played key roles in the Nittany Lions’ title run. Take a look back at their 1994 campaign through the Collegian archives.

January

Penn State had been eliminated in the NCAA Final Four in three consecutive seasons preceding the run to the championship match.

Hernández, a San Juan, Puerto Rico, native, entered the new year with a wealth of newly found responsibility as a senior leader for the spikers after being named an AVCA Third Team All-American in 1992 and 1993.

“Since I am a senior, I have a big responsibility for the team," Hernández told the Daily Collegian. “I see myself as the floor leader of the team… keeping the team together and making sure that everybody is doing the right things."

He developed his chemistry with Ortiz, in their time together on the Puerto Rico Junior National Team, and the relationship carried over to Penn State.

“We are very good friends,” Ortiz said. “Off the court, we hang out, but we are not that close of friends. All of that changes when we get on the court.”

Penn State opened the season by taking down a different California powerhouse. In the first match of three consecutive clashes with the Cardinal, the No. 6 Nittany Lions swept No. 7 Stanford in Rec Hall on Jan. 20. In a 1994 debut, Hernández led the way with 17 kills.

“This win was a great start for us this year,” Ortiz said after the game. ”We played together as a team and everything just fell into place.”

In the next two days, Penn State played Stanford two more times, splitting the pair before sweeping three straight matches to end the month.

February

Penn State moved up to No. 4 in the rankings at the start of February. That position drew some controversy, as the Nittany Lions’ 5-1 record was better than two higher-ranked squads.

“Until we beat one of the top teams, we will not move up,” Peterson said. “It is a total dogfight out there — they get to play against the best teams every weekend, whereas we don't have that opportunity.”

The blue and white went north of the border for Canadian clashes. Contreras found more time on the court, but the 6-foot-4 “die-hard dancer” spent some time on a different floor during the road trip.

"We went to Manitoba and we started dancing, and the girls that we were dancing with told Carlos [Ortiz] and me that they were impressed with our dancing," Contreras said. "None of the guys in Manitoba knew how to dance."

The passion didn’t hurt his skill, though. Through Feb. 24, the Tampico, Mexico, native was among the Nittany Lions’ leaders with 27 blocks and 91 kills on a .408 clip. It was enough of a performance to bounce Hernández from his previous position as a middle blocker to a new role as outside hitter.

“You can't say that I am displacing him,” Contreras said. “Because he is such a good player, [the coaches] put him on the outside to give him more balls to hit.”

By the end of the month, Penn State had surged to an 11-2 record after dropping just a single match to the University of Manitoba, landing the Nittany Lions at No. 3 in the rankings.

March

The Nittany Lions continued their crucial winning streak into March.

With the dominance that western schools held in the polls, dropping matches to lower-level schools in the east would have been fatal for Penn State in the race towards the postseason.

“We cannot lose any matches against any eastern teams, so all of these wins are very important,” Peterson said. “We want to win our division, we want to win the east, we can't lose for the polls. There's a lot of reasons why this is important.”

Hernández and Ortiz led the way with 19 and 11 kills, respectively, in the blue and white’s victory over Ohio State on March 25, the squad’s ninth consecutive win.

By March 31, Contreras’ performance had reached an even higher level as Penn State rose to No. 2 in the polls. Through 20 matches, he ranked No. 9 nationally with a .453 hitting percentage and No. 20 with 1.4 blocks per set.

"I just try to play as good as I can,” Contreras said. “One of my goals this season is to make the All-Freshman team, if I can.”

April

Adversity came in April.

The Nittany Lions lost their first two matches of the month, a five-set marathon to Ball State and a sweep by Indiana-Purdue at Fort Wayne. It was the first, and only, time all season that Penn State would lose back-to-back matches.

“I think that it is better to have to deal with the losses now than at the Final Four,” Contreras said. "I think we can all bounce back. I am looking forward to playing Brigham Young on Friday.”

Hernández echoed Contreras’ sentiment, looking at his team to be more prepared as the postseason drew closer and closer.

“I know that we were not ready to play at all this weekend," Hernández said. “If you are an athlete, you have to do some long-term preparation for the matches — sometimes hours, sometimes days. I think the team has to really practice this.”

In the remaining five matches, Penn State dropped just three sets. In the final regular-season match, Hernández and Ortiz were fueled by a contingent of fellow Puerto Ricans in the crowd as the Nittany Lions set up their berth in the EIVA Tournament.

Penn State delivered three straight sweeps, besting NJIT, Princeton and Rutgers-Newark, to claim the conference title and earn an automatic bid into the NCAA tournament, which was composed of just four teams at the time.

“It's as good a chance as we've had in a long time,” Peterson said. “If we play well, we can compete with anybody.”

May

To open the NCAA postseason, Penn State was faced with the season’s third match against Ball State after splitting the regular-season series. The Nittany Lions dropped the first set, but powered to win three straight and earn a bid in the national title match against UCLA.

They’d be faced with their toughest test of the season with the most on the line. UCLA entered the championship on a 27-match winning streak after dropping its season opener to BYU. It didn’t look great historically for Penn State, either, as they held a 3-9-1 all-time record against the Bruins before the clash.

The blue and white dropped two of the first three sets, and trailed 11-4 in the fourth until Peterson called a timeout to regroup his squad.

Hernández pulled the Nittany Lions from the ashes.

“Ramon just put us on his back,” former Penn State coach Mark Pavlik said after Hernández was inducted into the EIVA Hall of Fame in 2014. “Next thing you know, the tidal wave started and it was all Ramon that really pulled it together for us.”

Penn State rallied back to claim the set and level the match, and took an 8-4 lead in the decisive fifth frame. UCLA came back to even things at 12-12, but the Nittany Lions ripped off three straight points to seal the victory.

Hernández finished with a career-high 38 kills in the title match, the final of his time with Penn State. He’d go on to be named the tournament’s most outstanding player.

Building a legacy

Once his playing days were over, Hernández went into coaching. The three-time All-American led the Puerto Rican men’s national team in 2017 and spent time with Major League Volleyball’s Las Vegas Thrill in 2025.

Contreras would go on to be named the AVCA Player of the Year in 1997. He then started a professional career, playing for teams in Germany, Belgium, Turkey and Puerto Rico, and was enshrined in the EIVA Hall of Fame in 2013, a year prior to Hernández.

Ortiz finished sixth all-time with 4,609 assists for Penn State and was named an AVCA All-American in 1995.

title: 128.2 million eyes were on Bad Bunny’s halftime show. At Penn State, his impact lingers
author: Stella John | The Daily Collegian
description:
Six-time Grammy Award Winner Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio made history when he became the first ever Super Bowl solo headliner to perform almost entirely in Spanish during the 2026 Apple Music Super Bowl LX halftime show at Levi's Stadium on Feb. 8.

More famously recognized by his stage name, Bad Bunny, he made every second count during his performance. His show was modeled as a display of his Puerto Rican history, unity and belonging.

The halftime show had such an impact that A.K. Sandoval-Strausz, director of Latina and Latino studies, scrapped his lesson plan the day after to discuss it.

He said his students emphasized that a lot of discourse surrounding Latinx culture in the current political climate comes from a place of anger. But students were emotional to see a show rooted in love for their culture and the diversity within it, he added.

“I heard many of them saying, ‘I'm really glad that somebody got up and said what he did, because we often feel very alone in the United States, even if we're from here,’” Sandoval-Strausz said.

He said people have been fearful of ICE’s presence in their communities, and since Trump took office in 2025, being Latinx in the States means “being on the defensive.”

Many of his students told him they don’t speak Spanish in public anymore, he said, and others started carrying around documentation.

“A lot of them wanted to know, ‘Is this gonna change things? Are people gonna see this and realize how wrong some of these policies have been?’ Sometimes it takes one of the biggest recording artists in the world to say, ‘Aqui estamos, y no nos vamos.’ (We are here, and we are not leaving).”

Bad Bunny won all of his Grammys in the eight years since his debut album, “X 100PRE.” Exactly a week before he took to the field at Levi's Stadium, his most recent album, “DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOTos,” made history as the first fully Spanish-language album to win “Album of the Year” at the 2026 Grammys.

Sandoval-Strausz’s favorite song by Bad Bunny is “NEUVAYoL,” both because of his upbringing in the Bronx and for the song’s stylistic qualities. He said salsa being a central part of the performance was especially important, as it’s a traditional sound for Latinx New Yorkers and gives credence to generations of people and musicians.

Daniela Mendoza, who also grew up in New York, said her favorite song from the album was “LO QUE LE PASO HAWAii,” which tells the story of how damaging tourism has been for the land and locals of Hawaii.

In the song, Bad Bunny connects this to the creeping spread of tourism in Puerto Rico.

“I didn’t even know that,” Mendoza, a third-year studying criminology, said. “I’m not Puerto Rican, so this album brought me closer to the Puerto Rican friends I have here in college. It showed me that even within your own community, you’re always learning something new.”

It was announced that Bad Bunny would be the solo headliner for Super Bowl LX on Sept. 28, 2025. While there was a lot of excitement around the decision, there was also a lot of pushback, as the show was almost entirely in Spanish.

Sandoval-Strausz said the controversy was unsubstantiated. The idea of America being an immigrant and multicultural society, he said, has been around for a long time.

“There was a lot of ‘How dare he,’ That's un-American,’” Sandoval-Strausz said. “Puerto Ricans, since 1917, have been birthright-born American citizens… The great majority of people speak English, but under the law, there’s no official language of the United States.”

Mendoza said she heard discourse about whether or not Bad Bunny would mention anything about the federal administration’s increased, aggressive immigration enforcement. His statement was clear, she said, when he didn’t have any concerts in America during his album’s world tour.

“I was shocked. I didn’t think they were gonna let him perform,” Mendoza said. “There are still people who think he shouldn’t have.”

Caterina McGuigan, a student under Sandoval-Straus, said the backlash made her laugh.

“People were like ‘He shouldn’t be performing. Justin Bieber should be performing,’ and I was like, ‘Justin Bieber… is not a U.S. citizen and Bad Bunny is,’” McGuigan, a fourth-year studying broadcast journalism, said. “It just showed the arrogance of so many people, even people my age, because Bad Bunny was a U.S. citizen before we were, literally because he was born before we were.”

McGuigan’s mother is an immigrant from Argentina, and her father is the biggest “Bostonian,” so she saw the halftime show as a meshing of her two worlds. It was a special experience being able to watch her favorite team, the Patriots, and hear songs in her first language.

At one point in the show, dancers looked to be throwing a party on the rooftop of a casita, and as Bad Bunny walked through the scene, he stopped to wake up a boy who’d fallen asleep despite the commotion all around him. This was McGuigan’s favorite part of the show, because it reminded her of growing up in the Bronx with her sister and going to parties at their grandparents’ bodega.

“That is literally a canon event,” McGuigan said. “Any Latino kid looked at that and was like, ‘Yeah, that’s totally happened to me.’”

For the entirety of the performance, Bad Bunny spoke only three words in English: “God Bless America!” followed by a list of every country in North and South America, dancers alongside him raising the respective flags for each.

McGuigan said she interpreted the sequence as a reminder that all Latin-American countries are “a part of this side of the world,” and that “we’re not strangers, we’re neighbors.”

“I think it reminded us that we all speak different dialects of Spanish, but we all have so many things in common,” McGuigan said. “We forgot about that until this performance and y’know what, God bless all of us. God bless the fact that my mom could come here, that my grandparents could come here — we can come here.”

On the jumbotron behind Bad Bunny was a message that read, “The only thing stronger than hate is love.”

“We’re still here through our music, our shared language, our traditions,” Mendoza said. “Even a 13-minute performance, maybe people think, ‘What did he really do for you guys?’ I think he did so much.”
